blocks.text: Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:
Understand what programming is and why Python is the dominant language for AI/ML
Set up a complete Python development environment
Write and run your first Python program
Navigate the Python ecosystem for AI and Machine Learning
Understand how computers execute code at a conceptual level
Introduction
Welcome to your journey toward becoming an AI/ML Engineer. Before training models, building RAG pipelines, or deploying LLMs to production, every engineer must master the foundation: programming.

Python has become the universal language of AI. Whether you are at Google DeepMind, OpenAI, a Series A startup, or working on your first project, Python is what connects ideas to working systems. This chapter gets your environment ready and your mindset aligned with how professional engineers think and work.
What is Programming?
Programming is the process of giving a computer a precise set of instructions to solve a problem.

Computers are extraordinarily fast but completely literal. They do exactly what you tell them — nothing more, nothing less. A program is simply a sequence of instructions written in a language the computer can interpret and execute.
Think of it this way:
A recipe is a program for a cook
A GPS route is a program for a driver
A machine learning pipeline is a program for a computer to learn patterns from data
When you write Python code, you are authoring instructions that the Python interpreter translates into actions your computer performs.
Why Programming Matters for AI/ML
In AI/ML, programming is not just a supporting skill — it is the core skill. You will use it to:
Clean and transform raw data
Implement mathematical algorithms
Train and evaluate models
Build APIs that serve predictions
Orchestrate multi-agent AI systems
Deploy models to cloud infrastructure
Every concept in this handbook eventually becomes Python code.
How Computers Execute Code
Understanding this at a high level will make you a better debugger and a more intuitive engineer.
The Execution Stack

Your Python Code (.py file)
        ↓
Python Interpreter (CPython)
        ↓
Bytecode (.pyc)
        ↓
Python Virtual Machine (PVM)
        ↓
Operating System
        ↓
Hardware (CPU, RAM, GPU)
Key Concepts
Source Code is what you write — human-readable Python text.
Interpreter reads your source code line by line and executes it. Python is an interpreted language, which means there is no separate compilation step like in C++ or Java.
Bytecode is an intermediate representation that CPython (the standard Python implementation) compiles your source code into before execution.
RAM (Memory) is where your variables, data structures, and model weights live while your program runs.
CPU executes arithmetic, logic, and control flow operations.
GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) is massively parallel hardware used for training deep learning models. Libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow abstract GPU operations for you.
Interpreted vs Compiled

Python's speed disadvantage is largely solved in AI/ML because the heavy numerical operations (matrix multiplications, convolutions) run in optimized C/CUDA code through NumPy, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. You write Python; the expensive math runs in native code underneath.

Virtual environments isolate project dependencies. This is professional best practice.

# Create a new environment
conda create -n aiml_env python=3.11

# Activate it

Why virtual environments matter: Different projects need different library versions. Without isolation, projects break each other. Every professional project has its own environment.

Your First Python Program
Open VS Code, create a file called hello.py, and write:

# This is a comment. Python ignores lines starting with #
# Comments explain your code to humans (and your future self)
print("Hello, AI World!")
Run it from the terminal:
python hello.py
Output: Hello, AI World!
What Just Happened?
print() is a built-in Python function
Functions are reusable blocks of code that perform a specific action
"Hello, AI World!" is a string — text enclosed in quotes
Python read your file top to bottom and executed the print function
A Slightly More Interesting First Program

# A simple AI/ML themed introduction program

name = input("Enter your name: ")
goal = "AI/ML Engineer"

print(f"Welcome, {name}!")
print(f"Your goal: Become an {goal}")
print(f"This handbook will take you there step by step.")

# Simple calculation
weeks = 24
hours_per_week = 15
total_hours = weeks * hours_per_week

print(f"\nStudy plan: {weeks} weeks × {hours_per_week} hrs/week = {total_hours} total hours")
print("Let's build something great.")
Output:

Enter your name: Aryan
Welcome, Aryan!
Your goal: Become an AI/ML Engineer
This handbook will take you there step by step.

Study plan: 24 weeks × 15 hrs/week = 360 total hours
Let's build something great.
Line-by-Line Explanation
name = input("Enter your name: ")
input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type something. Whatever they type is stored in the variable name.
goal = "AI/ML Engineer"
We create a variable goal and assign it a string value.
print(f"Welcome, {name}!")
The f before the quote makes this an f-string (formatted string). Anything inside {} is evaluated as Python code and inserted into the string.
total_hours = weeks * hours_per_week
Python evaluates the right side first (24 × 15 = 360) and stores the result in total_hours.

Understanding the ecosystem before diving in gives you the map before the journey.
The Core Stack

Industry Best Practices
Even in Chapter 1, start building professional habits:
Use virtual environments always. Never install packages into your global Python installation.
Comment your code meaningfully. Not what the code does, but why you made the decision.
Use descriptive variable names. learning_rate = 0.001 is better than lr = 0.001 when starting out.
Commit code to Git frequently. Even personal learning projects. It builds the habit.
Keep a learning log. A simple markdown file noting what you learned each day compounds over months.
Common Mistakes
Installing packages globally instead of in a virtual environment. This causes dependency conflicts that waste hours.
Using Python 2. It is end-of-life. Always use Python 3.10 or higher (3.11 recommended in 2026).
Skipping the environment setup. Going straight to coding without a proper setup leads to messy, irreproducible projects.
Not reading error messages. Python error messages are precise and helpful. Read the full traceback from bottom to top.
Copying code without understanding it. You can use AI assistants and Stack Overflow, but always understand every line you write.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
Why is Python preferred for AI/ML over other languages?

Python offers a massive ecosystem of scientific libraries (NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow), clean readable syntax, rapid prototyping capability, and a huge community. The heavy numerical computations run in optimized C/CUDA code under the hood, so Python's interpreted speed is not a bottleneck for most ML workloads.
What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?

A compiler translates the entire source code to machine code before execution (C++, Java). An interpreter reads and executes source code line by line at runtime (Python, JavaScript). Python uses a hybrid: it first compiles to bytecode, then the Python Virtual Machine interprets that bytecode.
What is a virtual environment and why do we use it?

A virtual environment is an isolated Python installation with its own packages and dependencies. We use it so that different projects can use different library versions without conflicting with each other or the system Python installation.
Intermediate Level
What is CPython and how does it differ from other Python implementations?

CPython is the reference implementation of Python written in C. It is what you get when you download Python from python.org. Other implementations include PyPy (JIT-compiled, faster), Jython (Python on JVM), and MicroPython (for microcontrollers). CPython is the standard for AI/ML work.
What is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) in Python?

The GIL is a mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. This limits CPU-bound multi-threading in Python. For AI/ML, this is worked around by: using multiprocessing instead of threading, using NumPy/PyTorch which release the GIL during C-level operations, and using async I/O for I/O-bound tasks.

Mini Project: Personal AI Study Tracker
Build a simple command-line study tracker.

# study_tracker.py
# Personal AI/ML Study Tracker - Chapter 1 Mini Project

import datetime

def display_menu():
    print("\n" + "="*40)
    print("   AI/ML STUDY TRACKER")
    print("="*40)
    print("1. Log today's study session")
    print("2. View study history")
    print("3. View progress summary")
    print("4. Exit")
    print("="*40)

def log_session(sessions):
    """Log a new study session"""
    today = datetime.date.today().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    topic = input("What topic did you study? ")
    hours = float(input("How many hours? "))
    notes = input("Key takeaway from today: ")
    
    sessions.append({
        "date": today,
        "topic": topic,
        "hours": hours,
        "notes": notes
    })
    
    print(f"\n✓ Session logged! Keep going, {hours} hours closer to your goal.")
    return sessions

def view_history(sessions):
    """Display all logged sessions"""
    if not sessions:
        print("\nNo sessions logged yet. Start studying!")
        return
    
    print("\n--- STUDY HISTORY ---")
    for i, session in enumerate(sessions, 1):
        print(f"\nSession {i}:")
        print(f"  Date:  {session['date']}")
        print(f"  Topic: {session['topic']}")
        print(f"  Hours: {session['hours']}")
        print(f"  Notes: {session['notes']}")

def view_summary(sessions):
    """Display progress summary"""
    if not sessions:
        print("\nNo data yet!")
        return
    
    total_hours = sum(s['hours'] for s in sessions)
    total_sessions = len(sessions)
    topics_covered = set(s['topic'] for s in sessions)
    goal_hours = 360  # 24 weeks × 15 hours
    progress_pct = (total_hours / goal_hours) * 100
    
    print("\n--- PROGRESS SUMMARY ---")
    print(f"Total Sessions:  {total_sessions}")
    print(f"Total Hours:     {total_hours:.1f} / {goal_hours}")
    print(f"Progress:        {progress_pct:.1f}%")
    print(f"Topics Covered:  {len(topics_covered)}")
    print(f"Topics: {', '.join(topics_covered)}")
    
    # Progress bar
    filled = int(progress_pct / 5)
    bar = "█" * filled + "░" * (20 - filled)
    print(f"\n[{bar}] {progress_pct:.1f}%")

def main():
    """Main program loop"""
    print("Welcome to your AI/ML Study Tracker!")
    name = input("Enter your name: ")
    print(f"\nHello {name}! Let's track your path to AI/ML Engineer.")
    
    sessions = []
    
    while True:
        display_menu()
        choice = input("Choose an option (1-4): ").strip()
        
        if choice == "1":
            sessions = log_session(sessions)
        elif choice == "2":
            view_history(sessions)
        elif choice == "3":
            view_summary(sessions)
        elif choice == "4":
            print(f"\nGreat work today, {name}! Consistency beats intensity. See you tomorrow.")
            break
        else:
            print("Invalid choice. Please enter 1, 2, 3, or 4.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Introduction

Python fundamentals are the atoms of everything you will build. Every neural network, every RAG pipeline, every data cleaning script is ultimately built from variables, data types, and operators. Engineers who have a shaky foundation spend hours debugging trivial issues. Engineers who know this material cold move fast and think clearly.

This chapter goes deeper than most beginner resources. You will not just learn what these things are — you will understand how Python manages them in memory, why certain behaviors exist, and how professionals use them in real AI/ML code.
Variables and the Python Memory Model
What is a Variable?

A variable is a named reference to an object stored in memory. This is a crucial distinction from languages like C where a variable is a memory location. In Python, variables are labels that point to objects.
age = 25
What actually happens:
Python creates an integer object 25 somewhere in memory
Python creates a name age in the current namespace
age is bound to (points to) that object
The Python Memory Model

x = 42
y = x       # y points to the SAME object as x
z = 42      # z also points to the same object (Python caches small ints)

print(id(x)) # id() returns the memory address of the object
print(id(y)) # Same as x
print(id(z)) # Same as x (Python interns small integers -5 to 256)
 # Demonstrating that variables are references
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a           # b points to the SAME list object

b.append(4)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3, 4] — a is affected!
print(b)        # [1, 2, 3, 4]

# This surprises beginners but makes perfect sense once you understand
# that a and b are both labels pointing to the same list in memory
This behavior — called aliasing — is one of the most common sources of bugs in AI/ML code, especially when manipulating DataFrames and arrays.
Variable Naming Rules

# VALID variable names
learning_rate = 0.001       # snake_case (Python standard)
max_epochs = 100
model_v2 = None
_private_var = "internal"
CONSTANT_VALUE = 3.14       # ALL_CAPS for constants (convention)

# INVALID variable names
2nd_model = None    # Cannot start with a digit
my-model = None     # Hyphens not allowed
class = "NLP"       # 'class' is a reserved keyword

# Check reserved keywords
import keyword
print(keyword.kwlist)
Multiple Assignment

# Assign multiple variables in one line
x, y, z = 1, 2, 3

# Swap variables (Python does this elegantly)
x, y = y, x
print(x, y)   # 2, 1

# Assign same value to multiple variables
a = b = c = 0

# Augmented assignment
count = 0
count += 1      # count = count + 1
count -= 1
count *= 2
count /= 2
count **= 2     # exponentiation
count //= 3     # floor division
count %= 3      # modulo
Data Types

Python is dynamically typed — you do not declare the type of a variable. Python infers it from the value assigned. However, Python is also strongly typed — it will not silently convert between incompatible types.

x = 10
x = "hello"    # Perfectly valid — x now points to a string
x = [1, 2, 3]    # Now x points to a list
The Core Built-in Types

# Integer
age = 28
year = 2026
big_number = 1_000_000    # Underscores for readability (Python 3.6+)
negative = -42
binary = 0b1010           # Binary literal = 10
hexadecimal = 0xFF        # Hex literal = 255
octal = 0o17              # Octal literal = 15

print(type(age))          # <class 'int'>

# Float
pi = 3.14159
learning_rate = 0.001
scientific = 1.5e-4       # 0.00015 (scientific notation)
negative_exp = 2.5E10     # 25000000000.0

print(type(pi))           # <class 'float'>

# String
name = "GPT-4o"
framework = 'LangChain'
multiline = """
This is a
multi-line string
"""
raw_string = r"C:\Users\name\file"   # Raw string — backslashes are literal

print(type(name))         # <class 'str'>

# Boolean
is_trained = True
has_converged = False

print(type(is_trained))   # <class 'bool'>
print(isinstance(True, int))  # True — bool is a subclass of int!
print(True + True)            # 2 — this is valid Python

# NoneType
model = None              # Represents absence of value
result = None

print(type(model))        # <class 'NoneType'>
print(model is None)    # True — always use 'is' not '==' for None
Integers: Unlimited Precision

# Python integers have unlimited precision — no overflow!
factorial_100 = 1
for i in range(1, 101):
    factorial_100 *= i

print(factorial_100)
# Prints all 158 digits — this would overflow in C, Java, or JavaScript
Floats: Precision Pitfalls

# Float precision issues — critical for ML loss calculations
print(0.1 + 0.2)          # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)   # False!

# The right way to compare floats
import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))   # True

# For financial/precise calculations use Decimal
from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2')) # 0.3 exactly
Strings: Deep Dive
Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode characters.

text = "Machine Learning Engineer"

# Indexing — zero-based
print(text[0])      # M
print(text[-1])     # r (negative indexing from the end)

# Slicing — [start:stop:step]
print(text[0:7])    # Machine
print(text[8:])     # Learning Engineer
print(text[:7])     # Machine
print(text[::2])    # Mcieerig nier (every 2nd character)
print(text[::-1])   # reenignE gninraeL enihcaM (reversed)

# String methods
print(text.upper())           # MACHINE LEARNING ENGINEER
print(text.lower())           # machine learning engineer
print(text.split())           # ['Machine', 'Learning', 'Engineer']
print(text.replace("Learning", "Deep Learning"))
print(text.strip())           # removes leading/trailing whitespace
print(text.startswith("Mac")) # True
print(text.endswith("eer"))   # True
print(text.count("e"))        # counts occurrences
print(text.find("Learning"))  # returns starting index
print(",".join(["a", "b", "c"]))  # "a,b,c"

# String formatting approaches
name = "Claude"
score = 98.567

# f-string (recommended — Python 3.6+)
print(f"Model: {name}, Accuracy: {score:.2f}%")

# format() method
print("Model: {}, Accuracy: {:.2f}%".format(name, score))

# % formatting (old style — avoid in new code)
print("Model: %s, Accuracy: %.2f%%" % (name, score))
String Immutability in Practice

text = "hello"
# text[0] = "H"  # This raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

# To modify a string, create a new one
text = "H" + text[1:]
print(text)  # Hello

# In AI/ML this matters because heavy string operations
# inside loops create many temporary objects — use list + join instead

# Slow (creates new string each iteration)
result = ""
for word in ["large", "language", "model"]:
    result += word + " "

# Fast (recommended pattern)
result = " ".join(["large", "language", "model"])
Boolean Logic

# Truthy and Falsy values — critical for writing clean conditions
# Falsy values in Python:
falsy_values = [False, 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, set(), None, 0j]

for val in falsy_values:
    if not val:
        print(f"{repr(val)} is falsy")

# Truthy: everything else
if "non-empty string":
    print("This runs")

if [1, 2, 3]:
    print("Non-empty list is truthy")

# Practical use in ML code
model_results = []

# Pythonic check
if not model_results:
    print("No results yet — model has not been evaluated")

# Short-circuit evaluation
x = None
value = x or "default_value"   # Returns "default_value" because x is falsy
print(value)

threshold = 0.5
score = 0.87
label = "positive" if score > threshold else "negative"  # Ternary expression
Type Conversion
Implicit vs Explicit Conversion

# Implicit conversion (Python does it automatically when safe)
result = 10 + 3.5       # int + float → float (42 → 13.5)
print(type(result))     # <class 'float'>

result = True + 5       # bool + int → int
print(result)           # 6

# Explicit conversion (you control it)
# int()
print(int(3.9))         # 3 — truncates, does NOT round
print(int("42"))        # 42
print(int(True))        # 1
print(int("0xFF", 16))  # 255 — parse hex string

# float()
print(float("3.14"))    # 3.14
print(float(42))        # 42.0
print(float("inf"))     # inf

# str()
print(str(42))          # "42"
print(str(3.14))        # "3.14"
print(str(True))        # "True"

# bool()
print(bool(0))          # False
print(bool(1))          # True
print(bool(""))         # False
print(bool("hello"))    # True
print(bool([]))         # False
print(bool([0]))        # True — list with one element

# list(), tuple(), set()
print(list("hello"))    # ['h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o']
print(tuple([1,2,3]))   # (1, 2, 3)
print(set([1,1,2,3]))   # {1, 2, 3} — removes duplicates
Safe Type Conversion
Type Checking

x = 42
text = "hello"
items = [1, 2, 3]

# type() — exact type check
print(type(x))              # <class 'int'>
print(type(x) == int)       # True
print(type(x) == float)     # False

# isinstance() — preferred in professional code
# Checks if object is an instance of a class OR its subclasses
print(isinstance(x, int))          # True
print(isinstance(True, int))       # True (bool subclasses int)
print(isinstance(x, (int, float))) # True — check against multiple types

# Why isinstance() over type()
class Animal:
    pass

class Dog(Animal):
    pass

dog = Dog()
print(type(dog) == Animal)          # False
print(isinstance(dog, Animal))      # True — Dog IS an Animal

# In ML code this matters when functions need to accept multiple types
def process_input(data):
    if isinstance(data, str):
        return data.split()
    elif isinstance(data, list):
        return data
    elif isinstance(data, (int, float)):
        return [data]
    else:
        raise TypeError(f"Unsupported type: {type(data)}")
Operators
Arithmetic Operators

a, b = 17, 5

print(a + b)    # 22  — addition
print(a - b)    # 12  — subtraction
print(a * b)    # 85  — multiplication
print(a / b)    # 3.4 — true division (always returns float)
print(a // b)   # 3   — floor division (rounds down)
print(a % b)    # 2   — modulo (remainder)
print(a ** b)   # 1419857 — exponentiation

# Important: / always returns float in Python 3
print(10 / 2)   # 5.0 not 5

# Floor division with negatives (surprises many people)
print(-17 // 5)  # -4 (rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero)

Common Mistakes
Confusing = with ==

x = 10      # Assignment
x == 10     # Comparison (returns True/False)
if x = 10:  # SyntaxError — cannot assign inside if
Mutable default arguments

# WRONG — the list is created once and shared across all calls

    target.append(element)
    return target

print(append_to(1))   # [1]
print(append_to(2))   # [1, 2] — not [2]!

# CORRECT
def append_to(element, target=None):
    if target is None:
        target = []
    target.append(element)
    return target
Integer division surprises

count = 2
average = total / count    # 3.5 in Python 3
average = total // count   # 3 (floor division)
Comparing floats with ==

# WRONG
if 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3:  # False due to floating point

# CORRECT
import math
if math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3):  # True
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between is and == in Python?

== compares the values of two objects. is compares their identity — whether they are the exact same object in memory (same id()). Use == for value comparison. Use is only for comparing to None, True, or False singletons.
What are truthy and falsy values in Python?

Falsy values are: False, 0, 0.0, "" (empty string), [] (empty list), {} (empty dict), set() (empty set), None, and 0j (zero complex). Everything else is truthy. This matters when writing conditions without explicit comparisons: if my_list: is cleaner than if len(my_list) > 0:.
What is the difference between / and // in Python?
/ is true division and always returns a float (7/2 = 3.5). // is floor division and returns the floor of the result as an integer when both operands are integers (7//2 = 3).
Intermediate Level
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in Python?

Floating point numbers are stored in binary (IEEE 754 standard). 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in binary, so small rounding errors accumulate. The result of 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Always use math.isclose() for float comparisons.
What is the difference between mutable and immutable types? Give examples.

Immutable types cannot be changed after creation: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset, bool. Mutable types can be modified in place: list, dict, set. This matters because immutable objects can be used as dictionary keys and are safe to share across functions, while mutable objects passed to functions can be modified by those functions (aliasing).
Explain Python's memory model for integers from -5 to 256.

CPython pre-allocates (interns) integer objects from -5 to 256 at startup. Any time your code creates an integer in this range, Python returns the same cached object rather than creating a new one. This is why id(256) == id(256) is True but id(257) == id(257) may be False. This is a CPython implementation detail and should not be relied upon in production code.
Advanced Level
What is the difference between id(), hash(), and ==?

id() returns the memory address of the object (unique identity). hash() returns an integer computed from the object's value (used in dict keys and sets). == uses __eq__() to compare values. Two objects can have the same hash() and satisfy == without having the same id(). Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes. Mutable objects like lists are unhashable because their hash would change when their content changes.

# data_type_inspector.py
# Inspects a raw dataset record and produces a type analysis report

def inspect_record(record: dict) -> None:
    """
    Analyzes a dictionary record and reports:
    - Data type of each field
    - Whether the value is truthy/falsy
    - Suggested conversion for ML use
    """
    TYPE_SUGGESTIONS = {
        str: "Encode (Label/OneHot) or use NLP pipeline",
        int: "Ready for ML — consider scaling",
        float: "Ready for ML — consider normalization",
        bool: "Convert to int (0/1) for ML",
        type(None): "Missing value — needs imputation strategy",
        list: "Aggregate or extract features",
        dict: "Flatten or extract relevant keys"
    }

    print("\n" + "=" * 60)
    print(f"{'FIELD':<20} {'TYPE':<15} {'TRUTHY':<8} {'SUGGESTION'}")
    print("=" * 60)

    for field, value in record.items():
        field_type = type(value)
        type_name = field_type.__name__
        is_truthy = bool(value)
        suggestion = TYPE_SUGGESTIONS.get(field_type, "Unknown type")

        print(f"{field:<20} {type_name:<15} {str(is_truthy):<8} {suggestion}")

    print("=" * 60)

    # Summary statistics
    none_count = sum(1 for v in record.values() if v is None)
    total = len(record)
    missing_pct = (none_count / total) * 100

    print(f"\nTotal fields:   {total}")
    print(f"Missing values: {none_count} ({missing_pct:.1f}%)")

    numeric_types = (int, float, bool)
    numeric_count = sum(1 for v in record.values()
                       if isinstance(v, numeric_types) and v is not None)
    print(f"Numeric fields: {numeric_count}")
    print(f"Needs encoding: {total - numeric_count - none_count}")

Introduction

Control flow is what transforms a script that runs top-to-bottom into a program that makes decisions, repeats operations, and responds to data. Every machine learning training loop, every data preprocessing pipeline, every agent decision cycle is built on control flow.

In AI/ML specifically, you will write thousands of loops — loops over epochs, over batches, over tokens, over documents, over agent steps. Understanding how to write them efficiently, readably, and correctly is a core engineering skill.
This chapter covers not just the syntax but the professional patterns that separate beginner code from production-quality code.
Conditional Statements
The if Statement
The if statement evaluates a condition and executes a block of code only if that condition is True.

# Basic if statement
validation_accuracy = 0.94

if validation_accuracy > 0.90:
    print("Model meets production threshold")
    print("Ready for deployment review")
Python uses indentation to define code blocks. There are no curly braces. The standard is 4 spaces per level. This is enforced by the language — incorrect indentation causes an IndentationError.
if-elif-else

loss = 0.043

if loss < 0.01:
    status = "Excellent"
    action = "Deploy to production"
elif loss < 0.05:
    status = "Good"
    action = "Run additional validation"
elif loss < 0.10:
    status = "Acceptable"
    action = "Continue training"
elif loss < 0.20:
    status = "Poor"
    action = "Tune hyperparameters"
else:
    status = "Failed"
    action = "Debug model architecture"

print(f"Loss: {loss:.4f}")
print(f"Status: {status}")
print(f"Action: {action}")
Key rules:
Only one if per block
Zero or more elif clauses
At most one else clause
Python evaluates conditions top to bottom and stops at the first True
The else block runs only if all conditions above were False

def process_api_response(response):
    match response:
        case {"status": "success", "data": data}:
            return f"Success: {data}"
        case {"status": "error", "message": msg}:

        case {"status": "pending"}:

While Loops
The while loop executes as long as its condition remains True. Use it when you do not know in advance how many iterations are needed.
Basic While Loop

# Training until convergence
loss = 10.0
target_loss = 0.01
epoch = 0
max_epochs = 1000

while loss > target_loss and epoch < max_epochs:
    loss *= 0.85     # Simulate loss decreasing each epoch
    epoch += 1
    
    if epoch % 100 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch:4d} | Loss: {loss:.6f}")

print(f"\nStopped at epoch {epoch}")
print(f"Final loss: {loss:.6f}")
if loss <= target_loss:
    print("Converged successfully")
else:
    print("Reached max epochs without convergence")

Infinite Loops with Break

# Polling loop — common in agent systems and servers
import random

def check_model_status():
    """Simulates checking if async model training is complete"""
    return random.random() > 0.7   # 30% chance of being ready

attempt = 0
max_attempts = 20

while True:
    attempt += 1
    is_ready = check_model_status()
    
    print(f"Attempt {attempt}: {'Ready!' if is_ready else 'Still training...'}")
    
    if is_ready:
        print("Model training complete!")
        break
    
    if attempt >= max_attempts:
        print("Timeout: model training took too long")
        break
Loop Control: break, continue, pass
break — Exit the Loop Immediately
continue — Skip to the Next Iteration

# Process only valid data points — skip corrupted ones
dataset = [
    {"text": "Great product!", "label": 1},
    {"text": None,             "label": 1},   # corrupted
    {"text": "",               "label": 0},   # empty
    {"text": "Terrible",      "label": 0},
    {"text": "Amazing!",      "label": 1},
    {"text": "Bad quality",   "label": None}, # missing label
]

valid_samples = []

for i, sample in enumerate(dataset):
    # Skip samples with missing text
    if not sample["text"]:
        print(f"Sample {i}: Skipping — missing text")
        continue
    
    # Skip samples with missing label
    if sample["label"] is None:
        print(f"Sample {i}: Skipping — missing label")
        continue
    
    # Valid sample — process it
    valid_samples.append(sample)
    print(f"Sample {i}: ✓ Added to dataset")

print(f"\nValid samples: {len(valid_samples)}/{len(dataset)}")
pass — Do Nothing (Placeholder)

Python has an unusual feature: else clauses on loops. The else block runs if the loop completed without hitting a break.

# Search for a hyperparameter combination that works

    {"lr": 0.1,   "dropout": 0.5},
    {"lr": 0.01,  "dropout": 0.3},
    {"lr": 0.001, "dropout": 0.2},
]

TARGET_ACCURACY = 0.95

for params in param_combinations:
    # Simulate training with these params
    simulated_accuracy = 1 / (1 + params["lr"] * 10) * (1 - params["dropout"])
    print(f"Params: {params} → Accuracy: {simulated_accuracy:.3f}")
    
    if simulated_accuracy >= TARGET_ACCURACY:
        print(f"Found working params: {params}")
        break
else:
    # This runs only if no break occurred
    print("No combination achieved target accuracy — expand search space")

Generator Expressions
Generator expressions look like list comprehensions but use () instead of []. They are lazy — they compute values one at a time instead of building the entire list in memory.

# Generator expression — computes on demand

# Both produce the same values when iterated
print(next(squares_gen))    # 0
print(next(squares_gen))    # 1
print(next(squares_gen))    # 4

Control Flow Patterns in AI/ML
The Training Loop Pattern

def train_model(model, train_data, val_data, config):
    """
    Standard ML training loop structure.
    This pattern appears in virtually every ML codebase.
    """
    best_val_loss = float('inf')
    patience_counter = 0
    history = {"train_loss": [], "val_loss": [], "val_accuracy": []}

    for epoch in range(1, config["epochs"] + 1):

        # --- Training Phase ---
        train_losses = []
        for batch_idx, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(train_data):
            loss = model.train_step(inputs, targets)
            train_losses.append(loss)

            # Log every N batches
            if batch_idx % config["log_every"] == 0:
                print(f"  Epoch {epoch} | Batch {batch_idx} | Loss: {loss:.4f}")

        avg_train_loss = sum(train_losses) / len(train_losses)

        # --- Validation Phase ---
        val_losses, val_accuracies = [], []
        for inputs, targets in val_data:
            val_loss, accuracy = model.evaluate(inputs, targets)
            val_losses.append(val_loss)
            val_accuracies.append(accuracy)

        avg_val_loss = sum(val_losses) / len(val_losses)
        avg_val_acc = sum(val_accuracies) / len(val_accuracies)

        # --- Logging ---
        history["train_loss"].append(avg_train_loss)
        history["val_loss"].append(avg_val_loss)
        history["val_accuracy"].append(avg_val_acc)

        print(f"Epoch {epoch:3d}/{config['epochs']} | "
              f"Train Loss: {avg_train_loss:.4f} | "
              f"Val Loss: {avg_val_loss:.4f} | "
              f"Val Acc: {avg_val_acc:.2%}")

        # --- Early Stopping ---
        if avg_val_loss < best_val_loss:
            best_val_loss = avg_val_loss
            patience_counter = 0
            model.save("best_model.pt")
            print(f"  ✓ New best model saved (val_loss: {best_val_loss:.4f})")
        else:
            patience_counter += 1
            print(f"  ⚠ No improvement ({patience_counter}/{config['patience']})")

            if patience_counter >= config["patience"]:
                print(f"\nEarly stopping triggered at epoch {epoch}")
                break

    return history

Common Mistakes
Off-by-One Errors
Modifying a List While Iterating

# WRONG — modifying a list while iterating causes skipped items
scores = [0.9, 0.5, 0.8, 0.4, 0.7]
for score in scores:
    if score < 0.6:
        scores.remove(score)   # BUG: items get skipped
print(scores)   # [0.9, 0.8, 0.4, 0.7] — 0.4 was not removed!

# CORRECT — iterate over a copy, or build a new list
scores = [0.9, 0.5, 0.8, 0.4, 0.7]
scores = [s for s in scores if s >= 0.6]
print(scores)   # [0.9, 0.8, 0.7]
Infinite While Loop

# WRONG — forgetting to update the loop variable

# while count < 10:
#     print(count)
#     # Forgot count += 1 — infinite loop!

# ALWAYS make sure the condition can become False
count = 0
while count < 10:
    print(count)
    count += 1   # Must update!
Using range(len()) Instead of enumerate()

items = ["bert", "gpt", "t5"]

# WRONG — unnecessarily verbose
for i in range(len(items)):
    print(i, items[i])

# CORRECT — Pythonic
for i, item in enumerate(items):
    print(i, item)
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between break and continue?

break exits the loop entirely and resumes execution after the loop block. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one. break terminates the loop; continue only skips one iteration.
What does the else clause on a for loop do?

The else block on a for or while loop executes only if the loop completed normally — that is, without hitting a break statement. It is commonly used to handle the case where a search loop did not find what it was looking for.
What is the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?

Both produce sequences of values from an expression. A list comprehension [x for x in ...] computes all values immediately and stores them in a list in memory. A generator expression (x for x in ...) is lazy — it computes one value at a time when iterated, using constant memory regardless of size. Use generators for large datasets.
Intermediate Level
Why is it dangerous to modify a list while iterating over it?

Python's for loop maintains an internal index counter. When you remove items, the list shrinks and the index skips over the next item. For example, if you remove index 2, what was at index 3 shifts to index 2, but the loop counter moves to index 3, skipping the item that shifted. The safe alternatives are iterating over a copy, or building a new list with a comprehension.
What is the time complexity of a nested loop over n elements?

A single loop over n elements is O(n). Two nested loops each running over n elements is O(n²). Three levels deep is O(n³). In ML contexts, O(n²) can become a serious bottleneck — for example, computing pairwise distances between 100,000 embeddings would require 10 billion operations. This is why vectorized NumPy operations are essential.
How does Python's for loop work under the hood?

Python's for loop calls iter() on the iterable to get an iterator object, then repeatedly calls next() on it until a StopIteration exception is raised. This protocol (__iter__ and __next__ methods) is how custom iterable classes work and is the foundation of generators.
Advanced Level
What is the difference between yield and return in a generator function?

return exits the function and returns a value. yield suspends the function, saves its state (local variables, instruction pointer), and returns a value to the caller. When next() is called again, execution resumes from right after the yield statement. A function containing yield becomes a generator function — calling it returns a generator object without executing any code until the first next() call.

# experiment_runner.py
# Simulates running a grid search over hyperparameters
# Demonstrates control flow in a real ML context

import random
import time

def simulate_training(learning_rate, batch_size, dropout, epochs):
    """
    Simulates training a model with given hyperparameters.
    Returns (val_loss, val_accuracy, training_time)
    """
    random.seed(int(learning_rate * 10000 + batch_size + dropout * 100))
    
    # Simulate training dynamics
    base_accuracy = 0.70 + random.uniform(0, 0.25)
    
    # Penalize bad hyperparameter combinations
    if learning_rate > 0.1:
        base_accuracy -= 0.15  # Too high LR hurts
    if dropout > 0.6:
        base_accuracy -= 0.10  # Too much dropout hurts
    if batch_size < 8:
        base_accuracy -= 0.05  # Very small batches are unstable
    
    val_accuracy = min(max(base_accuracy, 0.50), 0.99)
    val_loss = -val_accuracy + 1.0 + random.uniform(0, 0.05)
    train_time = epochs * batch_size * 0.001 * random.uniform(0.8, 1.2)
    
    return val_loss, val_accuracy, train_time

def run_grid_search(param_grid, epochs=50):
    """
    Runs grid search over all hyperparameter combinations.
    """
    print("=" * 70)
    print("  HYPERPARAMETER GRID SEARCH")
    print("=" * 70)
    
    # Generate all combinations
    combinations = [
        {"lr": lr, "batch_size": bs, "dropout": do}
        for lr in param_grid["learning_rates"]
        for bs in param_grid["batch_sizes"]
        for do in param_grid["dropouts"]
    ]
    
    total = len(combinations)
    print(f"Total combinations to try: {total}\n")
    
    results = []
    best_result = None
    
    for i, params in enumerate(combinations, 1):
        print(f"[{i:3d}/{total}] Testing: lr={params['lr']:.4f} | "
              f"batch={params['batch_size']:3d} | "
              f"dropout={params['dropout']:.1f}", end=" → ")
        
        val_loss, val_acc, train_time = simulate_training(
            params["lr"], params["batch_size"],
            params["dropout"], epochs
        )
        
        result = {
            **params,
            "val_loss": val_loss,
            "val_accuracy": val_acc,
            "train_time": train_time
        }
        results.append(result)
        
        status = "⭐" if val_acc > 0.90 else "✓" if val_acc > 0.80 else "✗"
        print(f"Acc: {val_acc:.4f} | Loss: {val_loss:.4f} {status}")
        
        # Track best
        if best_result is None or val_acc > best_result["val_accuracy"]:
            best_result = result
    
    return results, best_result

def print_top_results(results, top_n=5):
    """Print top N results sorted by validation accuracy"""
    sorted_results = sorted(results, key=lambda r: r["val_accuracy"], reverse=True)
    
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"  TOP {top_n} CONFIGURATIONS")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    print(f"{'Rank':<6} {'LR':<8} {'Batch':<8} {'Dropout':<10} "
          f"{'Val Acc':<10} {'Val Loss':<10}")
    print("-" * 70)
    
    for rank, result in enumerate(sorted_results[:top_n], 1):
        print(f"{rank:<6} {result['lr']:<8.4f} {result['batch_size']:<8} "
              f"{result['dropout']:<10.1f} {result['val_accuracy']:<10.4f} "
              f"{result['val_loss']:<10.4f}")

def main():
    # Define hyperparameter search space
    param_grid = {
        "learning_rates": [0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001],
        "batch_sizes":    [8, 32, 64, 128],
        "dropouts":       [0.1, 0.3, 0.5]
    }
    
    start_time = time.time()
    results, best = run_grid_search(param_grid, epochs=50)
    elapsed = time.time() - start_time
    
    print_top_results(results, top_n=5)
    
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print("  BEST CONFIGURATION")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    print(f"  Learning Rate:  {best['lr']}")
    print(f"  Batch Size:     {best['batch_size']}")
    print(f"  Dropout:        {best['dropout']}")
    print(f"  Val Accuracy:   {best['val_accuracy']:.4f}")
    print(f"  Val Loss:       {best['val_loss']:.4f}")
    print(f"\nGrid search completed in {elapsed:.2f}s")
    print(f"Configurations tested: {len(results)}")
    
    # Analysis using comprehensions and control flow
    excellent = [r for r in results if r["val_accuracy"] >= 0.90]
    good = [r for r in results if 0.80 <= r["val_accuracy"] < 0.90]
    poor = [r for r in results if r["val_accuracy"] < 0.80]
    
    print(f"\nResults breakdown:")
    print(f"  Excellent (≥90%): {len(excellent)}")
    print(f"  Good (80-90%):    {len(good)}")
    print(f"  Poor (<80%):      {len(poor)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Introduction

Functions are the fundamental unit of reusable code. Every major AI/ML library you will ever use — PyTorch, LangChain, Scikit-learn, FastAPI — is built from thousands of carefully designed functions and methods.

The difference between a beginner who writes scripts and a professional who builds systems comes down largely to how they design functions. Good functions are small, focused, testable, and composable. They have clear inputs, predictable outputs, and no hidden side effects.
This chapter will take you from writing basic functions to understanding closures, decorators, and the functional programming patterns that appear throughout modern AI/ML codebases.
Defining and Calling Functions
Basic Function Structure

def function_name(parameters):
    """
    Docstring: describes what the function does,
    its parameters, and what it returns.
    """
    # Function body
    result = some_computation(parameters)
    return result
 def calculate_accuracy(correct_predictions, total_predictions):
    """
    Calculate classification accuracy.

    Args:
        correct_predictions (int): Number of correct predictions
        total_predictions (int): Total number of predictions

    Returns:
        float: Accuracy as a value between 0.0 and 1.0

    Raises:
        ValueError: If total_predictions is zero
    """
    if total_predictions == 0:
        raise ValueError("total_predictions cannot be zero")

    return correct_predictions / total_predictions

# DANGEROUS — this is one of Python's most common bugs

    return architecture

print(add_layer("conv2"))    # ['conv1', 'conv2'] — WRONG! Should be ['conv2']

    if architecture is None:
        architecture = []

print(add_layer("conv2"))    # ['conv2'] — correct

def ensemble_predict(*models, data):
    """
    Accept any number of model predictions.
    *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple.

    print(f"Ensembling {len(models)} models")
    predictions = [model.predict(data) for model in models]
    # Average the predictions
    avg = sum(predictions) / len(predictions)
    return avg

def create_model_config(**kwargs):
    """
    **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.
    Common in ML frameworks for flexible configuration.
    """
    defaults = {
        "hidden_size": 768,
        "num_layers": 12,
        "num_heads": 12,
        "dropout": 0.1,
        "activation": "gelu",
        "vocab_size": 30522
    }

    # Override defaults with provided values
    config = {**defaults, **kwargs}

    print("Model Configuration:")
    for key, value in config.items():
        marker = " ← custom" if key in kwargs else ""
        print(f"  {key}: {value}{marker}")

def full_training_pipeline(model_name,           # positional
                           dataset,              # positional
                           *augmentations,       # *args
                           epochs=10,            # keyword-only default
                           learning_rate=0.001,  # keyword-only default
                           **training_kwargs):   # **kwargs
    """
    Demonstrates the complete argument signature.

    Argument order rule:
    positional → *args → keyword-only → **kwargs
    """

def make_learning_rate_scheduler(initial_lr, decay_factor):
    """
    Returns a scheduler function that closes over
    initial_lr and decay_factor.
    """
    step_count = [0]   # Use list to allow mutation in closure

    def get_lr():
        current_lr = initial_lr * (decay_factor ** step_count[0])
        step_count[0] += 1
        return current_lr

    return get_lr   # Return the inner function

def make_early_stopper(patience):
    """
    Creates an early stopping checker using closure.
    Demonstrates nonlocal for modifying enclosing scope variables.
    """
    best_loss = float('inf')
    counter = 0

    def check(current_loss):
        nonlocal best_loss, counter   # Access enclosing variables

        if current_loss < best_loss:
            best_loss = current_loss
            counter = 0
            return False   # Do not stop
        else:
            counter += 1
            if counter >= patience:
                return True   # Stop training
            return False

    def reset():
        nonlocal best_loss, counter
        best_loss = float('inf')
        counter = 0

    return check, reset

class ModelCache:
    """
    A decorator class that caches model predictions.
    Avoids redundant computation for repeated inputs.
    """
    def __init__(self, func):
        functools.update_wrapper(self, func)
        self.func = func
        self.cache = {}
        self.hits = 0
        self.misses = 0

    def __call__(self, *args):
        cache_key = str(args)

        if cache_key in self.cache:
            self.hits += 1
            return self.cache[cache_key]

        self.misses += 1
        result = self.func(*args)
        self.cache[cache_key] = result
        return result

    def stats(self):
        total = self.hits + self.misses
        hit_rate = self.hits / total if total > 0 else 0
        return f"Cache: {self.hits} hits, {self.misses} misses ({hit_rate:.0%} hit rate)"

def iterative_tree_traversal(root):
    """Iterative DFS — avoids recursion limit for deep trees"""
    stack = [root]
    visited = []

    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        visited.append(node)

        # Add children to stack
        for child in node.get("children", []):
            stack.append(child)

    return visited

from typing import Optional, Union, List, Dict, Callable, Tuple
import random

def create_ml_pipeline(
    preprocessors: List[Callable],
    model: Callable,
    postprocessors: Optional[List[Callable]] = None,
    *,
    batch_size: int = 32,
    device: str = "cpu"
) -> Callable:
    """
    Factory function that builds a complete ML inference pipeline.

    Args:
        preprocessors: List of functions to apply to input data
        model: The model's inference function
        postprocessors: Optional list of post-processing functions
        batch_size: Number of samples to process at once
        device: Computation device

    Returns:
        A pipeline function ready for inference
    """
    if postprocessors is None:
        postprocessors = []

    def pipeline(raw_input: Union[str, List[str]]) -> Dict:
        # Normalize input to list
        if isinstance(raw_input, str):
            raw_input = [raw_input]

        results = []

        # Process in batches
        for i in range(0, len(raw_input), batch_size):
            batch = raw_input[i:i + batch_size]

            # Apply preprocessors sequentially
            processed = batch
            for preprocess_fn in preprocessors:
                processed = [preprocess_fn(x) for x in processed]

            # Run model inference
            predictions = model(processed)

            # Apply postprocessors
            for postprocess_fn in postprocessors:
                predictions = [postprocess_fn(p) for p in predictions]

            results.extend(predictions)

        return {
            "inputs": raw_input,
            "outputs": results,
            "count": len(results),
            "device": device
        }

    # Attach metadata to the pipeline
    pipeline.__name__ = "ml_pipeline"
    pipeline.preprocessors = preprocessors
    pipeline.model = model
    pipeline.config = {"batch_size": batch_size, "device": device}

    return pipeline

Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

A parameter is the variable listed in the function definition. An argument is the actual value passed to the function when it is called. In def add(x, y), x and y are parameters. In add(3, 5), 3 and 5 are arguments.
What does *args and **kwargs do?

*args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple inside the function. **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. They allow functions to accept a variable number of arguments. The names args and kwargs are conventions — the * and ** are what matter syntactically.
What is a lambda function and when should you use it?

A lambda is an anonymous single-expression function. Use it for short, simple functions passed as arguments to sorted(), map(), or filter(). Do not use lambdas for complex logic — use a named function with a docstring instead.
Intermediate Level
Explain Python's LEGB scope rule with an example.

Python resolves names by searching four scopes in order: Local (inside current function), Enclosing (in outer functions for closures), Global (module level), Built-in (Python builtins like len, print). If a name is not found in any scope, Python raises a NameError. The global keyword allows a function to modify a global variable. The nonlocal keyword allows an inner function to modify a variable in an enclosing function's scope.
What is a closure and how is it used in ML?

A closure is a function that retains access to variables from its enclosing scope even after that scope has finished executing. In ML, closures are used to create factory functions — for example, make_lr_scheduler(initial_lr, decay) returns a scheduler function that remembers initial_lr and decay. Each call to the factory creates an independent scheduler with its own state.
How do decorators work, and what is @functools.wraps for?

A decorator is a function that takes a function as input and returns a modified function. The @decorator syntax is equivalent to func = decorator(func). @functools.wraps(func) is applied to the wrapper function inside a decorator to copy the original function's __name__, __doc__, and other metadata to the wrapper. Without it, tools like help(), logging, and debugging see the wrapper's metadata instead of the original function's.
Advanced Level
What is the difference between a decorator and a decorator factory?

A decorator takes a function and returns a function: @my_decorator. A decorator factory is a function that takes configuration arguments and returns a decorator: @my_decorator(param=value). When you use @retry(max_attempts=3), retry(max_attempts=3) is called first and must return a decorator function, which is then applied to the decorated function. This is the three-level pattern: outer (config) → middle (receives function) → inner (wrapper).

# experiment_framework.py
# A lightweight experiment tracking framework built entirely with functions
# Demonstrates closures, decorators, higher-order functions, and *args/**kwargs

import time
import functools
from typing import Callable, Dict, Any, List

# ── Experiment Registry ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────

_experiments: Dict[str, Dict] = {}

def experiment(name: str, tags: List[str] = None):
    """
    Decorator factory that registers a function as an ML experiment.
    Tracks execution time, parameters, and results automatically.
    """
    def decorator(func: Callable) -> Callable:
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            print(f"\n{'='*60}")
            print(f"  EXPERIMENT: {name}")
            print(f"  Tags: {tags or []}")
            print(f"{'='*60}")

            start_time = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                result = func(*args, **kwargs)
                status = "SUCCESS"
            except Exception as e:
                result = None
                status = f"FAILED: {e}"
                raise
            finally:
                elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
                _experiments[name] = {
                    "status": status,
                    "duration": elapsed,
                    "tags": tags or [],
                    "result": result,
                    "kwargs": kwargs
                }
                print(f"\n  Duration: {elapsed:.3f}s | Status: {status}")
                print(f"{'='*60}")

            return result
        return wrapper
    return decorator


# ── Metric Tracker ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def make_metric_tracker():
    """
    Closure-based metric tracker.
    Each call creates an independent tracker with its own state.
    """
    _metrics: Dict[str, List] = {}

    def log(metric_name: str, value: float, step: int = None):
        if metric_name not in _metrics:
            _metrics[metric_name] = []
        _metrics[metric_name].append({
            "value": value,
            "step": step or len(_metrics[metric_name])
        })

    def get(metric_name: str) -> List:
        return _metrics.get(metric_name, [])

    def best(metric_name: str, mode: str = "min") -> float:
        values = [entry["value"] for entry in get(metric_name)]
        if not values:
            return None
        return min(values) if mode == "min" else max(values)

    def summary() -> None:
        print("\n  Metrics Summary:")
        print("  " + "-" * 40)
        for name, entries in _metrics.items():
            values = [e["value"] for e in entries]
            print(f"  {name}:")
            print(f"    Steps logged: {len(values)}")
            print(f"    Last:  {values[-1]:.6f}")
            print(f"    Best:  {min(values):.6f}")
            print(f"    Worst: {max(values):.6f}")

    return log, get, best, summary


# ── Pipeline Builder ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def build_pipeline(*steps: Callable) -> Callable:
    """
    Build a data pipeline from a sequence of functions.
    Each function's output becomes the next function's input.
    """
    def pipeline(data: Any) -> Any:
        result = data
        for step in steps:
            step_name = getattr(step, '__name__', str(step))
            result = step(result)
            print(f"  ✓ {step_name}: {type(result).__name__}")
        return result

    pipeline.__name__ = " → ".join(
        getattr(s, '__name__', '?') for s in steps
    )
    return pipeline


# ── Experiments ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

import random

@experiment(name="linear_baseline", tags=["baseline", "linear"])

    for epoch in range(1, training_kwargs.get("epochs", 20) + 1):
        complexity_bonus = sum(hidden_sizes) / 1000
        train_loss = 1.5 * (0.90 ** epoch) + random.uniform(-0.02, 0.02)
        val_loss = train_loss + random.uniform(0.005, 0.03)
        accuracy = min(0.99, 0.65 + complexity_bonus + (1 - val_loss))

        log("train_loss", train_loss, epoch)
        log("val_loss", val_loss, epoch)
        log("accuracy", accuracy, epoch)

        if epoch % 5 == 0:
            print(f"  Epoch {epoch:3d} | train_loss={train_loss:.4f} "
                  f"| val_loss={val_loss:.4f} | acc={accuracy:.4f}")

    summary()
    return {"best_val_l
oss": best("val_loss"), "best_accuracy": best("accuracy", mode="max")}

Chapter Summary
Functions are first-class objects in Python — they can be assigned, passed, returned, and stored
Argument types in order: positional → *args → keyword-only → **kwargs
Never use mutable objects as default arguments — use None and initialize inside
Python resolves names using LEGB: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in
global modifies module-level variables; nonlocal modifies enclosing function variables
Closures retain access to enclosing scope variables — powerful for factory functions
Lambda functions are anonymous single-expression functions — use for short, simple cases only
map(), filter(), reduce() apply functions to iterables — often replaced by comprehensions
Decorators wrap functions to add behavior — always use @functools.wraps inside decorators
Decorator factories add configuration to decorators using the three-level pattern
@lru_cache memoizes recursive functions and eliminates redundant computation
Recursion requires a base case and a recursive case — Python defaults to 1000 call depth

# Function definition

    return result

# Lambda

# Decorator template
import functools
def decorator(func):
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        # before
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        # after
        return result
    return wrapper

# Decorator factory template
def decorator_factory(config):
    def decorator(func):
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator

# Higher-order functions
map(fn, iterable)          # Apply fn to each element
filter(fn, iterable)       # Keep elements where fn is True
reduce(fn, iterable)       # Accumulate with fn

# Memoization
from functools import lru_cache
@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def expensive(n): ...

Introduction

Data structures are the containers that hold your data as it flows through an AI/ML system. Raw text documents, model predictions, training batches, configuration parameters, vocabulary mappings, tokenized sequences — all of these live in Python data structures at some point in their lifecycle.

Choosing the wrong data structure is one of the most common causes of slow, buggy, and hard-to-read ML code. A lookup that should take one microsecond takes one second because someone used a list instead of a set. A configuration that should be immutable gets accidentally modified because someone used a list instead of a tuple.

This chapter goes deep into Python's four core data structures — lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries — plus strings as sequences, and collections module extras. You will understand not just how to use them but why they behave the way they do.
Lists
A list is an ordered, mutable, heterogeneous sequence. It is the most versatile Python data structure and the one you will use most often in AI/ML code.
Internal Implementation

Python lists are implemented as dynamic arrays. They store references (pointers) to objects, not the objects themselves. When the array fills up, Python allocates a new larger array and copies all references — this is why appending to a list is O(1) amortized but occasionally O(n).

List in memory:
[ref0][ref1][ref2][ref3][ref4][....][....][....]
  ↓     ↓     ↓     ↓     ↓
obj0  obj1  obj2  obj3  obj4

List Methods — Complete Reference

data = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3, 5]

# Adding elements
data.append(7)          # Add to end — O(1) amortized
data.insert(0, 0)       # Insert at index — O(n)
data.extend([8, 9, 10]) # Add multiple — O(k)
data += [11, 12]        # Same as extend

# Removing elements
data.remove(1)          # Remove first occurrence of value — O(n)
popped = data.pop()     # Remove and return last element — O(1)
popped = data.pop(2)    # Remove and return element at index — O(n)
del data[0]             # Delete by index — O(n)
data.clear()            # Remove all elements

# Searching
data = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
print(data.index(1))    # Index of first occurrence — O(n)
print(data.count(1))    # Count occurrences — O(n)
print(5 in data)        # Membership test — O(n)

# Ordering
data.sort()                          # In-place sort — O(n log n)
data.sort(reverse=True)              # Descending
data.sort(key=lambda x: abs(x-5))   # Sort by distance from 5
sorted_copy = sorted(data)           # Returns new sorted list

# Other
data.reverse()          # In-place reversal — O(n)
copy = data.copy()      # Shallow copy — O(n)
copy = data[:]          # Equivalent shallow copy

print(len(data))        # Length — O(1)
print(min(data))        # Minimum — O(n)
print(max(data))        # Maximum — O(n)
print(sum(data))        # Sum — O(n)

Operation              Average    Worst
──────────────────────────────────────
Index access (list[i])  O(1)       O(1)
Append                  O(1)       O(n)  ← occasional resize
Insert at beginning     O(n)       O(n)
Delete at beginning     O(n)       O(n)
Search (in)             O(n)       O(n)
Sort                    O(n log n) O(n log n)
Length (len)            O(1)       O(1)
Slice [i:j]             O(k)       O(k)
Deep vs Shallow Copy

import copy

original = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]

# Shallow copy — copies the list but not the nested objects
shallow = original.copy()
shallow[0][0] = 99      # Modifies the SHARED inner list!
print(original[0][0])   # 99 — original affected

# Deep copy — copies everything recursively
original = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
deep[0][0] = 99
print(original[0][0])   # 1 — original NOT affected

# In ML: be careful with deepcopy on large objects like model weights
# Use model.state_dict() and copy.deepcopy(state_dict) patterns

A set is an unordered, mutable collection of unique hashable elements. Sets are implemented as hash tables, giving O(1) average-case lookup, insertion, and deletion.

# Remove duplicate documents from a dataset
def deduplicate_dataset(documents):
    """Remove exact duplicate texts from a dataset"""
    seen = set()
    unique_docs = []

    for doc in documents:
        # Use text as fingerprint
        fingerprint = doc["text"].lower().strip()
        if fingerprint not in seen:
            seen.add(fingerprint)
            unique_docs.append(doc)

    removed = len(documents) - len(unique_docs)
    print(f"Removed {removed} duplicates ({removed/len(documents):.1%})")
    return unique_docs

Dictionaries
A dictionary is an unordered (insertion-ordered in Python 3.7+), mutable mapping of unique keys to values. It is implemented as a hash table.

Dictionaries are perhaps the most important data structure in Python. JSON objects, model configurations, label encodings, feature maps, API responses, word-to-index mappings — virtually everything in AI/ML uses dictionaries.

counter_a = Counter({"a": 3, "b": 2, "c": 1})
counter_b = Counter({"b": 1, "c": 2, "d": 3})

print(counter_a + counter_b)   # {'d': 3, 'a': 3, 'c': 3, 'b': 3}
print(counter_a - counter_b)   # {'a': 3, 'b': 1}
print(counter_a & counter_b)   # Intersection (min): {'b': 1, 'c': 1}
print(counter_a | counter_b)   # Union (max): {'a': 3, 'c': 2, 'd': 3, 'b': 2}


# ── deque ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Double-ended queue — O(1) append and pop from both ends
# Lists have O(n) for insert/remove at the beginning

from collections import deque

# Sliding window of recent losses
window_size = 5
recent_losses = deque(maxlen=window_size)

all_losses = [2.1, 1.9, 1.7, 1.5, 1.4, 1.3, 1.2, 1.15, 1.1, 1.08]
for loss in all_losses:
    recent_losses.append(loss)   # Auto-removes oldest when full
    smoothed = sum(recent_losses) / len(recent_losses)
    print(f"Loss: {loss:.2f} | Smoothed: {smoothed:.3f}")

# BFS queue — O(1) popleft vs O(n) list.pop(0)
queue = deque(["node_1", "node_2", "node_3"])
queue.appendleft("node_0")    # Add to front
front = queue.popleft()       # Remove from front — O(1)

Lookup Time Comparison

import time
import random

n = 100_000
data = list(range(n))
target = n - 1   # Worst case — at the end

# List lookup: O(n)
data_list = list(range(n))
start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    _ = target in data_list
list_time = time.perf_counter() - start

# Set lookup: O(1)
data_set = set(range(n))
start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    _ = target in data_set
set_time = time.perf_counter() - start

# Dict lookup: O(1)
data_dict = {i: True for i in range(n)}
start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(1000):
    _ = target in data_dict
dict_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"List lookup:   {list_time:.4f}s")
print(f"Set lookup:    {set_time:.4f}s  ({list_time/set_time:.0f}x faster)")
print(f"Dict lookup:   {dict_time:.4f}s  ({list_time/dict_time:.0f}x faster)")
Common Mistakes
Using a List When You Should Use a Set

# SLOW — O(n) lookup
visited_urls = []
if url not in visited_urls:   # Searches entire list
    visited_urls.append(url)

# FAST — O(1) lookup
visited_urls = set()
if url not in visited_urls:   # Hash table lookup
    visited_urls.add(url)
Modifying a Dictionary While Iterating

Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between a list and a tuple?

Both are ordered sequences. A list is mutable — elements can be added, removed, or changed after creation. A tuple is immutable — once created, it cannot be modified. Tuples are faster and use less memory than lists. Tuples can be used as dictionary keys and set elements; lists cannot. Use tuples when the data should not change (coordinates, RGB values, function return of multiple values) and lists when you need to modify the collection.
What makes a dictionary key valid?

A dictionary key must be hashable — it must implement __hash__() and __eq__() methods, and its hash value must not change during its lifetime. Immutable types (int, float, str, tuple, frozenset) are hashable and valid as keys. Mutable types (list, dict, set) are not hashable and cannot be used as keys.
What is the time complexity of in for lists vs sets vs dicts?

For lists, in is O(n) — Python must check each element one by one. For sets and dictionary keys, in is O(1) average case — Python computes the hash of the target value and directly looks up the hash table bucket. This makes sets and dicts dramatically faster for membership testing on large collections.
Intermediate Level
How does Python's dict maintain insertion order?

Since Python 3.7, dictionaries are guaranteed to maintain insertion order as part of the language specification. This is implemented using a combination of a hash table for O(1) lookups and a compact array that stores key-value pairs in insertion order. Before Python 3.7, you needed collections.OrderedDict for ordered behavior.
What is the difference between dict.copy() and copy.deepcopy(dict)?

dict.copy() creates a shallow copy — a new dictionary object with the same key-value references. If values are mutable objects (lists, other dicts), both the original and the copy point to the same objects, so modifying a nested object affects both. copy.deepcopy() recursively copies all nested objects, creating completely independent copies. For flat dicts with immutable values, shallow copy is sufficient. For nested structures like experiment configs, deepcopy is safer.
When would you use defaultdict over a regular dict?

Use defaultdict when you are building a collection where you will be accessing or modifying values for keys that may not yet exist, and you want a sensible default value rather than a KeyError. Common use cases: counting (default int → 0), grouping (default list → []), building graphs (default set → empty set). It eliminates the if key not in dict: dict[key] = default_value boilerplate.
Advanced Level
Explain how Python's hash table works and why worst-case dict lookup is O(n).

Python dictionaries use open addressing with pseudo-random probing. When inserting a key, Python computes hash(key) % table_size to find a slot. If the slot is occupied (collision), Python probes other slots using a pseudo-random sequence until an empty slot is found. For lookup, the same process finds the key or confirms absence. With a good hash function and low load factor (Python maintains load factor < 2/3), collisions are rare and average lookup is O(1). However, if all keys hash to the same value (adversarial input or poor hash function), every lookup probes all n occupied slots — O(n) worst case. This is why Python randomizes hash seeds between runs (PYTHONHASHSEED).

# dataset_analyzer.py
# Comprehensive dataset analysis using all four core data structures
# Produces a full statistical report on any list-of-dict dataset

from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from typing import List, Dict, Any, Optional
import json


def analyze_dataset(records: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> Dict:
    """
    Analyze a dataset and produce comprehensive statistics.

    Args:
        records: List of dictionaries representing data records

    Returns:
        Dictionary containing full analysis results
    """
    if not records:
        return {"error": "Empty dataset"}

    total = len(records)
    all_keys = set()
    key_presence = Counter()
    type_distribution = defaultdict(Counter)
    value_distribution = defaultdict(Counter)
    numeric_stats = defaultdict(list)
    missing_by_field = defaultdict(int)

    # ── Pass 1: Collect all information ──────────────────────────
    for record in records:
        all_keys.update(record.keys())

        for key, value in record.items():
            key_presence[key] += 1

            # Track type distribution
            type_name = type(value).__name__
            type_distribution[key][type_name] += 1

            # Handle missing / None
            if value is None or value == "" or value == []:
                missing_by_field[key] += 1
                continue

            # Track value distribution for categorical fields
            if isinstance(value, (str, bool, int)) and not isinstance(value, bool):
                if isinstance(value, str) and len(value) < 50:
                    value_distribution[key][str(value)] += 1
                elif isinstance(value, int) and value < 1000:
                    value_distribution[key][str(value)] += 1

            # Collect numeric values
            if isinstance(value, (int, float)) and not isinstance(value, bool):
                numeric_stats[key].append(float(value))

    # ── Pass 2: Compute statistics ────────────────────────────────
    field_stats = {}
    for key in sorted(all_keys):
        present = key_presence[key]
        missing = total - present + missing_by_field.get(key, 0)

        stats = {
            "present": present,
            "missing": missing,
            "missing_pct": round(missing / total * 100, 2),
            "coverage": round(present / total * 100, 2),
            "types": dict(type_distribution[key]),
            "dominant_type": type_distribution[key].most_common(1)[0][0]
                             if type_distribution[key] else "unknown"
        }

        # Add numeric statistics if applicable
        if key in numeric_stats and numeric_stats[key]:
            values = numeric_stats[key]
            values_sorted = sorted(values)
            n = len(values)

            stats["numeric"] = {
                "count": n,
                "min": round(min(values), 6),
                "max": round(max(values), 6),
                "mean": round(sum(values) / n, 6),
                "median": round(values_sorted[n // 2], 6),
                "range": round(max(values) - min(values), 6),
                "std": round(
                    (sum((v - sum(values)/n)**2 for v in values) / n) ** 0.5,
                    6
                )
            }

        # Add top values for categorical fields
        if key in value_distribution and value_distribution[key]:
            top_values = value_distribution[key].most_common(5)
            stats["top_values"] = [
                {"value": v, "count": c,
                 "pct": round(c / total * 100, 1)}
                for v, c in top_values
            ]
            stats["unique_count"] = len(value_distribution[key])

        field_stats[key] = stats

    # ── Dataset-level summary ────────────────────────────────────
    complete_records = sum(
        1 for r in records
        if all(r.get(k) not in (None, "", []) for k in all_keys)
    )

    summary = {
        "total_records": total,
        "total_fields": len(all_keys),
        "complete_records": complete_records,
        "completeness": round(complete_records / total * 100, 2),
        "fields": sorted(all_keys)
    }

    return {"summary": summary, "fields": field_stats}


def print_analysis_report(analysis: Dict) -> None:
    """Print a formatted analysis report"""

    if "error" in analysis:
        print(f"Error: {analysis['error']}")
        return

    summary = analysis["summary"]
    fields = analysis["fields"]

    print("\n" + "═" * 65)
    print("  DATASET ANALYSIS REPORT")
    print("═" * 65)
    print(f"  Total Records:     {summary['total_records']:,}")
    print(f"  Total Fields:      {summary['total_fields']}")
    print(f"  Complete Records:  {summary['complete_records']:,} "
          f"({summary['completeness']}%)")
    print(f"  Fields: {', '.join(summary['fields'])}")

    print("\n" + "─" * 65)
    print("  FIELD-LEVEL ANALYSIS")
    print("─" * 65)

    for field_name, stats in fields.items():
        print(f"\n  📊 {field_name.upper()}")
        print(f"     Coverage:  {stats['coverage']}% "
              f"| Missing: {stats['missing']} ({stats['missing_pct']}%)")
        print(f"     Type:      {stats['dominant_type']} "
              f"| Types: {stats['types']}")

        if "numeric" in stats:
            num = stats["numeric"]
            print(f"     Range:     [{num['min']} → {num['max']}]")
            print(f"     Mean:      {num['mean']} | Median: {num['median']}")
            print(f"     Std Dev:   {num['std']}")

        if "top_values" in stats:
            print(f"     Unique:    {stats['unique_count']}")
            print(f"     Top values:")
            for item in stats["top_values"][:3]:
                bar = "█" * int(item["pct"] / 5)
                print(f"       {str(item['value']):<15} {item['count']:>4} "
                      f"({item['pct']:>5.1f}%) {bar}")

    print("\n" + "═" * 65)

Classes and Objects
The Core Concept
A class is a blueprint. An object (instance) is a concrete realization of that blueprint.

# The class is the blueprint

A Complete Class Example

import math
from typing import List, Optional


class Neuron:
    """
    Represents a single artificial neuron.

    This class demonstrates:
    - Instance attributes (unique per object)
    - Methods (behaviors)
    - Proper docstrings
    - Type hints
    """

    def __init__(self, num_inputs: int, activation: str = "relu"):
        """
        Initialize a neuron with random weights and zero bias.

        Args:
            num_inputs: Number of input connections
            activation: Activation function name
        """
        import random
        # Instance attributes — unique to each neuron object
        self.num_inputs = num_inputs
        self.activation = activation
        self.weights = [random.gauss(0, 1) * (2/num_inputs)**0.5
                        for _ in range(num_inputs)]
        self.bias = 0.0
        self.last_output = None   # Cache for backward pass

    def forward(self, inputs: List[float]) -> float:
        """
        Compute the neuron's output for given inputs.

        Args:
            inputs: List of input values

        Returns:
            Activated output value
        """
        if len(inputs) != self.num_inputs:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Expected {self.num_inputs} inputs, got {len(inputs)}"
            )

        # Weighted sum: z = w·x + b
        weighted_sum = sum(w * x for w, x in zip(self.weights, inputs))
        weighted_sum += self.bias

        # Apply activation
        output = self._apply_activation(weighted_sum)
        self.last_output = output
        return output

    def _apply_activation(self, z: float) -> float:
        """
        Apply the activation function.
        Leading underscore signals this is an internal method.
        """
        if self.activation == "relu":
            return max(0.0, z)
        elif self.activation == "sigmoid":
            return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-z))
        elif self.activation == "tanh":
            return math.tanh(z)
        elif self.activation == "linear":
            return z
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown activation: {self.activation}")

    def update_weights(self, gradients: List[float],
                       learning_rate: float = 0.01) -> None:
        """Update weights using gradient descent"""
        if len(gradients) != self.num_inputs:
            raise ValueError("Gradient size must match number of inputs")

        self.weights = [w - learning_rate * g
                        for w, g in zip(self.weights, gradients)]

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return (f"Neuron(inputs={self.num_inputs}, "
                f"activation='{self.activation}', "
                f"bias={self.bias:.4f})")

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"Neuron[{self.activation}]({self.num_inputs} inputs)"


# Creating and using neuron objects
neuron = Neuron(num_inputs=4, activation="relu")
print(neuron)                   # Neuron[relu](4 inputs)
print(repr(neuron))             # Full repr

output = neuron.forward([0.5, -0.3, 0.8, 0.2])
print(f"Output: {output:.4f}")

# Each neuron has independent weights
neuron2 = Neuron(num_inputs=4, activation="sigmoid")
print(neuron.weights == neuron2.weights)   # Almost certainly False
