# model_evaluation_viz.py
# A complete, reusable visualization suite for ML model evaluation
# Covers classification metrics, training curves, and feature analysis

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Tuple

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")


class ModelEvaluationVisualizer:
    """
    Complete visualization suite for evaluating ML model performance.
    Designed to be called after training to produce a standard report.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, model_name: str = "Model",
                 class_names: Optional[List[str]] = None,
                 figsize_scale: float = 1.0):
        self.model_name = model_name
        self.class_names = class_names
        self.figsize_scale = figsize_scale
        self.colors = sns.color_palette("colorblind")
    
    def plot_training_curves(self,
                             train_loss: List[float],
                             val_loss: List[float],
                             train_metric: Optional[List[float]] = None,
                             val_metric: Optional[List[float]] = None,
                             metric_name: str = "Accuracy") -> plt.Figure:
        """Plot training and validation curves with best-epoch annotation"""
        
        has_metric = train_metric is not None and val_metric is not None
        n_panels = 2 if has_metric else 1
        
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n_panels,
                                 figsize=(7*n_panels*self.figsize_scale, 5))
        if n_panels == 1:
            axes = [axes]
        
        epochs = np.arange(1, len(train_loss) + 1)
        
        # Loss panel
        axes[0].plot(epochs, train_loss, color=self.colors[0],
                    linewidth=2, label="Train")
        axes[0].plot(epochs, val_loss, color=self.colors[1],
                    linewidth=2, linestyle="--", label="Validation")
        
        best_epoch = np.argmin(val_loss) + 1
        best_loss = min(val_loss)
        axes[0].scatter([best_epoch], [best_loss], color="red", s=80,
                       zorder=5, label=f"Best (epoch {best_epoch})")
        axes[0].axvline(best_epoch, color="red", alpha=0.3, linestyle=":")
        
        axes[0].set_title(f"{self.model_name}: Loss Curves", fontweight="bold")
        axes[0].set_xlabel("Epoch")
        axes[0].set_ylabel("Loss")
        axes[0].legend()
        axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3)
        
        # Metric panel
        if has_metric:
            axes[1].plot(epochs, train_metric, color=self.colors[0],
                        linewidth=2, label="Train")
            axes[1].plot(epochs, val_metric, color=self.colors[1],
                        linewidth=2, linestyle="--", label="Validation")
            
            best_metric_epoch = np.argmax(val_metric) + 1
            best_metric_val = max(val_metric)
            axes[1].scatter([best_metric_epoch], [best_metric_val],
                           color="red", s=80, zorder=5)
            
            axes[1].set_title(f"{self.model_name}: {metric_name}", fontweight="bold")
            axes[1].set_xlabel("Epoch")
            axes[1].set_ylabel(metric_name)
            axes[1].legend()
            axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig
    
    def plot_confusion_matrix(self,
                              y_true: np.ndarray,
                              y_pred: np.ndarray,
                              normalize: bool = False) -> plt.Figure:
        """Plot confusion matrix with optional normalization"""
        
        classes = self.class_names or sorted(set(y_true) | set(y_pred))
        n_classes = len(classes)
        
        cm = np.zeros((n_classes, n_classes), dtype=int)
        class_to_idx = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(classes)}
        
        for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred):
            cm[class_to_idx[t], class_to_idx[p]] += 1
        
        if normalize:
            cm_display = cm.astype(float) / cm.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
            fmt = ".2%"
        else:
            cm_display = cm
            fmt = "d"
        
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6*self.figsize_scale, 5*self.figsize_scale))
        sns.heatmap(cm_display, annot=True, fmt=fmt, cmap="Blues",
                   xticklabels=classes, yticklabels=classes,
                   square=True, cbar_kws={"label": "Count" if not normalize else "Proportion"},
                   ax=ax)
        ax.set_xlabel("Predicted Label")
        ax.set_ylabel("True Label")
        ax.set_title(f"{self.model_name}: Confusion Matrix"
                    f"{' (Normalized)' if normalize else ''}", fontweight="bold")
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig
    
    def plot_roc_curve(self,
                       y_true: np.ndarray,
                       y_scores: np.ndarray) -> plt.Figure:
        """Plot ROC curve with AUC for binary classification"""
        
        # Manual ROC computation (no sklearn dependency)
        thresholds = np.sort(np.unique(y_scores))[::-1]
        tpr_list, fpr_list = [], []
        
        n_pos = np.sum(y_true == 1)
        n_neg = np.sum(y_true == 0)
        
        for thresh in thresholds:
            y_pred = (y_scores >= thresh).astype(int)
            tp = np.sum((y_pred == 1) & (y_true == 1))
            fp = np.sum((y_pred == 1) & (y_true == 0))
            tpr_list.append(tp / n_pos if n_pos > 0 else 0)
            fpr_list.append(fp / n_neg if n_neg > 0 else 0)
        
        tpr_arr = np.array([0] + tpr_list + [1])
        fpr_arr = np.array([0] + fpr_list + [1])
        
        # AUC via trapezoidal rule
        sorted_idx = np.argsort(fpr_arr)
        auc = np.trapz(tpr_arr[sorted_idx], fpr_arr[sorted_idx])
        
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6*self.figsize_scale, 6*self.figsize_scale))
        ax.plot(fpr_arr[sorted_idx], tpr_arr[sorted_idx],
               color=self.colors[0], linewidth=2.5,
               label=f"{self.model_name} (AUC = {auc:.3f})")
        ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", linestyle="--",
               linewidth=1.5, label="Random classifier")
        
        ax.fill_between(fpr_arr[sorted_idx], tpr_arr[sorted_idx],
                        alpha=0.1, color=self.colors[0])
        
        ax.set_xlabel("False Positive Rate")
        ax.set_ylabel("True Positive Rate")
        ax.set_title("ROC Curve", fontweight="bold")
        ax.legend(loc="lower right")
        ax.set_xlim(-0.02, 1.02)
        ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig
    
    def plot_feature_importance(self,
                                feature_names: List[str],
                                importances: List[float],
                                top_n: int = 15) -> plt.Figure:
        """Plot sorted feature importance"""
        
        sorted_pairs = sorted(zip(feature_names, importances),
                             key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:top_n]
        names, values = zip(*sorted_pairs)
        
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8*self.figsize_scale,
                                        max(4, len(names)*0.35)))
        
        colors = [self.colors[0] if v == max(values) else self.colors[2]
                 for v in values]
        
        y_pos = np.arange(len(names))
        ax.barh(y_pos, values, color=colors)
        ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
        ax.set_yticklabels(names)
        ax.invert_yaxis()
        ax.set_xlabel("Importance")
        ax.set_title(f"{self.model_name}: Top {top_n} Feature Importances",
                    fontweight="bold")
        
        for i, v in enumerate(values):
            ax.text(v + max(values)*0.01, i, f"{v:.3f}",
                   va="center", fontsize=9)
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig
    
    def plot_prediction_distribution(self,
                                     y_true: np.ndarray,
                                     y_scores: np.ndarray) -> plt.Figure:
        """Plot predicted probability distributions by true class"""
        
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8*self.figsize_scale, 5))
        
        df = pd.DataFrame({"true_label": y_true, "score": y_scores})
        
        for label in sorted(df["true_label"].unique()):
            subset = df[df["true_label"] == label]["score"]
            sns.kdeplot(subset, ax=ax, fill=True, alpha=0.4,
                       label=f"Class {label}")
        
        ax.set_xlabel("Predicted Probability")
        ax.set_ylabel("Density")
        ax.set_title(f"{self.model_name}: Prediction Distribution by True Class",
                    fontweight="bold")
        ax.legend()
        ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig
    
    def plot_calibration_curve(self,
                               y_true: np.ndarray,
                               y_scores: np.ndarray,
                               n_bins: int = 10) -> plt.Figure:
        """Plot calibration curve (reliability diagram)"""
        
        bins = np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)
        bin_indices = np.digitize(y_scores, bins) - 1
        bin_indices = np.clip(bin_indices, 0, n_bins - 1)
        
        bin_true_freq = []
        bin_pred_mean = []
        bin_counts = []
        
        for i in range(n_bins):
            mask = bin_indices == i
            if mask.sum() > 0:
                bin_true_freq.append(y_true[mask].mean())
                bin_pred_mean.append(y_scores[mask].mean())
                bin_counts.append(mask.sum())
        
        fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7*self.figsize_scale, 8),
                                       gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 1]},
                                       sharex=True)
        
        ax1.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color="gray", linestyle="--",
                label="Perfectly calibrated")
        ax1.plot(bin_pred_mean, bin_true_freq, marker="o",
                color=self.colors[0], linewidth=2, label=self.model_name)
        ax1.set_ylabel("Fraction of Positives")
        ax1.set_title(f"{self.model_name}: Calibration Curve", fontweight="bold")
        ax1.legend()
        ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
        
        ax2.bar(bin_pred_mean, bin_counts, width=0.08, color=self.colors[0], alpha=0.6)
        ax2.set_xlabel("Mean Predicted Probability")
        ax2.set_ylabel("Count")
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        return fig
    
    def generate_full_report(self,
                             y_true: np.ndarray,
                             y_pred: np.ndarray,
                             y_scores: Optional[np.ndarray] = None,
                             train_loss: Optional[List[float]] = None,
                             val_loss: Optional[List[float]] = None,
                             feature_names: Optional[List[str]] = None,
                             feature_importances: Optional[List[float]] = None,

Introduction

Modern AI engineering is API-driven. You call OpenAI's API to access GPT models. You call HuggingFace's Inference API to run hosted models. You call vector database APIs to store and search embeddings. You call your own model's API once it's deployed. Nearly every GenAI application is fundamentally a system of API calls orchestrated together.

Understanding APIs deeply — not just calling requests.get() but understanding status codes, authentication, retries, rate limits, and error handling — is what separates a fragile prototype from a production system. A RAG application that crashes the first time OpenAI returns a 429 rate limit error is not production-ready. This chapter builds that production-grade understanding.
What is an API and REST Architecture
Core Concepts

CLIENT (your Python code)              SERVER (e.g., api.openai.com)
        │                                        │
        │──────── HTTP Request ─────────────────▶│
        │  Method: POST                          │
        │  URL: /v1/chat/completions             │
        │  Headers: {Authorization: Bearer ...}  │
        │  Body: {"model": "gpt-4o", ...}        │
        │                                        │
        │◀─────── HTTP Response ─────────────────│
        │  Status: 200 OK                        │
        │  Body: {"choices": [...]}               │
        │                                        │
API (Application Programming Interface): a contract that allows two systems to communicate — typically over HTTP for web APIs.
REST (Representational State Transfer): an architectural style for APIs built on HTTP, using standard methods to operate on "resources" identified by URLs.
HTTP Methods

"""
GET     — Retrieve data (should not modify server state)
POST    — Create new data / submit data for processing
PUT     — Replace an existing resource entirely
PATCH   — Partially update an existing resource
DELETE  — Remove a resource

Examples in an ML context:
GET    /v1/models                    → List available models
POST   /v1/chat/completions          → Generate a completion
POST   /v1/embeddings                → Generate embeddings
GET    /v1/fine_tuning/jobs/{id}     → Check fine-tuning job status
DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}           → Delete an uploaded file
"""
HTTP Status Codes

"""
1xx — Informational (rarely seen directly)

2xx — Success
  200 OK              — Request succeeded
  201 Created         — Resource created successfully
  202 Accepted        — Request accepted for async processing
  204 No Content      — Success, but no response body

3xx — Redirection
  301 Moved Permanently
  304 Not Modified    — Cached version is still valid

4xx — Client Errors (YOUR request was wrong)
  400 Bad Request           — Malformed request
  401 Unauthorized          — Missing/invalid authentication
  403 Forbidden             — Authenticated but not allowed
  404 Not Found             — Resource doesn't exist
  409 Conflict               — Request conflicts with current state
  422 Unprocessable Entity  — Validation failed
  429 Too Many Requests    — Rate limit exceeded

5xx — Server Errors (THEIR system failed)
  500 Internal Server Error
  502 Bad Gateway
  503 Service Unavailable   — Server temporarily overloaded
  504 Gateway Timeout
"""

# Why this matters for ML engineers:
# 429 → implement exponential backoff and retry
# 401/403 → check API key configuration, don't retry blindly
# 500/503 → transient, safe to retry with backoff
# 400/422 → your request is malformed, retrying won't help — fix the request

def safe_api_call(url: str, **kwargs) -> dict:
    """
    Production pattern: always check status before parsing.
    """
    try:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=10, **kwargs)
        
        # raise_for_status() raises an exception for 4xx/5xx responses
        response.raise_for_status()
        
        return response.json()
    
    except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as e:
        print(f"HTTP error: {e.response.status_code} — {e.response.text[:200]}")
        raise
    
    except requests.exceptions.ConnectionError:
        print(f"Connection failed — check network or URL: {url}")
        raise
    
    except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
        print(f"Request timed out after 10s: {url}")
        raise
    
    except requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError:
        print(f"Response was not valid JSON: {response.text[:200]}")
        raise
    
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        print(f"Request failed: {e}")
        raise

OAuth 2.0 Flow (Conceptual Overview)

"""
OAuth 2.0 is used when an application needs to act on behalf of a user
(e.g., "Sign in with Google", accessing a user's Google Drive files).

Simplified Authorization Code Flow:

1. User clicks "Login with Provider" in your app
2. Your app redirects user to provider's authorization URL
3. User logs in and grants permission on the provider's site
4. Provider redirects back to your app with an authorization CODE
5. Your app exchanges the CODE for an ACCESS TOKEN (server-to-server)
6. Your app uses the ACCESS TOKEN in API requests
7. Access tokens expire — use REFRESH TOKEN to get a new one
"""

import requests

def exchange_code_for_token(auth_code: str,
                             client_id: str,
                             client_secret: str,
                             redirect_uri: str,
                             token_url: str) -> dict:
    """Step 5: Exchange authorization code for access token"""
    response = requests.post(token_url, data={
        "grant_type": "authorization_code",
        "code": auth_code,
        "client_id": client_id,
        "client_secret": client_secret,
        "redirect_uri": redirect_uri
    })
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()   # Contains access_token, refresh_token, expires_in


def refresh_access_token(refresh_token: str,
                         client_id: str,
                         client_secret: str,
                         token_url: str) -> dict:
    """Step 7: Get a new access token using the refresh token"""
    response = requests.post(token_url, data={
        "grant_type": "refresh_token",
        "refresh_token": refresh_token,
        "client_id": client_id,
        "client_secret": client_secret
    })
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()


class OAuthSession:
    """Manages an OAuth token lifecycle automatically"""
    
    def __init__(self, client_id: str, client_secret: str, token_url: str):
        self.client_id = client_id
        self.client_secret = client_secret
        self.token_url = token_url
        self.access_token = None
        self.refresh_token = None
        self.expires_at = 0
    
    def authenticate(self, auth_code: str, redirect_uri: str) -> None:
        token_data = exchange_code_for_token(
            auth_code, self.client_id, self.client_secret,
            redirect_uri, self.token_url
        )
        self._store_tokens(token_data)
    
    def _store_tokens(self, token_data: dict) -> None:
        import time
        self.access_token = token_data["access_token"]
        self.refresh_token = token_data.get("refresh_token", self.refresh_token)
        self.expires_at = time.time() + token_data.get("expires_in", 3600)
    
    def get_valid_token(self) -> str:
        """Returns a valid access token, refreshing if necessary"""
        import time
        if time.time() >= self.expires_at - 60:   # Refresh 60s before expiry
            token_data = refresh_access_token(
                self.refresh_token, self.client_id,
                self.client_secret, self.token_url
            )
            self._store_tokens(token_data)
        return self.access_token

Rate Limiting and Error Handling
Exponential Backoff with Retries

import time
import random
from functools import wraps
from typing import Callable, Type, Tuple


def retry_with_backoff(
    max_retries: int = 5,
    base_delay: float = 1.0,
    max_delay: float = 60.0,
    exceptions: Tuple[Type[Exception], ...] = (requests.exceptions.RequestException,)
) -> Callable:
    """
    Decorator implementing exponential backoff with jitter.
    Standard production pattern for API resilience.
    """
    def decorator(func: Callable) -> Callable:
        @wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            last_exception = None
            
            for attempt in range(max_retries):
                try:
                    return func(*args, **kwargs)
                
                except exceptions as e:
                    last_exception = e
                    
                    # Check if this is a retryable error
                    if isinstance(e, requests.exceptions.HTTPError):
                        status_code = e.response.status_code
                        
                        # Don't retry client errors (except 429)
                        if status_code in (400, 401, 403, 404, 422):
                            print(f"Non-retryable error ({status_code}): {e}")
                            raise
                        
                        # Respect Retry-After header for rate limits
                        if status_code == 429:
                            retry_after = e.response.headers.get("Retry-After")
                            if retry_after:
                                delay = float(retry_after)
                                print(f"Rate limited. Waiting {delay}s as instructed...")
                                time.sleep(delay)
                                continue
                    
                    if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                        print(f"Max retries ({max_retries}) exceeded")
                        raise
                    
                    # Exponential backoff with jitter
                    delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
                    jitter = random.uniform(0, delay * 0.1)
                    total_delay = delay + jitter
                    
                    print(f"Attempt {attempt + 1}/{max_retries} failed: {e}. "
                          f"Retrying in {total_delay:.2f}s...")
                    time.sleep(total_delay)
            
            raise last_exception
        
        return wrapper
    return decorator


@retry_with_backoff(max_retries=4, base_delay=1.0)
def fetch_with_retry(url: str) -> dict:
    """Example function with automatic retry on failure"""
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

Client-Side Rate Limiting

import time
from collections import deque
from threading import Lock


class RateLimiter:
    """
    Token bucket / sliding window rate limiter.
    Prevents YOUR client from exceeding API rate limits proactively,
    rather than reactively handling 429 errors.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, max_calls: int, period_seconds: float):
        self.max_calls = max_calls
        self.period = period_seconds
        self.call_times = deque()
        self.lock = Lock()
    
    def acquire(self) -> None:
        """Block until a call can be made within rate limits"""
        with self.lock:
            now = time.time()
            
            # Remove timestamps outside the current window
            while self.call_times and self.call_times[0] <= now - self.period:
                self.call_times.popleft()
            
            if len(self.call_times) >= self.max_calls:
                # Need to wait until the oldest call exits the window
                sleep_time = self.period - (now - self.call_times[0])
                if sleep_time > 0:
                    time.sleep(sleep_time)
                # Clean up again after waiting
                now = time.time()
                while self.call_times and self.call_times[0] <= now - self.period:
                    self.call_times.popleft()
            
            self.call_times.append(time.time())
    
    def __enter__(self):
        self.acquire()
        return self
    
    def __exit__(self, *args):
        pass


# Usage: limit to 10 calls per second
limiter = RateLimiter(max_calls=10, period_seconds=1.0)

def rate_limited_api_call(url: str) -> dict:
    with limiter:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()

class OpenAIClient(BaseAPIClient):
    """
    Production-ready OpenAI API client built on BaseAPIClient.
    Demonstrates a real-world LLM API integration pattern.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, api_key: Optional[str] = None):
        api_key = api_key or os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY")
        if not api_key:
            raise ValueError("OPENAI_API_KEY not found in environment")
        
        config = APIClientConfig(
            base_url="https://api.openai.com/v1",
            api_key=api_key,
            timeout=60.0,
            max_retries=3,
            rate_limit_calls=50,
            rate_limit_period=60.0
        )
        super().__init__(config)
    
    def chat_completion(self,
                        messages: List[Dict[str, str]],
                        model: str = "gpt-4o-mini",
                        temperature: float = 0.7,
                        max_tokens: Optional[int] = None,
                        **kwargs) -> Dict:
        """Send a chat completion request"""
        payload = {
            "model": model,
            "messages": messages,
            "temperature": temperature,
            **kwargs
        }
        if max_tokens:
            payload["max_tokens"] = max_tokens
        
        return self.post("chat/completions", json_data=payload)
    
    def get_completion_text(self, messages: List[Dict[str, str]],
                            **kwargs) -> str:
        """Convenience method: returns just the text response"""
        response = self.chat_completion(messages, **kwargs)
        return response["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
    
    def create_embedding(self, text: str,
                         model: str = "text-embedding-3-small") -> List[float]:
        """Generate an embedding vector for text"""
        response = self.post("embeddings", json_data={
            "model": model,
            "input": text
        })
        return response["data"][0]["embedding"]
    
    def create_embeddings_batch(self, texts: List[str],
                                model: str = "text-embedding-3-small") -> List[List[float]]:
        """Generate embeddings for multiple texts in one request (more efficient)"""
        response = self.post("embeddings", json_data={
            "model": model,
            "input": texts
        })
        # Results may not preserve order — sort by index to be safe
        sorted_data = sorted(response["data"], key=lambda x: x["index"])
        return [item["embedding"] for item in sorted_data]

"""
Some APIs use webhooks for long-running operations instead of polling.

POLLING pattern (simpler, used for fine-tuning jobs, batch jobs):
"""

def poll_until_complete(client: BaseAPIClient,
                        job_id: str,
                        poll_interval: float = 5.0,
                        max_wait: float = 600.0) -> Dict:
    """Poll a long-running job until it completes"""
    start_time = time.time()
    
    while time.time() - start_time < max_wait:
        job_status = client.get(f"jobs/{job_id}")
        
        status = job_status.get("status")
        print(f"Job {job_id}: {status}")
        
        if status in ("completed", "succeeded"):
            return job_status
        if status in ("failed", "cancelled"):
            raise APIError(f"Job {job_id} ended with status: {status}")
        
        time.sleep(poll_interval)
    
    raise TimeoutError(f"Job {job_id} did not complete within {max_wait}s")


"""
WEBHOOK pattern (more efficient, requires a publicly accessible endpoint):

1. Your app registers a webhook URL with the API provider
2. Your app starts a long-running job and gets back a job ID
3. The provider calls YOUR webhook URL when the job completes
4. Your webhook handler (a small web server) processes the notification

This requires running a web server (FastAPI/Flask) to receive callbacks —
covered in depth in Part 12 (MLOps & Deployment).
"""

Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between GET and POST requests?

GET retrieves data and should not modify server state — parameters are typically passed in the URL query string, and GET requests can be cached and are idempotent (calling it multiple times has the same effect as calling it once). POST submits data to create a resource or trigger processing — parameters go in the request body, POST requests are not idempotent by default (calling twice may create two resources), and POST responses are generally not cached.
What does a 429 status code mean and how should you handle it?

429 "Too Many Requests" means you have exceeded the API's rate limit. The correct handling is to check for a Retry-After header (which tells you how many seconds to wait) and pause before retrying, ideally with exponential backoff if no header is present. You should never retry immediately in a tight loop, as this worsens the situation and may lead to your API key being temporarily or permanently blocked.
Why should API keys never be hardcoded in source code?

Hardcoded keys get committed to version control history permanently — even if removed in a later commit, they remain accessible in the git history and can be extracted by anyone with repository access, including in public repositories where automated bots actively scan for leaked credentials. The correct practice is to store keys in environment variables or secret management systems, loaded at runtime, with the actual .env file or secrets excluded via .gitignore.
Intermediate Level
Explain exponential backoff and why jitter is added to it.

Exponential backoff increases the wait time between retries exponentially (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) rather than retrying immediately or at a fixed interval. This gives a struggling server time to recover and reduces load during outages. Jitter adds a small random amount to each delay to prevent the "thundering herd" problem — if many clients all failed at the same moment and all retry using the exact same backoff schedule, they will all hit the server simultaneously again at each retry attempt, effectively synchronizing their retries into repeated traffic spikes. Random jitter spreads out these retries.
What is the difference between client-side rate limiting and handling 429 responses reactively?

Reactive handling waits for the server to reject a request with 429, then backs off — this wastes a request attempt and risks the API provider flagging excessive violations. Proactive client-side rate limiting (e.g., a token bucket or sliding window limiter) tracks your own request history and deliberately paces requests to stay under the known limit before sending them, preventing 429 errors from occurring in the first place. Production systems typically use both: proactive limiting as the primary defense, with reactive backoff as a safety net for unexpected limit changes or shared-quota scenarios.
How would you design an API client to handle both transient and permanent failures differently?

Classify errors by type: 5xx server errors, timeouts, and connection errors are transient and should be retried with exponential backoff, since the same request will likely succeed once the underlying issue resolves. 4xx client errors (except 429) — like 400 Bad Request or 422 Validation Error — are permanent for that exact request because the request itself is malformed; retrying without modification will fail identically every time. 401/403 authentication errors should not be retried blindly either, since retrying with the same invalid credentials will never succeed — instead, trigger a credential refresh flow if available, or fail immediately with a clear error pointing to configuration. This classification logic should live centrally in the API client's error handling, not scattered across calling code.
Advanced Level
Design a resilient batch processing system for sending thousands of requests to an LLM API with rate limits.

Use an async architecture with asyncio and a Semaphore to limit concurrent in-flight requests to a safe number below the provider's concurrent connection limit. Implement a token bucket rate limiter that tracks both request-per-minute AND token-per-minute limits (LLM APIs often have both). Queue requests with priority levels if some are more time-sensitive. Implement per-request retry with exponential backoff and jitter, capped at a reasonable max attempt count, with permanently failed requests written to a dead-letter file for later inspection rather than blocking the entire batch. Track and log token usage and costs in real time. Implement checkpointing so that if the batch process crashes partway through, it can resume from where it left off rather than reprocessing already-completed requests — this is typically done by writing completed results to a JSONL file incrementally and checking on resume which IDs are already present.

# A complete, production-grade gateway for calling LLM APIs
# Combines: authentication, retries, rate limiting, caching,
# cost tracking, and multi-provider fallback

import time
import json
import hashlib
import logging
from pathlib import Path
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional, Dict, List, Callable, Any
from enum import Enum
from collections import deque
from threading import Lock

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s | %(levelname)s | %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger("llm_gateway")


# ── Enums and Data Classes ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class ProviderStatus(Enum):
    HEALTHY = "healthy"
    DEGRADED = "degraded"
    DOWN = "down"


@dataclass
class LLMRequest:
    messages: List[Dict[str, str]]
    model: str
    temperature: float = 0.7
    max_tokens: Optional[int] = None
    
    def cache_key(self) -> str:
        """Generate a deterministic cache key for this request"""
        payload = json.dumps({
            "messages": self.messages,
            "model": self.model,
            "temperature": self.temperature,
            "max_tokens": self.max_tokens
        }, sort_keys=True)
        return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()


@dataclass
class LLMResponse:
    text: str
    provider: str
    model: str
    input_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int
    latency_ms: float
    cached: bool = False
    
    @property
    def total_tokens(self) -> int:
        return self.input_tokens + self.output_tokens


@dataclass
class ProviderConfig:
    name: str
    cost_per_1k_input: float
    cost_per_1k_output: float
    max_retries: int = 3
    rate_limit_rpm: int = 60   # requests per minute


# ── Rate Limiter ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class TokenBucketLimiter:
    """Thread-safe sliding-window rate limiter"""
    
    def __init__(self, max_calls: int, period_seconds: float = 60.0):
        self.max_calls = max_calls
        self.period = period_seconds
        self._calls = deque()
        self._lock = Lock()
    
    def acquire(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            now = time.time()
            while self._calls and self._calls[0] <= now - self.period:
                self._calls.popleft()
            
            if len(self._calls) >= self.max_calls:
                wait = self.period - (now - self._calls[0])
                if wait > 0:
                    logger.debug(f"Rate limiting: sleeping {wait:.2f}s")
                    time.sleep(wait)
            
            self._calls.append(time.time())
    
    def current_usage(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            now = time.time()
            while self._calls and self._calls[0] <= now - self.period:
                self._calls.popleft()
            return len(self._calls)


# ── Response Cache ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class ResponseCache:
    """Simple file-based cache for LLM responses (avoids redundant API costs)"""
    
    def __init__(self, cache_dir: str = ".llm_cache", ttl_seconds: float = 3600):
        self.cache_dir = Path(cache_dir)
        self.cache_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        self.ttl = ttl_seconds
        self._memory_cache: Dict[str, tuple] = {}   # key -> (response, timestamp)
    
    def get(self, key: str) -> Optional[LLMResponse]:
        # Check memory cache first (fastest)
        if key in self._memory_cache:
            response, timestamp = self._memory_cache[key]
            if time.time() - timestamp < self.ttl:
                return response
            del self._memory_cache[key]
        
        # Check disk cache
        cache_file = self.cache_dir / f"{key}.json"
        if cache_file.exists():
            age = time.time() - cache_file.stat().st_mtime
            if age < self.ttl:
                with open(cache_file, "r") as f:
                    data = json.load(f)
                response = LLMResponse(**data, cached=True)
                self._memory_cache[key] = (response, time.time())
                return response
            else:
                cache_file.unlink()   # Expired
        
        return None
    
    def set(self, key: str, response: LLMResponse) -> None:
        self._memory_cache[key] = (response, time.time())
        
        cache_file = self.cache_dir / f"{key}.json"
        data = {
            "text": response.text,
            "provider": response.provider,
            "model": response.model,
            "input_tokens": response.input_tokens,
            "output_tokens": response.output_tokens,
            "latency_ms": response.latency_ms
        }
        with open(cache_file, "w") as f:
            json.dump(data, f)


# ── Cost Tracker ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class CostTracker:
    """Tracks API usage and costs across providers"""
    
    def __init__(self, log_file: str = "llm_usage.jsonl"):
        self.log_file = log_file
        self.total_cost = 0.0
        self.total_calls = 0
        self.provider_costs: Dict[str, float] = {}
    
    def record(self, response: LLMResponse, config: ProviderConfig) -> float:
        if response.cached:
            cost = 0.0   # Cached responses cost nothing
        else:
            cost = (
                (response.input_tokens / 1000) * config.cost_per_1k_input +
                (response.output_tokens / 1000) * config.cost_per_1k_output
            )
        
        self.total_cost += cost
        self.total_calls += 1
        self.provider_costs[response.provider] = (
            self.provider_costs.get(response.provider, 0) + cost
        )
        
        record = {
            "timestamp": time.time(),
            "provider": response.provider,
            "model": response.model,
            "input_tokens": response.input_tokens,
            "output_tokens": response.output_tokens,
            "cost": round(cost, 6),
            "cached": response.cached,
            "latency_ms": response.latency_ms
        }
        
        with open(self.log_file, "a") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")
        
        return cost
    
    def summary(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "total_calls": self.total_calls,
            "total_cost_usd": round(self.total_cost, 4),
            "cost_by_provider": {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in self.provider_costs.items()},
            "avg_cost_per_call": round(self.total_cost / max(self.total_calls, 1), 6)
        }


# ── Mock Providers (simulating real API behavior) ────────────────────────────

class MockLLMProvider:
    """
    Simulates an LLM API provider with realistic behavior:
    occasional failures, rate limits, and variable latency.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, config: ProviderConfig, failure_rate: float = 0.1):
        self.config = config
        self.failure_rate = failure_rate
        self.status = ProviderStatus.HEALTHY
        self._consecutive_failures = 0
        self.limiter = TokenBucketLimiter(config.rate_limit_rpm, 60.0)
    
    def call(self, request: LLMRequest) -> LLMResponse:
        import random
        
        self.limiter.acquire()
        
        start = time.perf_counter()
        
        # Simulate occasional failures
        if random.random() < self.failure_rate:
            self._consecutive_failures += 1
            if self._consecutive_failures >= 3:
                self.status = ProviderStatus.DEGRADED
            raise ConnectionError(f"{self.config.name}: simulated transient failure")
        
        self._consecutive_failures = 0
        self.status = ProviderStatus.HEALTHY
        
        # Simulate processing time
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0.05, 0.2))
        
        input_text = " ".join(m["content"] for m in request.messages)
        input_tokens = len(input_text.split()) * 2   # Rough approximation
        output_text = f"[{self.config.name} response to: {input_text[:50]}...]"
        output_tokens = len(output_text.split()) * 2
        
        latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
        
        return LLMResponse(
            text=output_text,
            provider=self.config.name,
            model=request.model,
            input_tokens=input_tokens,
            output_tokens=output_tokens,
            latency_ms=latency_ms
        )


# ── Circuit Breaker ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class CircuitBreaker:
    """Prevents repeated calls to a failing provider"""
    
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold: int = 3, recovery_timeout: float = 10.0):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.failures = 0
        self.opened_at: Optional[float] = None
    
    def is_open(self) -> bool:
        if self.opened_at is None:
            return False
        if time.time() - self.opened_at >= self.recovery_timeout:
            logger.info("Circuit breaker entering half-open state (trial allowed)")
            return False
        return True
    
    def record_success(self) -> None:
        self.failures = 0
        self.opened_at = None
    
    def record_failure(self) -> None:
        self.failures += 1
        if self.failures >= self.failure_threshold and self.opened_at is None:
            self.opened_at = time.time()
            logger.warning(f"Circuit breaker OPENED after {self.failures} failures")


# ── Main Gateway ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class LLMGateway:
    """
    Production-grade gateway for LLM API calls.
    Handles: caching, multi-provider fallback, circuit breaking,
    cost tracking, and retries — all transparently.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, providers: List[tuple],
                 cache_enabled: bool = True,
                 cache_ttl: float = 3600):
        """
        providers: list of (MockLLMProvider, priority) tuples,
                   ordered by preference (first = primary)
        """
        self.providers = providers
        self.circuit_breakers = {
            provider.config.name: CircuitBreaker()
            for provider, _ in providers
        }
        self.cache = ResponseCache(ttl_seconds=cache_ttl) if cache_enabled else None
        self.cost_tracker = CostTracker()
    
    def call(self, request: LLMRequest) -> LLMResponse:
        """
        Execute an LLM request with full resilience:
        1. Check cache
        2. Try each provider in priority order
        3. Skip providers with open circuit breakers
        4. Track cost and log the result
        """
        
        # Step 1: Check cache
        if self.cache:
            cache_key = request.cache_key()
            cached_response = self.cache.get(cache_key)
            if cached_response:
                logger.info(f"Cache HIT for request to {request.model}")
                return cached_response
        
        # Step 2: Try providers in order
        last_error = None
        
        for provider, config in self.providers:
            breaker = self.circuit_breakers[config.name]
            
            if breaker.is_open():
                logger.info(f"Skipping {config.name}: circuit breaker open")
                continue
            
            try:
                logger.info(f"Trying provider: {config.name}")
                response = self._call_with_retry(provider, request, config)
                
                breaker.record_success()
                
                # Step 3: Cache successful response
                if self.cache:
                    self.cache.set(request.cache_key(), response)
                
                # Step 4: Track cost
                cost = self.cost_tracker.record(response, config)
                logger.info(f"Success via {config.name} | "
                          f"tokens={response.total_tokens} | "
                          f"cost=${cost:.6f} | "
                          f"latency={response.latency_ms:.1f}ms")
                
                return response
            
            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning(f"{config.name} failed: {e}")
                breaker.record_failure()
                last_error = e
                continue
        
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"All providers failed or unavailable. Last error: {last_error}"
        )
    
    def _call_with_retry(self, provider: MockLLMProvider,
                         request: LLMRequest,
                         config: ProviderConfig) -> LLMResponse:
        """Retry logic for a single provider"""
        last_error = None
        
        for attempt in range(config.max_retries):
            try:
                return provider.call(request)
            except Exception as e:
                last_error = e
                if attempt < config.max_retries - 1:
                    wait = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.debug(f"{config.name} attempt {attempt+1} failed, "
                                f"retrying in {wait}s")
                    time.sleep(wait)
        
        raise last_error
    
    def get_stats(self) -> Dict:
        """Get gateway statistics"""
        return {
            "cost_summary": self.cost_tracker.summary(),
            "circuit_breaker_states": {
                name: "OPEN" if cb.is_open() else "CLOSED"
                for name, cb in self.circuit_breakers.items()
            }
        }

Chapter Summary
REST APIs use HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) on resource URLs, with status codes communicating success (2xx), client errors (4xx), and server errors (5xx)
Always set explicit timeout values and call raise_for_status() to fail fast and clearly on errors
Store credentials in environment variables or .env files — never hardcode API keys in source code
429 (rate limit) errors should be handled with exponential backoff and respect for Retry-After headers; 4xx client errors generally should not be retried unmodified
Proactive client-side rate limiting (token bucket / sliding window) prevents hitting limits rather than just reacting to them
A production API client should centralize error classification, retry logic, and authentication in a reusable base class
Cache deterministic API responses (especially for LLM calls) to reduce cost and latency on repeated requests
Circuit breakers stop calling a failing service temporarily, preventing wasted retries and cascading failures
Multi-provider fallback patterns increase resilience for critical LLM-dependent applications
Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations (like payment or resource creation) when retrying

session.get(url)

# Environment variables for secrets
api_key = os.environ.get("API_KEY")

# Retry with exponential backoff (manual pattern)
for attempt in range(max_retries):
    try:
        response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
        response.raise_for_status()
        break
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException:
        time.sleep(2 ** attempt)

# Status code categories
# 2xx success | 4xx your error (don't retry except 429) | 5xx their error (retry)
Revision Notes
GET = read (idempotent, cacheable); POST = create/process (not idempotent by default)
429 = rate limited → backoff + respect Retry-After; 401/403 = auth issue → don't blindly retry
Always: timeout=, raise_for_status(), never hardcode keys
requests.Session() reuses TCP connections — use for multiple calls to the same host
Exponential backoff + jitter prevents thundering herd on retries
Client-side rate limiting (proactive) > reactive 429 handling alone
Circuit breaker: stop calling a failing service for a cooldown period, then allow a trial request
Cache deterministic LLM responses by hashing the full request payload
Idempotency keys make retries of resource-creating POST requests safe

Introduction

Version control is non-negotiable in professional software engineering, and AI/ML work is no exception — arguably it matters even more, because ML projects involve not just code but data, models, configurations, and experiments that all evolve together. A model that performed well last week and poorly today is often explained by an undocumented code change, a silently swapped dataset, or a hyperparameter nobody wrote down.

Beyond protecting your work, your GitHub profile is the single most important artifact recruiters and hiring managers look at when evaluating AI/ML candidates. A clean, well-documented, active GitHub profile with real projects often matters more than a resume line. This chapter teaches you Git as a tool and GitHub as a career asset.
Why Version Control Matters for AI/ML

TRADITIONAL SOFTWARE              ML PROJECTS
─────────────────────             ─────────────────────────────
Track code changes                Track code changes
                                   + Track data versions
                                   + Track model versions
                                   + Track experiment configs
                                   + Track hyperparameters
                                   + Reproduce exact training runs
                                   + Collaborate on notebooks (hard!)
 """
Common ML disasters that version control (done right) prevents:

1. "It worked yesterday" — someone changed preprocessing code without
   committing, and now results aren't reproducible

2. "Which model is in production?" — no tag/commit links the deployed
   model artifact to the exact code that trained it

3. "Why did accuracy drop?" — a teammate silently changed a hyperparameter
   in a shared config file, no record of who or why

4. "I can't reproduce the paper's result" — the exact commit, data version,
   and random seed used for a reported number were never recorded

5. Notebook chaos — five different versions of "final_model_v2_REAL.ipynb"
   floating around with no clear lineage

Merging

# Merge feature branch into main

git merge feature/add-attention-mechanism

# Fast-forward merge (when main hasn't diverged) — clean, linear history
# Merge commit (when both branches have new commits) — preserves branch history

# Abort a merge if conflicts are too messy to resolve right now
git merge --abort
Resolving Merge Conflicts

# When Git cannot automatically merge changes, it marks conflicts in the file:
 # Example conflict markers in a file:
def compute_loss(predictions, targets):
<<<<<<< HEAD
    return cross_entropy_loss(predictions, targets)
=======
    return focal_loss(predictions, targets, gamma=2.0)
>>>>>>> experiment/try-focal-loss
 # Resolution process:
# 1. Open the file, find <<<<<<< markers
# 2. Decide which version to keep (or combine both)
# 3. Remove the conflict markers entirely
# 4. Stage the resolved file
# 5. Complete the merge with a commit

git add resolved_file.py
git commit -m "merge: resolve conflict, keep focal loss implementation"

# Tools to help with conflicts
git mergetool                    # Opens configured merge tool
# VS Code has excellent built-in merge conflict UI — strongly recommended
Rebasing (Alternative to Merging)

# Rebase replays your branch's commits on top of the latest main
# Produces a CLEANER, LINEAR history (no merge commits)

git switch feature/my-feature
git rebase main

# Interactive rebase — clean up commit history before opening a PR
git rebase -i HEAD~3       # Interactively edit the last 3 commits

# In the interactive editor, you can:
# pick   — keep commit as-is
# reword — keep commit, edit message
# squash — combine with previous commit
# drop   — remove commit entirely

"""
RULE OF THUMB:
- Merge: when working on shared/public branches (preserves true history)
- Rebase: when cleaning up YOUR OWN local feature branch before sharing
- NEVER rebase a branch that others have already pulled and built upon
  (it rewrites commit hashes, causing painful conflicts for collaborators)
"""
Stashing — Temporary Storage

# Save uncommitted changes temporarily without committing
git stash                          # Stash all changes
git stash save "WIP: trying new optimizer"

git stash pop                      # Apply and remove the most recent stash
git stash apply                    # Apply but KEEP the stash (can apply again later)
git stash drop                     # Delete a stash without applying

git stash
git switch main
# ... fix urgent issue, commit, push ...

git stash pop                       # Resume exactly where you left off

"""
AS A REVIEWER, look for:

1. Correctness — does the code do what it claims?
2. Edge cases — empty inputs, None values, very large/small numbers
3. Test coverage — are the important paths actually tested?
4. Reproducibility — are random seeds set? Is the experiment documented?

   fitting in any way? (extremely common and serious ML-specific bug)

8. Performance — any obvious O(n²) operations on large datasets?

2. Respond to every comment (even just "Good catch, fixed in abc123")
3. If you disagree, explain your reasoning rather than just reverting
4. Thank reviewers for their time — it's a gift, not an obligation
"""

jobs:

      matrix:

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Set up Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:

        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pip
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-pip-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}
      
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install -r requirements.txt
          pip install pytest pytest-cov flake8

        run: |
          flake8 src/ --max-line-length=100 --extend-ignore=E203
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: |
          pytest tests/ --cov=src --cov-report=xml -v
      
      - name: Upload coverage report

 # scripts/validate_model.py — example referenced by the workflow above
"""
A simple model validation gate.
Fails the CI pipeline if model performance drops below an acceptable threshold,
preventing regressions from reaching production.
"""
import argparse
import sys
import json

def validate_model(min_accuracy: float) -> bool:
    with open("model_metrics.json") as f:
        metrics = json.load(f)
    
    accuracy = metrics.get("accuracy", 0.0)
    print(f"Model accuracy: {accuracy:.4f} (threshold: {min_accuracy})")
    
    if accuracy < min_accuracy:
        print(f"FAILED: Model accuracy {accuracy:.4f} below threshold {min_accuracy}")
        return False
    
    print("PASSED: Model meets performance threshold")
    return True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--min-accuracy", type=float, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    success = validate_model(args.min_accuracy)
    sys.exit(0 if success else 1)

git add model_checkpoint_500MB.pt
git add __pycache__/
git add .ipynb_checkpoints/

# CORRECT — set up .gitignore BEFORE your first commit
Vague or Missing Commit Messages

# WRONG
git commit -m "stuff"
git commit -m "wip"

# CORRECT — even quick commits should explain WHAT and ideally WHY
git commit -m "wip: scaffold RAG pipeline, embeddings not yet connected"
Force Pushing to Shared Branches

# DANGEROUS on shared branches — destroys teammates' work silently
git push --force origin main

# If you must force push (e.g., after an interactive rebase on YOUR
# OWN feature branch that only you use), use the safer variant:
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/my-branch
# This fails safely if someone else pushed commits you don't have locally
Working Directly on main

# WRONG — no safety net, can't easily abandon bad experiments
git switch main
# ... make changes directly ...
git commit -m "try new approach"

# CORRECT — always branch first, even for "quick" changes
git switch -c experiment/quick-test
# ... make changes ...
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

git fetch downloads new commits and branches from the remote repository but does NOT integrate them into your current branch — it lets you inspect what changed before deciding to merge. git pull is essentially git fetch followed immediately by git merge, automatically integrating remote changes into your current branch. git fetch is the safer choice when you want to review incoming changes first.
What is the difference between git add and git commit?

git add moves changes from the working directory into the "staging area" — a preparation zone where you build up exactly what will go into the next commit. git commit takes everything currently staged and permanently records it as a new snapshot in the repository's history, along with a message describing the change. This two-step process lets you commit only some of your changes, even if multiple files were modified.
What does .gitignore do and why is it especially important for ML projects?

.gitignore lists file patterns that Git should never track or stage, even if they exist in the working directory. It's especially critical for ML projects because datasets, model checkpoints, and experiment logs can be gigabytes in size — committing them would bloat the repository permanently (since Git history is largely immutable) and make every clone slow. It also prevents accidentally committing .env files containing API keys and secrets.
Intermediate Level
Explain the difference between merging and rebasing, and when you would use each.

Merging combines two branches' histories by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents, preserving the exact history of when and how branches diverged and reconverged. Rebasing takes your branch's commits and replays them one-by-one on top of the target branch's latest state, producing a clean, linear history as if you had branched off more recently — but it rewrites commit hashes. Use merging for integrating shared/public branches (preserves true collaborative history). Use rebasing to clean up your own local feature branch before opening a PR, making the history easier to read. Never rebase a branch that others have already pulled, since it creates painful conflicts when their local history diverges from the rewritten remote history.
How would you remove a sensitive file (like an API key) that was committed several commits ago?

Simply deleting the file in a new commit does NOT remove it from history — anyone can still find it by checking out the earlier commit. You need history-rewriting tools: git filter-repo (the modern recommended tool) or BFG Repo-Cleaner can scan the entire history and strip the file/content from every commit. After rewriting history, you must force-push (coordinating carefully with any collaborators, since this changes commit hashes for everyone). Critically, the leaked credential must also be rotated/invalidated at the source immediately — rewriting Git history doesn't undo any damage already done by the exposure, especially if the repository was ever public or forked.
What is the purpose of a feature branch workflow, and how does it specifically benefit ML experimentation?

A feature branch workflow isolates work-in-progress from the stable main branch, so main always represents a known-good, deployable state. For ML specifically, this means failed experiments — which are common and expected in ML research — never destabilize the working codebase. An engineer can freely try a risky architecture change or new hyperparameter sweep on an experiment/ branch; if it doesn't pan out, the branch is simply abandoned or deleted with zero impact on main. If it succeeds, it goes through review and merges cleanly, with the commit history documenting exactly what was tried and why.
Advanced Level
Design a Git-based workflow for a team running dozens of ML experiments per week, where many experiments fail and only a few succeed.

Use short-lived experiment/<descriptive-name> branches for every individual experiment, created from the latest main. Require that each experiment branch's final commit message include the key results (metrics achieved, configuration used) even if the experiment ultimately fails, creating a searchable history of what's been tried (git log --all --grep="focal loss" becomes a literature review of past attempts). Pair this with an experiment tracking tool (MLflow, Weights & Biases) that logs the exact git commit hash alongside metrics, so any historical run can be traced back to its exact code. Failed experiment branches can be deleted after a retention period (e.g., 30 days) to avoid branch clutter, while successful ones go through PR review and merge into main, with squashed commits to keep main's history clean and meaningful. Tag commits that correspond to production model deployments (git tag model-v2.3-prod) for instant traceability between a deployed artifact and its exact source code.

# experiment_git_tracker.py
# Demonstrates integrating Git metadata directly into ML experiment tracking
# This pattern ensures every experiment result is traceable to exact code

import subprocess
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, Optional, List


def run_git_command(args: List[str]) -> str:
    """Run a git command and return its output, or empty string on failure"""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["git"] + args,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True
        )
        return result.stdout.strip()
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, FileNotFoundError):
        return ""


@dataclass
class GitMetadata:
    """Captures the exact state of the repository at experiment time"""
    commit_hash: str
    branch_name: str
    is_dirty: bool          # True if there are uncommitted changes
    uncommitted_files: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    remote_url: str = ""
    commit_message: str = ""
    author: str = ""
    
    @classmethod
    def capture(cls) -> "GitMetadata":
        """Capture current git state — call this at the start of every experiment"""
        commit_hash = run_git_command(["rev-parse", "HEAD"]) or "no-git-repo"
        branch_name = run_git_command(["rev-parse", "--abbrev-ref", "HEAD"]) or "unknown"
        status_output = run_git_command(["status", "--porcelain"])
        is_dirty = bool(status_output)
        uncommitted_files = [
            line[3:].strip() for line in status_output.splitlines()
        ] if status_output else []
        remote_url = run_git_command(["config", "--get", "remote.origin.url"])
        commit_message = run_git_command(["log", "-1", "--pretty=%s"])
        author = run_git_command(["log", "-1", "--pretty=%an"])
        
        return cls(
            commit_hash=commit_hash,
            branch_name=branch_name,
            is_dirty=is_dirty,
            uncommitted_files=uncommitted_files,
            remote_url=remote_url,
            commit_message=commit_message,
            author=author
        )
    
    def to_dict(self) -> Dict:
        return {
            "commit_hash": self.commit_hash,
            "commit_hash_short": self.commit_hash[:8] if len(self.commit_hash) >= 8 else self.commit_hash,
            "branch": self.branch_name,
            "is_dirty": self.is_dirty,
            "uncommitted_files": self.uncommitted_files,
            "remote_url": self.remote_url,
            "commit_message": self.commit_message,
            "author": self.author
        }
    
    def warn_if_dirty(self) -> None:
        """Print a warning if there are uncommitted changes — results may not be reproducible"""
        if self.is_dirty:
            print("⚠️  WARNING: Uncommitted changes detected!")
            print("    This experiment's results may NOT be reproducible from git history alone.")
            print(f"    Uncommitted files: {self.uncommitted_files}")
            print("    Consider committing your changes before running important experiments.")


class GitAwareExperimentTracker:
    """
    Experiment tracker that automatically links every run to its
    exact git commit, branch, and dirty-state — solving the
    'which code produced this result?' problem permanently.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, log_dir: str = "experiments"):
        self.log_dir = Path(log_dir)
        self.log_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)
        self.log_file = self.log_dir / "experiment_log.jsonl"
    
    def run_experiment(self,
                       name: str,
                       config: Dict,
                       train_fn,
                       warn_on_dirty: bool = True) -> Dict:
        """
        Run an experiment with automatic git tracking.
        
        train_fn should be a callable that takes config and returns
        a metrics dictionary.
        """
        git_metadata = GitMetadata.capture()
        
        if warn_on_dirty:
            git_metadata.warn_if_dirty()
        
        print(f"\n{'='*60}")
        print(f"  EXPERIMENT: {name}")
        print(f"{'='*60}")
        print(f"  Branch: {git_metadata.branch_name}")
        print(f"  Commit: {git_metadata.commit_hash[:8]}")
        print(f"  Config: {config}")
        
        start_time = time.time()
        
        try:
            metrics = train_fn(config)
            status = "completed"
            error = None
        except Exception as e:
            metrics = {}
            status = "failed"
            error = str(e)
            print(f"  ERROR: {error}")
        
        duration = time.time() - start_time
        
        record = {
            "experiment_name": name,
            "timestamp": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"),
            "status": status,
            "error": error,
            "duration_seconds": round(duration, 2),
            "config": config,
            "metrics": metrics,
            "git": git_metadata.to_dict()
        }
        
        with open(self.log_file, "a") as f:
            f.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")
        
        print(f"  Status: {status} ({duration:.2f}s)")
        if metrics:
            for key, value in metrics.items():
                print(f"  {key}: {value}")
        print(f"{'='*60}\n")
        
        return record
    
    def get_history(self, name_filter: Optional[str] = None) -> List[Dict]:
        """Load all experiment history, optionally filtered by name"""
        if not self.log_file.exists():
            return []
        
        records = []
        with open(self.log_file, "r") as f:
            for line in f:
                record = json.loads(line)
                if name_filter is None or name_filter in record["experiment_name"]:
                    records.append(record)
        return records
    
    def find_best_run(self, metric_name: str,
                      mode: str = "max") -> Optional[Dict]:
        """Find the best historical run by a given metric"""
        history = self.get_history()
        valid_runs = [
            r for r in history
            if r["status"] == "completed" and metric_name in r["metrics"]
        ]
        
        if not valid_runs:
            return None
        
        key_fn = lambda r: r["metrics"][metric_name]
        return (max(valid_runs, key=key_fn) if mode == "max"
                else min(valid_runs, key=key_fn))
    
    def reproduce_command(self, record: Dict) -> str:
        """
        Generate the exact git command to checkout the code
        used for a specific historical experiment.
        """
        commit = record["git"]["commit_hash"]
        return f"git checkout {commit}  # Reproduces: {record['experiment_name']}"
    
    def print_summary_table(self, metric_name: str = "accuracy") -> None:
        """Print a clean summary of all experiments"""
        history = self.get_history()
        
        print(f"\n{'Experiment':<25} {'Branch':<20} {'Commit':<10} "
              f"{'Status':<10} {metric_name:<12}")
        print("-" * 80)
        
        for record in history:
            metric_val = record["metrics"].get(metric_name, "N/A")
            metric_str = f"{metric_val:.4f}" if isinstance(metric_val, float) else str(metric_val)
            dirty_flag = " *" if record["git"]["is_dirty"] else ""
            
            print(f"{record['experiment_name']:<25} "
                  f"{record['git']['branch']:<20} "
                  f"{record['git']['commit_hash_short']:<10} "
                  f"{record['status']:<10} "
                  f"{metric_str:<12}{dirty_flag}")
        
        print("\n(* = run had uncommitted changes — may not be reproducible)")

def mock_train_function(config: Dict) -> Dict:

    import random
    random.seed(config.get("seed", 42))
    
    base_accuracy = 0.75

    }

Version control matters more in ML than traditional software because results depend on code, data, configuration, and randomness all evolving together
The core workflow is add (stage) → commit (snapshot) → push (share); use fetch before pull when you want to inspect remote changes first
Write commit messages that explain WHY a change was made, not just what — future you (and your team) will thank you
Use feature/experiment branches for all ML work; never commit experimental work directly to main
Merge preserves true collaborative history; rebase creates clean linear history but should only be used on your own unpushed/unshared branches

Use Git LFS or DVC for large binary files (models, datasets) that genuinely need versioning
GitHub Actions automate testing, linting, and even model performance validation gates directly in your CI pipeline
Your GitHub profile is a primary recruiting signal — invest in clean READMEs, organized repository structure, and genuine, working projects

Introduction

Linear algebra is the mathematical language of machine learning. Every neural network forward pass is a sequence of matrix multiplications. Every embedding is a vector. Every image is a tensor. Every PCA reduction, every recommendation system, every transformer's attention mechanism is, underneath the abstractions, linear algebra.

Many engineers learn to call model.fit() without understanding what is mathematically happening inside. This chapter closes that gap — not as abstract theory, but as the direct mathematical foundation beneath the code you already write.
Scalars, Vectors, Matrices, Tensors
The Hierarchy of Mathematical Objects

Scalar  → a single number                    5
Vector  → a 1D array of numbers               [5, 3, 8]
Matrix  → a 2D array of numbers               [[1,2],[3,4]]
Tensor  → an N-dimensional array of numbers   [[[1,2],[3,4]],[[5,6],[7,8]]]

Rank (number of dimensions):
Scalar: rank 0
Vector: rank 1
Matrix: rank 2
Tensor: rank ≥ 3
