Introduction

Intermediate SQL is where the real power of relational databases becomes visible. Basic SELECT queries retrieve data. Intermediate SQL transforms, combines, and summarizes it — turning raw tables into insights, training datasets, and business metrics.

Every data-intensive interview at a tech company tests this material. Joins, aggregations, and subqueries are not optional knowledge for an AI/ML engineer. They are the difference between waiting for a data engineer to hand you a file and pulling exactly the dataset you need in thirty seconds.
This chapter covers the full intermediate SQL toolkit with real examples drawn from data scenarios you will actually encounter in AI/ML work.
Aggregate Functions
Aggregate functions collapse multiple rows into a single summary value. They are the foundation of every analytics query.
The Core Aggregate Functions
Aggregate Functions and NULLs
Understanding how aggregates handle NULL is critical:

SELECT
    COUNT(*)    AS total_rows,        -- 10: counts all rows
    COUNT(age)  AS non_null_age,      -- 9: skips the NULL age
    COUNT(city) AS non_null_city,     -- 9: skips the NULL city
    AVG(age)    AS avg_age,           -- Computed over 9 rows, ignores NULL
    SUM(age)    AS sum_age            -- Sums 9 values, treats NULL as absent
FROM customers;
The rule: all aggregate functions except COUNT(*) ignore NULL values. This is usually correct behavior but can produce misleading results — always verify your NULL handling matches your intent.
GROUP BY
GROUP BY partitions rows into groups based on one or more columns, then applies aggregate functions to each group independently.

-- Count customers per city
SELECT
    city,
    COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;
 -- Total and average order amount by status
SELECT
    status,
    COUNT(*)            AS order_count,
    SUM(amount)         AS total_amount,
    ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_amount,
    MIN(amount)         AS min_amount,
    MAX(amount)         AS max_amount
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY total_amount DESC;
 -- Group by multiple columns
SELECT
    city,
    plan_type,
    COUNT(*) AS count
FROM customers
WHERE city IS NOT NULL
  AND plan_type IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY city, plan_type
ORDER BY city, count DESC;
The GROUP BY Rule
Every column in SELECT must either:
Appear in the GROUP BY clause, or
Be inside an aggregate function

-- WRONG — name is not in GROUP BY and not aggregated
SELECT city, name, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY city;   -- ERROR in most databases

-- CORRECT
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM customers
GROUP BY city;

-- CORRECT — name inside aggregate
SELECT city, COUNT(*), MAX(name) AS sample_name
FROM customers
GROUP BY city;
Grouping with NULLs
GROUP BY treats all NULL values as a single group:

SELECT
    COALESCE(city, '[No City]') AS city,
    COUNT(*) AS count
FROM customers
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY count DESC;
-- NULL city customers appear as one group
HAVING — Filtering Groups
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has been applied. It is the WHERE clause for groups.

-- Cities with more than 1 customer
SELECT
    city,
    COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers
WHERE city IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;
 -- Plan types with average customer age above 30
SELECT
    plan_type,
    COUNT(*)          AS count,
    ROUND(AVG(age),1) AS avg_age
FROM customers
WHERE age IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY plan_type
HAVING AVG(age) > 30
ORDER BY avg_age DESC;
 -- Customers with more than one order (multi-order buyers)
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*)   AS order_count,
    SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
WHERE vs HAVING Side by Side

-- WHERE filters BEFORE grouping — reduces the rows being grouped
-- HAVING filters AFTER grouping — reduces the groups in the output

-- "Among completed orders, which customers spent over 3000 total?"
SELECT
    customer_id,
    SUM(amount) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'        -- Filter rows first (only completed orders)
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 3000         -- Then filter groups (only big spenders)
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
 -- Common mistake: putting aggregate conditions in WHERE
-- WRONG
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount)
FROM orders
WHERE SUM(amount) > 3000     -- ERROR: aggregate in WHERE
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- CORRECT
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > 3000;
JOINs
A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column — usually a primary key and a foreign key relationship.
Visual Overview of JOIN Types### INNER JOIN
Returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables. Non-matching rows from either table are excluded.

-- Customers and their orders (only customers who have ordered)
SELECT
    c.name,
    c.city,
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    o.status,
    o.order_date
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY c.name, o.order_date;
 -- Table aliases (c and o) make queries readable
-- ON specifies the join condition — usually a primary/foreign key match
-- Multiple joins can be chained:

SELECT
    c.name,
    o.product_name,
    o.amount,
    p.category,
    p.price AS list_price
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
INNER JOIN products AS p
    ON o.product_name = p.product_name
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
ORDER BY o.amount DESC;
 -- Aggregation with JOIN
-- Total spent per customer (only customers who have orders)
SELECT
    c.name,
    c.city,
    c.plan_type,
    COUNT(o.order_id)    AS order_count,
    SUM(o.amount)        AS total_spent,
    ROUND(AVG(o.amount), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name, c.city, c.plan_type
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
LEFT JOIN
Returns all rows from the left table. For rows in the left table with no match in the right table, the right-side columns are filled with NULL.

-- ALL customers and their orders (including customers with no orders)
SELECT
    c.name,
    c.city,
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    o.status
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY c.name;
-- Customers with no orders appear with NULL in all order columns
 -- Find customers who have NEVER placed an order
-- Classic pattern: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL on the right table's key
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    c.city,
    c.plan_type
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
-- o.order_id is NULL only when no matching order exists
 -- Count orders per customer including zero-order customers
SELECT
    c.name,
    c.city,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count,   -- COUNT(col) ignores NULLs → shows 0
    COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name, c.city
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
RIGHT JOIN

Returns all rows from the right table. For rows in the right table with no match in the left table, left-side columns are NULL. In practice, most engineers rewrite RIGHT JOINs as LEFT JOINs by swapping table order — it is easier to reason about.

-- All orders and their customer details
-- (RIGHT JOIN orders means all orders appear even without a matching customer)
SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    o.status
FROM customers AS c
RIGHT JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- Equivalent LEFT JOIN (swap table order):
SELECT
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.amount,
    o.status
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customers AS c
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
FULL OUTER JOIN
Returns all rows from both tables. Where there is no match, NULLs fill the missing side. Note: SQLite does not support FULL OUTER JOIN natively — it is emulated with UNION.

-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server syntax
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    o.order_id,
    o.amount
FROM customers AS c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- SQLite equivalent (LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT-side-only):
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
UNION
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
CROSS JOIN
Returns the Cartesian product — every row from the left table paired with every row from the right table. N × M rows total.

-- Generate all possible customer-product combinations
-- Useful for recommendation system candidate generation
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.name,
    p.product_name,
    p.category,
    p.price
FROM customers AS c
CROSS JOIN products AS p
ORDER BY c.customer_id, p.price;
-- 10 customers × 10 products = 100 rows
 -- Practical use: generate a date × category grid for reporting
-- even when some combinations have no data
SELECT dates.report_date, cats.category
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT order_date AS report_date FROM orders) AS dates
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) AS cats
ORDER BY dates.report_date, cats.category;
SELF JOIN
A table joined to itself. Used when rows within the same table have a relationship to each other.

-- Find pairs of customers from the same city
SELECT
    a.name AS customer_1,
    b.name AS customer_2,
    a.city
FROM customers AS a
INNER JOIN customers AS b
    ON a.city = b.city
    AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id  -- Avoid duplicates and self-pairs
ORDER BY a.city, a.name;
 -- Practical ML use: find similar customers
-- (customers with same plan type and city — candidate pairs for collaborative filtering)
SELECT
    a.customer_id AS customer_a,
    b.customer_id AS customer_b,
    a.city,
    a.plan_type
FROM customers AS a
INNER JOIN customers AS b
    ON a.city = b.city
    AND a.plan_type = b.plan_type
    AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id
ORDER BY a.city, a.plan_type;
Subqueries
A subquery is a query nested inside another query. It can appear in SELECT, FROM, or WHERE clauses.
Scalar Subquery
Returns exactly one row and one column. Can be used anywhere a single value is expected.

-- Show each order's amount and how it compares to the overall average
SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount,
    (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) AS overall_avg,
    amount - (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) AS diff_from_avg,
    CASE
        WHEN amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) THEN 'Above average'
        ELSE 'Below average'
    END AS classification
FROM orders
ORDER BY amount DESC;
 -- Find customers older than the average customer age
SELECT name, age, city
FROM customers
WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM customers WHERE age IS NOT NULL)
ORDER BY age DESC;
Subquery in FROM (Inline View / Derived Table)
A subquery in the FROM clause creates a temporary table for the outer query.

-- Average revenue per city (requires two levels of aggregation)
-- Step 1 (inner): total revenue per customer
-- Step 2 (outer): average of those totals per city

SELECT
    city,
    ROUND(AVG(customer_total), 2) AS avg_customer_revenue,
    COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM (
    SELECT
        c.customer_id,
        c.city,
        COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS customer_total
    FROM customers AS c
    LEFT JOIN orders AS o
        ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE c.city IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.city
) AS customer_revenue
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY avg_customer_revenue DESC;
 -- Classify customers by spend tier, then count each tier
SELECT
    spend_tier,
    COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM (
    SELECT
        c.customer_id,
        SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent,
        CASE
            WHEN SUM(o.amount) >= 10000 THEN 'High Value'
            WHEN SUM(o.amount) >= 3000  THEN 'Medium Value'
            WHEN SUM(o.amount) > 0      THEN 'Low Value'
            ELSE 'No Orders'
        END AS spend_tier
    FROM customers AS c
    LEFT JOIN orders AS o
        ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.customer_id
) AS classified
GROUP BY spend_tier
ORDER BY customer_count DESC;
Subquery in WHERE

-- Find customers who have placed at least one completed order
SELECT name, city, plan_type
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
)
ORDER BY name;
 -- Find customers who have NEVER placed a completed order
SELECT name, city, plan_type
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
        AND customer_id IS NOT NULL  -- Critical: NOT IN fails with NULLs
)
ORDER BY name;
 -- Products that have been ordered
SELECT product_name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE product_name IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT product_name FROM orders
)
ORDER BY price DESC;
Correlated Subquery
A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query. It executes once per row of the outer query — powerful but can be slow on large tables.

-- For each customer, show their highest order amount
SELECT
    c.name,
    c.city,
    (
        SELECT MAX(o.amount)
        FROM orders AS o
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id  -- References outer query's c
    ) AS max_order_amount
FROM customers AS c
ORDER BY max_order_amount DESC NULLS LAST;
 -- Find orders that are above the average for that specific customer
-- (not the global average, but each customer's personal average)
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.customer_id,
    o.amount,
    o.product_name
FROM orders AS o
WHERE o.amount > (
    SELECT AVG(o2.amount)
    FROM orders AS o2
    WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id  -- Per-customer average
)
ORDER BY o.customer_id, o.amount DESC;
EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
EXISTS checks whether a subquery returns any rows. It stops as soon as the first matching row is found — often faster than IN for large tables.

-- Customers who have placed at least one order (using EXISTS)
SELECT name, city
FROM customers AS c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders AS o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
ORDER BY name;
 -- Customers who have no orders at all (using NOT EXISTS)
SELECT name, city, plan_type
FROM customers AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders AS o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
ORDER BY name;
 -- EXISTS is safer than NOT IN when subquery might return NULLs
-- These two are equivalent in behavior when no NULLs are present,
-- but NOT EXISTS is always safe:

-- Potentially dangerous (if customer_id can be NULL in orders):
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)

-- Always safe:
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
These set operators combine the results of two or more SELECT statements.
Rules for Set Operators
Both SELECT statements must return the same number of columns
Corresponding columns must have compatible data types
Column names come from the first SELECT
UNION — Combine and Deduplicate

-- All cities where customers live OR where orders were shipped
-- (hypothetical — here combining premium and high-spend customers)

-- Premium plan customers
SELECT customer_id, name, 'premium_plan' AS source
FROM customers
WHERE plan_type = 'premium'

UNION

-- High-spend customers (any plan)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, 'high_spender' AS source
FROM customers AS c
INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 5000;
-- UNION removes duplicates — a customer who is both premium AND high-spend
-- appears only once
UNION ALL — Combine Without Deduplication

-- Combine completed and pending orders into one result set
-- Use UNION ALL when you want all rows including duplicates
-- (and it's faster than UNION since no deduplication step)

SELECT order_id, amount, status, order_date, 'recent' AS batch
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-02-01'

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, amount, status, order_date, 'older' AS batch
FROM orders
WHERE order_date < '2026-02-01'

ORDER BY order_date DESC;
INTERSECT — Common Rows

-- Customers who are both premium AND have placed completed orders
SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE plan_type = 'premium'
INTERSECT
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed';
EXCEPT — Rows in First Set Not in Second

-- Premium customers who have NOT placed any completed order
SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE plan_type = 'premium'
EXCEPT
SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed';
Putting It All Together — Real ML Query Patterns
Pattern 1: Building a Feature Table for ML

-- Assemble a customer feature table for churn prediction
-- Combines: customer attributes + order behavior + recency
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.age,
    COALESCE(c.city, 'Unknown')      AS city,
    COALESCE(c.plan_type, 'basic')   AS plan_type,
    COUNT(o.order_id)                AS total_orders,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0)       AS total_spent,
    COALESCE(AVG(o.amount), 0)       AS avg_order_value,
    COALESCE(MAX(o.amount), 0)       AS max_order_value,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders,
    MAX(o.order_date)                AS last_order_date
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.age IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY
    c.customer_id, c.age, c.city, c.plan_type
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
Pattern 2: Class Distribution Check

-- Check label distribution before training — critical for imbalance detection
SELECT
    churn_label,
    COUNT(*) AS count,
    ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 2) AS percentage
FROM training_data
GROUP BY churn_label;
Pattern 3: Identifying Data Quality Issues with JOIN

-- Find orphaned orders (orders with no matching customer)
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.amount
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customers AS c
    ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
Common Mistakes
Forgetting GROUP BY Includes All Non-Aggregated SELECT Columns

-- WRONG
SELECT city, plan_type, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY city;  -- Missing plan_type → error in strict SQL databases

-- CORRECT
SELECT city, plan_type, COUNT(*)
FROM customers
GROUP BY city, plan_type;
Using WHERE Instead of HAVING for Aggregate Conditions

-- WRONG
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE COUNT(*) > 2           -- ERROR: aggregate in WHERE
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- CORRECT
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) Confusion

-- COUNT(*) — counts all rows including NULLs
-- COUNT(col) — counts only non-NULL values in that column
-- These give different results when the column has NULLs!

SELECT
    COUNT(*)   AS all_rows,         -- 10
    COUNT(age) AS rows_with_age,    -- 9 (one NULL age)
    COUNT(city) AS rows_with_city   -- 9 (one NULL city)
FROM customers;
NOT IN With Possible NULLs
Joining on the Wrong Column

-- WRONG — joining on name instead of the unique key
SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.name = o.product_name;  -- Accidental cross-join!

-- CORRECT — always join on the primary/foreign key
SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?

INNER JOIN returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables — non-matching rows are excluded from the result. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table regardless of whether they match the right table. For left-table rows with no match, right-side columns are filled with NULL. Use INNER JOIN when you only want matched pairs. Use LEFT JOIN when you need all records from one table, including those with no corresponding record in the other.
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping — it runs before GROUP BY. HAVING filters groups after grouping — it runs after GROUP BY. Aggregate functions like COUNT(), SUM(), and AVG() cannot be used in WHERE because aggregation has not happened yet. They belong in HAVING. A simple rule: if the filter involves an aggregate function, use HAVING. Otherwise use WHERE.
What does COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) return?

COUNT(*) counts every row in the result set, including rows where all columns are NULL. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that specific column is NOT NULL. They give different results when the column contains NULL values. Use COUNT(*) to count total rows. Use COUNT(column) when you specifically want to know how many rows have a value in that column.
Intermediate Level
How do you find rows in Table A that have no match in Table B?

The two standard patterns are LEFT JOIN with IS NULL check and NOT EXISTS. For LEFT JOIN: SELECT a.* FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.id = B.a_id WHERE B.a_id IS NULL. For NOT EXISTS: SELECT * FROM A WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B WHERE B.a_id = A.id). Both work correctly. The NOT EXISTS form is often more readable and avoids the NULL trap that affects NOT IN when the subquery might return NULLs.
What is a correlated subquery and when would you use it?

A correlated subquery is a subquery that references a column from the outer query. It executes once for each row processed by the outer query, making it potentially slow on large tables. Use it when you need a per-row computation that depends on the current outer row — for example, finding orders above each customer's personal average, or returning the most recent order for each customer. For performance-critical queries, correlated subqueries can often be rewritten as window functions.
What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?

Both combine result sets from two SELECT statements. UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result — it performs a deduplication step. UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates and is faster because it skips deduplication. Use UNION ALL when you know there are no duplicates or when duplicates are intentional. Use UNION only when deduplication is required, as it adds computational overhead.
Advanced Level
When would you use EXISTS over IN, and why?

EXISTS is preferred over IN in several scenarios. First, safety with NULLs: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery produces any NULL values, while NOT EXISTS handles NULLs correctly. Second, performance on large subqueries: EXISTS short-circuits — it stops at the first matching row. IN typically materializes the entire subquery result. Third, readability for existence checks: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ...) clearly expresses intent. Use IN when comparing against a small list of values. Prefer EXISTS for subquery-based membership tests, especially with NOT.
Explain the difference between a derived table and a correlated subquery.

A derived table is a subquery in the FROM clause — it executes once, produces a temporary result set, and the outer query operates on that result. It is independent of the outer query. A correlated subquery is a subquery in SELECT or WHERE that references the outer query's columns — it executes once per row of the outer query. Derived tables are generally more efficient because they execute once. Correlated subqueries are more flexible for per-row operations but can be slow for large datasets. In modern SQL, window functions often replace both patterns more elegantly.

Chapter Summary
Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) collapse rows into summary values — they ignore NULLs except COUNT(*)
GROUP BY partitions rows into groups; every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after grouping — aggregate functions belong in HAVING
INNER JOIN returns only matching rows; LEFT JOIN returns all left rows with NULLs for unmatched right rows
The LEFT JOIN + WHERE right_key IS NULL pattern finds rows in one table with no match in another
Subqueries can appear in SELECT (scalar), FROM (derived table), or WHERE (filter or EXISTS check)
NOT IN is dangerous when the subquery can return NULLs — prefer NOT EXISTS for safety
UNION deduplicates; UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster; INTERSECT finds common rows; EXCEPT finds set differences
Correlated subqueries execute once per outer row — powerful but potentially slow on large tables
Cheat Sheet

-- Aggregation
SELECT col, COUNT(*), SUM(x), AVG(x), MIN(x), MAX(x)
FROM t GROUP BY col HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Conditional aggregation
SUM(CASE WHEN status='done' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
COUNT(CASE WHEN status='done' THEN 1 END)

-- JOIN patterns
FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id   -- matched rows only
FROM a LEFT  JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id   -- all a, NULL for unmatched b
FROM a LEFT  JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id WHERE b.id IS NULL  -- a with no b

-- Subquery locations
WHERE col IN (SELECT col FROM t WHERE ...)   -- filter by list
FROM (SELECT ... FROM t) AS sub             -- derived table
SELECT (SELECT MAX(x) FROM t) AS max_x     -- scalar

-- EXISTS patterns
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.id = a.id)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.id = a.id)

-- Set operators
SELECT ... UNION     SELECT ...  -- combine, deduplicate
SELECT ... UNION ALL SELECT ...  -- combine, keep duplicates
SELECT ... INTERSECT SELECT ...  -- common rows
SELECT ... EXCEPT    SELECT ...  -- first minus second
Revision Notes
COUNT(*) = all rows; COUNT(col) = non-NULL rows only
GROUP BY + HAVING always pair together; WHERE cannot use aggregates
LEFT JOIN IS NULL = anti-join (find unmatched rows)
NOT IN with NULLs in subquery → 0 rows returned (use NOT EXISTS)
Correlated subquery = runs once per outer row (slow); derived table = runs once (fast)
UNION deduplicates (slower); UNION ALL does not (faster)
Join condition goes in ON; row filters go in WHERE; group filters go in HAVING
Always alias tables when joining (c for customers, o for orders)

Introduction
Most SQL knowledge at the beginner and intermediate level gets you through the front door. Advanced SQL is what keeps you employed and valued.

As an AI/ML engineer, you will constantly need to pull features from databases, analyze model performance metrics over time, build cohorts, and audit data quality — all in SQL. The tools in this chapter are what data teams at companies like Airbnb, Stripe, Uber, and every serious ML-driven company use daily.

Window functions alone transformed how analysts work with data. CTEs made complex analytical queries maintainable. JSON support brought SQL into the era of semi-structured data. Together, these features make SQL powerful enough to handle surprisingly sophisticated data science tasks before a single line of Python is written.
Window Functions
A window function performs a calculation across a set of rows that are somehow related to the current row — without collapsing those rows into a single output row the way GROUP BY does.
Think of it this way: GROUP BY collapses five rows into one. A window function keeps all five rows and adds a new calculated column to each one.

-- Compare: GROUP BY collapses rows
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
-- Result: one row per department, individual employees disappear

-- Window function: keeps all rows, adds the avg to each
SELECT
    name,
    department,
    salary,
    AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg_salary,
    salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS diff_from_avg
FROM employees;
-- Result: all employees visible, with their dept avg added
The anatomy of a window function:

function_name() OVER (
    PARTITION BY column1, column2   -- defines the "window" (group)
    ORDER BY column3                -- defines the order within the window
    ROWS BETWEEN ... AND ...        -- defines the frame (optional)
)
Ranking Functions

-- Sample dataset: model evaluation results per experiment
CREATE TABLE model_results (
    experiment_id   INT,
    model_name      VARCHAR(50),
    dataset         VARCHAR(50),
    accuracy        FLOAT,
    f1_score        FLOAT,
    run_date        DATE
);

-- ROW_NUMBER: unique rank, no ties
SELECT
    model_name,
    dataset,
    accuracy,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY dataset
        ORDER BY accuracy DESC
    ) AS row_num
FROM model_results;

-- RANK: ties get the same rank, next rank skips
-- Example: if two models tie for 1st, next is 3rd (not 2nd)
SELECT
    model_name,
    dataset,
    accuracy,
    RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY dataset
        ORDER BY accuracy DESC
    ) AS rank_position
FROM model_results;

-- DENSE_RANK: ties get same rank, next rank does NOT skip
-- Example: if two models tie for 1st, next is 2nd
SELECT
    model_name,
    dataset,
    accuracy,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY dataset
        ORDER BY accuracy DESC
    ) AS dense_rank_position
FROM model_results;

-- NTILE(n): divides rows into n buckets
-- Useful for splitting data into percentile groups
SELECT
    model_name,
    accuracy,
    NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY accuracy) AS quartile
    -- quartile 1 = bottom 25%, quartile 4 = top 25%
FROM model_results;
A practical example — find the best-performing model on each dataset:

-- Find top model per dataset using ROW_NUMBER
WITH ranked_models AS (
    SELECT
        model_name,
        dataset,
        accuracy,
        f1_score,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY dataset
            ORDER BY accuracy DESC, f1_score DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM model_results
)
SELECT
    model_name,
    dataset,
    accuracy,
    f1_score
FROM ranked_models
WHERE rn = 1;
This pattern — rank inside a CTE, filter on rank in the outer query — is one of the most used patterns in data analytics and interviews.
Aggregate Window Functions
Any aggregate function can be used as a window function by adding OVER():

-- Training metrics table
SELECT
    epoch,
    train_loss,
    val_loss,
    -- Running average of val_loss up to current epoch
    AVG(val_loss) OVER (
        ORDER BY epoch
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_avg_val_loss,
    -- Total epochs run so far
    COUNT(*) OVER (
        ORDER BY epoch
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS epochs_run,
    -- Best val_loss seen so far
    MIN(val_loss) OVER (
        ORDER BY epoch
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS best_val_loss_so_far,
    -- How many epochs since we last improved (simplified)
    val_loss - MIN(val_loss) OVER (
        ORDER BY epoch
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS gap_from_best
FROM training_runs
WHERE experiment_id = 42
ORDER BY epoch;
LAG and LEAD
LAG accesses a value from a previous row. LEAD accesses a value from a future row. Both are window functions that are essential for trend analysis.

LAG(column, offset, default_value)  OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
LEAD(column, offset, default_value) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
 -- Epoch-by-epoch loss comparison
SELECT
    epoch,
    val_loss,
    LAG(val_loss, 1) OVER (ORDER BY epoch) AS prev_epoch_loss,
    val_loss - LAG(val_loss, 1) OVER (ORDER BY epoch) AS loss_change,
    CASE
        WHEN val_loss < LAG(val_loss, 1) OVER (ORDER BY epoch)
        THEN 'Improving'
        WHEN val_loss > LAG(val_loss, 1) OVER (ORDER BY epoch)
        THEN 'Degrading'
        ELSE 'No Change'
    END AS trend
FROM training_runs
WHERE experiment_id = 42
ORDER BY epoch;
 -- Real use case: detecting training stalls
-- An epoch where loss hasn't improved in 3 consecutive epochs
WITH loss_with_lag AS (
    SELECT
        epoch,
        val_loss,
        LAG(val_loss, 1) OVER (ORDER BY epoch) AS loss_1_ago,
        LAG(val_loss, 2) OVER (ORDER BY epoch) AS loss_2_ago,
        LAG(val_loss, 3) OVER (ORDER BY epoch) AS loss_3_ago
    FROM training_runs
    WHERE experiment_id = 42
)
SELECT
    epoch,
    val_loss,
    loss_1_ago,
    loss_2_ago,
    loss_3_ago
FROM loss_with_lag
WHERE
    val_loss >= loss_1_ago AND
    loss_1_ago >= loss_2_ago AND
    loss_2_ago >= loss_3_ago
ORDER BY epoch;
-- These are early stopping candidates
 -- LEAD example: looking ahead to next row
-- Useful for session analysis — how long until next user action?
SELECT
    user_id,
    event_type,
    event_timestamp,
    LEAD(event_timestamp, 1) OVER (
        PARTITION BY user_id
        ORDER BY event_timestamp
    ) AS next_event_time,
    EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (
        LEAD(event_timestamp, 1) OVER (
            PARTITION BY user_id
            ORDER BY event_timestamp
        ) - event_timestamp
    )) / 60.0 AS minutes_to_next_event
FROM user_events
ORDER BY user_id, event_timestamp;
Running Totals and Moving Averages
These are the most common analytical patterns in business intelligence and ML monitoring.
Running Total

-- Cumulative API cost tracking for LLM usage
SELECT
    usage_date,
    model_name,
    daily_tokens_used,
    daily_cost_usd,
    SUM(daily_cost_usd) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name
        ORDER BY usage_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS cumulative_cost_usd
FROM llm_usage_log
ORDER BY model_name, usage_date;
Moving Average
A moving average smooths out noise in time series data. Common in financial analysis and ML loss curve monitoring.

-- 7-day moving average of model accuracy (for production monitoring)
SELECT
    metric_date,
    model_name,
    daily_accuracy,
    -- 7-day simple moving average
    AVG(daily_accuracy) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name
        ORDER BY metric_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS ma_7day,
    -- 30-day moving average
    AVG(daily_accuracy) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name
        ORDER BY metric_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS ma_30day,
    -- Count of days in the window (useful early in the series when < 7 days exist)
    COUNT(*) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name
        ORDER BY metric_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS days_in_window
FROM model_production_metrics
ORDER BY model_name, metric_date;
Understanding the Frame Clause
The frame clause specifies which rows are included in the window relative to the current row:

-- Frame clause options:
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW  -- From first row to current
ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW          -- Last 7 rows including current
ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING          -- Previous, current, next
ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING  -- Current to last row
ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING -- All rows in partition

Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

A CTE is a temporary, named result set that you define at the top of a query with the WITH keyword. It exists only for the duration of the query that follows it. CTEs make complex queries readable by breaking them into named logical steps.

-- Without CTE — deeply nested, hard to read
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT model_name, AVG(accuracy) AS avg_acc FROM (
        SELECT * FROM model_results WHERE run_date >= '2026-01-01'
    ) AS recent
    GROUP BY model_name
) AS averages
WHERE avg_acc > 0.85;

-- With CTE — reads like English
WITH recent_results AS (
    SELECT *
    FROM model_results
    WHERE run_date >= '2026-01-01'
),
model_averages AS (
    SELECT
        model_name,
        AVG(accuracy) AS avg_acc,
        COUNT(*) AS num_runs
    FROM recent_results
    GROUP BY model_name
)
SELECT
    model_name,
    avg_acc,
    num_runs
FROM model_averages
WHERE avg_acc > 0.85
ORDER BY avg_acc DESC;
Chaining Multiple CTEs

-- Multi-step data pipeline in SQL
-- Use case: find users who used an AI feature and churned within 30 days

WITH feature_users AS (
    -- Step 1: users who used the AI feature
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_ai_use
    FROM user_events
    WHERE event_type = 'ai_feature_used'
    GROUP BY user_id
),
churned_users AS (
    -- Step 2: users who cancelled subscription
    SELECT user_id, cancellation_date
    FROM subscriptions
    WHERE status = 'cancelled'
),
at_risk AS (
    -- Step 3: join and find users who churned within 30 days of using AI feature
    SELECT
        fu.user_id,
        fu.first_ai_use,
        cu.cancellation_date,
        cu.cancellation_date - fu.first_ai_use AS days_to_churn
    FROM feature_users fu
    JOIN churned_users cu ON fu.user_id = cu.user_id
    WHERE cu.cancellation_date BETWEEN fu.first_ai_use
                                   AND fu.first_ai_use + INTERVAL '30 days'
)
SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS churned_after_ai,
    AVG(days_to_churn) AS avg_days_to_churn,
    MIN(days_to_churn) AS min_days,
    MAX(days_to_churn) AS max_days
FROM at_risk;
CTEs vs Subqueries vs Temp Tables
Recursive CTEs
Recursive CTEs let a query reference itself. They are the standard SQL tool for traversing hierarchical data: org charts, category trees, file systems, and graph paths.

-- Structure of a recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE cte_name AS (
    -- Anchor member: the starting point (non-recursive part)
    SELECT ...
    FROM table
    WHERE base_condition

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references cte_name itself
    SELECT ...
    FROM table
    JOIN cte_name ON join_condition
)
SELECT * FROM cte_name;
Org Chart Traversal

-- employees table
-- id | name        | manager_id | department | level
-- ---|-------------|------------|------------|------
-- 1  | CEO         | NULL       | Executive  | 1
-- 2  | CTO         | 1          | Tech       | 2
-- 3  | VP Eng      | 2          | Tech       | 3
-- 4  | ML Lead     | 3          | ML         | 4
-- 5  | ML Engineer | 4          | ML         | 5

-- Find the full org hierarchy under a given person
WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
    -- Anchor: start at CEO (or any starting node)
    SELECT
        id,
        name,
        manager_id,
        department,
        1 AS depth,
        name::TEXT AS path
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL   -- Root node (CEO)

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive: join each employee to their manager in the CTE
    SELECT
        e.id,
        e.name,
        e.manager_id,
        e.department,
        ot.depth + 1,
        ot.path || ' → ' || e.name
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_tree ot ON e.manager_id = ot.id
)
SELECT
    id,
    REPEAT('    ', depth - 1) || name AS indented_name,
    department,
    depth,
    path
FROM org_tree
ORDER BY path;

-- Output:
-- CEO
--     CTO
--         VP Eng
--             ML Lead
--                 ML Engineer
Category Tree (e-commerce or ML taxonomy)

-- Find all subcategories under "Computer Vision"
WITH RECURSIVE category_tree AS (
    -- Anchor: the root category we're starting from
    SELECT id, name, parent_id, 0 AS level
    FROM ml_categories
    WHERE name = 'Computer Vision'

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive: all children of current nodes
    SELECT c.id, c.name, c.parent_id, ct.level + 1
    FROM ml_categories c
    JOIN category_tree ct ON c.parent_id = ct.id
)
SELECT
    REPEAT('  ', level) || name AS category,
    level
FROM category_tree
ORDER BY level, name;
Preventing Infinite Recursion

-- Always add a depth limit to recursive CTEs
-- to handle circular references in dirty data
WITH RECURSIVE safe_traversal AS (
    SELECT id, parent_id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM nodes
    WHERE id = 1

    UNION ALL

    SELECT n.id, n.parent_id, n.name, st.depth + 1
    FROM nodes n
    JOIN safe_traversal st ON n.parent_id = st.id
    WHERE st.depth < 50    -- Safety limit — prevents infinite loop
)
SELECT * FROM safe_traversal;
CASE Statements
CASE is SQL's conditional expression — equivalent to if-elif-else in Python. It can be used anywhere an expression is valid: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY.
Simple CASE

-- Map numeric labels to human-readable categories
SELECT
    prediction_id,
    predicted_label,
    CASE predicted_label
        WHEN 0 THEN 'Negative'
        WHEN 1 THEN 'Positive'
        WHEN 2 THEN 'Neutral'
        ELSE 'Unknown'
    END AS label_name
FROM predictions;
Searched CASE

-- More powerful: each WHEN can have an independent condition
SELECT
    model_name,
    accuracy,
    f1_score,
    CASE
        WHEN accuracy >= 0.95 AND f1_score >= 0.90 THEN 'Production Ready'
        WHEN accuracy >= 0.90 AND f1_score >= 0.85 THEN 'Needs Validation'
        WHEN accuracy >= 0.80                       THEN 'Under Development'
        ELSE                                             'Rejected'
    END AS deployment_status,
    CASE
        WHEN accuracy >= 0.95 THEN 1
        WHEN accuracy >= 0.90 THEN 2
        WHEN accuracy >= 0.80 THEN 3
        ELSE 4
    END AS priority_rank
FROM model_results
ORDER BY priority_rank, accuracy DESC;
CASE Inside Aggregations
This is one of the most powerful SQL patterns — it lets you pivot counts into different columns:

-- Pivot model results by status in a single query
-- Instead of multiple queries, get counts for all statuses at once
SELECT
    experiment_name,
    COUNT(*) AS total_runs,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN accuracy >= 0.95 THEN 1 END) AS excellent_runs,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN accuracy >= 0.85 AND accuracy < 0.95 THEN 1 END) AS good_runs,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN accuracy < 0.85 THEN 1 END) AS poor_runs,
    ROUND(
        100.0 * COUNT(CASE WHEN accuracy >= 0.90 THEN 1 END) / COUNT(*), 2
    ) AS pct_above_90
FROM model_results
GROUP BY experiment_name
ORDER BY total_runs DESC;
 -- CASE in ORDER BY — custom sort order
SELECT model_name, deployment_status
FROM model_results
ORDER BY
    CASE deployment_status
        WHEN 'Production Ready' THEN 1
        WHEN 'Needs Validation' THEN 2
        WHEN 'Under Development' THEN 3
        ELSE 4
    END;
String Functions
Data from real sources is messy. String functions are your cleaning tools.

-- Common string operations for data cleaning
SELECT
    -- Case manipulation
    UPPER('bert-base-uncased'),           -- BERT-BASE-UNCASED
    LOWER('GPT-4o'),                      -- gpt-4o
    INITCAP('machine learning engineer'), -- Machine Learning Engineer

    -- Trimming whitespace
    TRIM('  hello world  '),              -- 'hello world'
    LTRIM('   left spaces'),              -- 'left spaces'
    RTRIM('right spaces   '),             -- 'right spaces'
    TRIM(BOTH '#' FROM '##hello##'),      -- 'hello'

    -- Length
    LENGTH('transformer'),                -- 11
    CHAR_LENGTH('GPT-4o'),               -- 6

    -- Substring extraction
    SUBSTRING('bert-base-uncased' FROM 1 FOR 4),  -- bert
    LEFT('bert-base-uncased', 4),         -- bert
    RIGHT('bert-base-uncased', 8),        -- uncased

    -- Search and replace
    REPLACE('hello world', 'world', 'AI'),-- hello AI
    POSITION('base' IN 'bert-base-uncased'), -- 6

    -- Concatenation
    CONCAT('GPT', '-', '4o'),             -- GPT-4o
    'GPT' || '-' || '4o',                 -- GPT-4o (PostgreSQL syntax)

    -- Padding
    LPAD('7', 3, '0'),                    -- 007
    RPAD('bert', 10, '-'),                -- bert------

    -- Split
    SPLIT_PART('bert-base-uncased', '-', 1), -- bert (PostgreSQL)
    SPLIT_PART('bert-base-uncased', '-', 2); -- base
Real-World String Cleaning

-- Clean a model registry table with messy data
WITH cleaned_models AS (
    SELECT
        TRIM(LOWER(model_name)) AS model_name,
        TRIM(LOWER(framework)) AS framework,
        -- Extract version number from strings like "v1.2.3" or "version 2.0"
        REGEXP_REPLACE(version_string, '[^0-9.]', '', 'g') AS version_number,
        -- Normalize dataset name
        CASE
            WHEN LOWER(dataset) LIKE '%imagenet%' THEN 'ImageNet'
            WHEN LOWER(dataset) LIKE '%cifar%'    THEN 'CIFAR'
            WHEN LOWER(dataset) LIKE '%coco%'     THEN 'COCO'
            ELSE INITCAP(TRIM(dataset))
        END AS dataset_normalized,
        accuracy
    FROM raw_model_registry
    WHERE model_name IS NOT NULL
    AND LENGTH(TRIM(model_name)) > 0
)
SELECT * FROM cleaned_models;
Date and Time Functions
Date functions are used constantly in time series analysis, cohort analysis, and model monitoring.

-- Getting current time
SELECT
    NOW(),                              -- Current timestamp with timezone
    CURRENT_DATE,                       -- Current date only
    CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,                  -- Same as NOW()

-- Date arithmetic
    NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days',          -- 7 days ago
    NOW() + INTERVAL '1 month',         -- 1 month from now
    DATE '2026-06-01' + 30,            -- Add 30 days

-- Extracting parts
    EXTRACT(YEAR  FROM NOW()),          -- 2026
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM NOW()),          -- Current month number
    EXTRACT(DOW   FROM NOW()),          -- Day of week (0=Sunday)
    EXTRACT(HOUR  FROM NOW()),          -- Current hour

-- Truncating
    DATE_TRUNC('month', NOW()),         -- First day of current month
    DATE_TRUNC('week',  NOW()),         -- First day of current week
    DATE_TRUNC('day',   NOW()),         -- Start of today (midnight)

-- Formatting
    TO_CHAR(NOW(), 'YYYY-MM-DD'),       -- '2026-06-28'
    TO_CHAR(NOW(), 'Month DD, YYYY'),   -- 'June 28, 2026'

-- Differences
    AGE(NOW(), '2000-01-01'::DATE),                  -- interval between dates
    EXTRACT(DAY FROM NOW() - '2026-01-01'::DATE);    -- days since Jan 1
Date Functions in Analytics

-- Weekly model performance report
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('week', evaluation_date) AS week_start,
    model_name,
    COUNT(*) AS evaluations_this_week,
    AVG(accuracy) AS avg_accuracy,
    MIN(accuracy) AS min_accuracy,
    MAX(accuracy) AS max_accuracy,
    STDDEV(accuracy) AS accuracy_stddev
FROM model_evaluations
WHERE evaluation_date >= NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('week', evaluation_date), model_name
ORDER BY week_start DESC, model_name;
 -- Cohort analysis: group users by the week they first used the product
-- Track how many return each subsequent week
WITH first_use AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('week', MIN(event_date)) AS cohort_week
    FROM user_events
    GROUP BY user_id
),
weekly_activity AS (
    SELECT
        fu.user_id,
        fu.cohort_week,
        DATE_TRUNC('week', e.event_date) AS activity_week,
        EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (
            DATE_TRUNC('week', e.event_date) - fu.cohort_week
        )) / 604800 AS weeks_since_join  -- 604800 seconds in a week
    FROM first_use fu
    JOIN user_events e ON fu.user_id = e.user_id
)
SELECT
    cohort_week,
    weeks_since_join::INT AS week_number,
    COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS retained_users
FROM weekly_activity
GROUP BY cohort_week, weeks_since_join
ORDER BY cohort_week, weeks_since_join;
JSON in SQL

Modern applications store semi-structured data in JSON columns. PostgreSQL has excellent JSON support that AI engineers use frequently when working with model metadata, configuration objects, and API responses.

-- Creating a table with JSON columns
CREATE TABLE model_experiments (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    model_name  VARCHAR(100),
    run_date    TIMESTAMP,
    hyperparams JSONB,      -- JSONB: binary JSON, indexed and queryable
    metrics     JSONB,
    tags        TEXT[]      -- Array column
);

-- Inserting JSON data
INSERT INTO model_experiments (model_name, run_date, hyperparams, metrics, tags)
VALUES (
    'bert-base',
    NOW(),
    '{"learning_rate": 0.0001, "batch_size": 32, "epochs": 10, "optimizer": "adam"}',
    '{"accuracy": 0.924, "f1": 0.918, "precision": 0.921, "recall": 0.915}',
    ARRAY['nlp', 'classification', 'bert']
);
 -- Querying JSON fields
SELECT
    model_name,
    -- Extract a value from JSON
    hyperparams->>'learning_rate' AS lr,       -- Returns text
    hyperparams->'batch_size' AS batch_size,   -- Returns JSON
    (hyperparams->>'batch_size')::INT AS batch_size_int,  -- Cast to int
    metrics->>'accuracy' AS accuracy,
    (metrics->>'f1')::FLOAT AS f1_score,

    -- Access nested JSON
    hyperparams->'optimizer' AS optimizer

FROM model_experiments
WHERE
    -- Filter on JSON values
    (hyperparams->>'learning_rate')::FLOAT < 0.001
    AND (metrics->>'accuracy')::FLOAT > 0.90;
 -- Aggregate over JSON fields — finding best hyperparameters
SELECT
    hyperparams->>'optimizer' AS optimizer,
    AVG((metrics->>'accuracy')::FLOAT) AS avg_accuracy,
    COUNT(*) AS num_experiments
FROM model_experiments
GROUP BY hyperparams->>'optimizer'
ORDER BY avg_accuracy DESC;
 -- Check if a JSON key exists
SELECT model_name, hyperparams
FROM model_experiments
WHERE hyperparams ? 'dropout_rate';    -- Has this key?

-- Check if JSON contains a specific object
WHERE hyperparams @> '{"optimizer": "adam"}';  -- Contains this?

-- Expand JSON array to rows
SELECT
    model_name,
    jsonb_array_elements_text(metrics->'per_class_f1') AS class_f1
FROM model_experiments;

-- Build JSON from query results
SELECT
    jsonb_build_object(
        'model', model_name,
        'accuracy', metrics->>'accuracy',
        'hyperparams', hyperparams
    ) AS experiment_summary
FROM model_experiments;
Query Performance Optimization
Understanding EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN shows you what the database query planner intends to do. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows what it did.
Key things to look for in the output:
Seq Scan — full table scan, no index used (expensive on large tables)
Index Scan — using an index (fast)
Hash Join / Nested Loop — join strategies (hash join is usually faster for large tables)
rows= — estimated row count (if very wrong, statistics need updating)
actual time= — real execution time in milliseconds

Real Interview Questions
These are actual SQL questions asked at data science and ML engineering interviews at top companies.
Question 1: Find the second highest accuracy model for each dataset

WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        model_name,
        dataset,
        accuracy,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY dataset
            ORDER BY accuracy DESC
        ) AS rnk
    FROM model_results
)
SELECT model_name, dataset, accuracy
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;
Question 2: Find users who logged in on three consecutive days

WITH daily_logins AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date::DATE AS login_date
    FROM user_sessions
),
with_lag AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        login_date,
        LAG(login_date, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS prev1,
        LAG(login_date, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS prev2
    FROM daily_logins
)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM with_lag
WHERE
    login_date - prev1 = 1
    AND prev1 - prev2 = 1;
Question 3: Calculate month-over-month accuracy change per model

WITH monthly_avg AS (
    SELECT
        model_name,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', run_date) AS month,
        AVG(accuracy) AS avg_accuracy
    FROM model_results
    GROUP BY model_name, DATE_TRUNC('month', run_date)
)
SELECT
    model_name,
    month,
    avg_accuracy,
    LAG(avg_accuracy) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY month
    ) AS prev_month_accuracy,
    avg_accuracy - LAG(avg_accuracy) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY month
    ) AS mom_change,
    ROUND(
        100.0 * (avg_accuracy - LAG(avg_accuracy) OVER (
            PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY month
        )) /
        NULLIF(LAG(avg_accuracy) OVER (
            PARTITION BY model_name ORDER BY month
        ), 0),
    2) AS pct_change
FROM monthly_avg
ORDER BY model_name, month;

    run_date,
    model_name,
    api_cost,
    SUM(api_cost) OVER (
        PARTITION BY model_name, DATE_TRUNC('month', run_date)
        ORDER BY run_date
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

    department,
    PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS median_salary,

Common Mistakes
Confusing WHERE with HAVING

-- WRONG: WHERE cannot filter on window function results
SELECT model_name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY accuracy DESC) AS rnk
FROM model_results
WHERE rnk <= 3;  -- Error: column "rnk" does not exist

-- CORRECT: wrap in a subquery or CTE
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT model_name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY accuracy DESC) AS rnk
    FROM model_results
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 3;
Forgetting NULLIF when dividing

-- WRONG: division by zero crashes the query
SELECT model_name, correct_predictions / total_predictions AS accuracy
FROM model_results;

-- CORRECT: handle zero denominator
SELECT model_name,
       correct_predictions / NULLIF(total_predictions, 0) AS accuracy
FROM model_results;
Using GROUP BY when you need a window function

-- WRONG: GROUP BY collapses rows, losing individual records
SELECT user_id, SUM(spend) FROM purchases GROUP BY user_id;
-- You can no longer see individual purchase details

-- If you need both the detail AND the aggregate, use a window function
SELECT user_id, purchase_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS total_spend
FROM purchases;
Recursive CTEs without a depth limit

-- DANGEROUS: if there are circular references in data, this runs forever
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, manager_id FROM employees WHERE id = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.manager_id FROM employees e JOIN org ON e.manager_id = org.id
    -- No depth limit!
)
SELECT * FROM org;

-- SAFE: always add WHERE depth < N
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has been applied. You cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE but you can in HAVING. Window function aliases cannot be used in WHERE or HAVING — they must be wrapped in a CTE or subquery.
What is a CTE and why use it instead of a subquery?

A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named temporary result set defined with WITH at the start of a query. It is preferable to subqueries because it can be named descriptively, referenced multiple times in the same query (a subquery cannot), and it formats the query as sequential readable steps rather than nesting. Some databases also optimize CTEs differently.
What is the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK, and ROW_NUMBER?

All three assign a number to each row within a partition. ROW_NUMBER always gives unique sequential integers with no ties. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then skips — if two rows tie for rank 1, the next rank is 3. DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number but does not skip — if two rows tie for rank 1, the next rank is 2.
Intermediate Level
How do you find the Nth highest value in a column?

Use DENSE_RANK() inside a CTE, then filter on rnk = N. Using OFFSET N-1 LIMIT 1 is simpler but returns the Nth highest distinct value unreliably when there are ties. DENSE_RANK handles ties correctly and is the preferred interview answer.
What is the difference between ROWS and RANGE in window frame specifications?

ROWS counts physical rows — ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW always includes exactly 3 rows. RANGE counts logical values — RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes all rows whose ORDER BY value is within 2 units of the current row's value. If the column has duplicates, RANGE can include more rows than you expect. ROWS is more predictable and is more commonly used.
When would you use a recursive CTE over a self-join?

A recursive CTE is needed when you do not know the depth of the hierarchy in advance — org charts, category trees, and graph paths can be arbitrarily deep. A self-join can only traverse a fixed number of levels. For a 2-level hierarchy you could self-join twice, but for unknown depth you need recursion.
Advanced Level
How does a database decide whether to use an index?

The query planner uses statistics about table size, column cardinality, and data distribution to estimate the cost of a sequential scan vs an index scan. If the query returns a large fraction of the table (typically above 5-20%), a sequential scan is often faster than random-access index lookups. The planner also considers whether the query can be satisfied entirely from the index (an index-only scan). You can view the decision with EXPLAIN.
Explain how window functions are executed in a query's logical order

SQL's logical query order is: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Window functions are evaluated in the SELECT phase, after WHERE and GROUP BY but before ORDER BY. This means you can use window functions on already-grouped data, but you cannot filter on window function results with WHERE or HAVING — you must wrap the query in a CTE or subquery and filter the outer query.

-- Schema setup
CREATE TABLE experiments (
    id              SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    experiment_name VARCHAR(100),
    model_name      VARCHAR(100),
    created_by      VARCHAR(100),
    created_at      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
    status          VARCHAR(20),  -- 'running', 'completed', 'failed'
    hyperparams     JSONB,
    tags            TEXT[]
);

CREATE TABLE training_epochs (
    id              SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    experiment_id   INT REFERENCES experiments(id),
    epoch           INT,
    train_loss      FLOAT,
    val_loss        FLOAT,
    train_accuracy  FLOAT,
    val_accuracy    FLOAT,
    learning_rate   FLOAT,
    recorded_at     TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- ============================================================
-- QUERY 1: Experiment leaderboard with rankings
-- ============================================================
WITH final_metrics AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (experiment_id)
        experiment_id,
        epoch AS final_epoch,
        val_accuracy AS final_accuracy,
        val_loss AS final_loss
    FROM training_epochs
    ORDER BY experiment_id, epoch DESC
),
experiment_stats AS (
    SELECT
        e.id,
        e.experiment_name,
        e.model_name,
        e.created_by,
        e.status,
        fm.final_epoch,
        fm.final_accuracy,
        fm.final_loss,
        e.hyperparams->>'learning_rate' AS lr,
        e.hyperparams->>'batch_size' AS batch_size
    FROM experiments e
    JOIN final_metrics fm ON e.id = fm.experiment_id
    WHERE e.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY final_accuracy DESC) AS rank,
    experiment_name,
    model_name,
    created_by,
    final_accuracy,
    final_loss,
    final_epoch,
    lr,
    batch_size
FROM experiment_stats
ORDER BY rank;

-- ============================================================
-- QUERY 2: Per-experiment training curve (epoch-by-epoch analysis)
-- ============================================================
SELECT
    experiment_id,
    epoch,
    val_loss,
    LAG(val_loss) OVER (
        PARTITION BY experiment_id ORDER BY epoch
    ) AS prev_val_loss,
    val_loss - LAG(val_loss) OVER (
        PARTITION BY experiment_id ORDER BY epoch
    ) AS loss_delta,
    AVG(val_loss) OVER (
        PARTITION BY experiment_id
        ORDER BY epoch
        ROWS BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS val_loss_ma5,
    MIN(val_loss) OVER (
        PARTITION BY experiment_id
        ORDER BY epoch
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS best_val_loss_so_far,
    CASE
        WHEN val_loss <= MIN(val_loss) OVER (
            PARTITION BY experiment_id
            ORDER BY epoch
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
        ) THEN 'New Best'
        WHEN val_loss > LAG(val_loss) OVER (
            PARTITION BY experiment_id ORDER BY epoch
        ) THEN 'Degrading'
        ELSE 'Improving'
    END AS epoch_status
FROM training_epochs
WHERE experiment_id = 1
ORDER BY epoch;

-- ============================================================
-- QUERY 3: Early stopping analysis — how many epochs before plateau?
-- ============================================================
WITH epoch_data AS (
    SELECT
        experiment_id,
        epoch,
        val_loss,
        MIN(val_loss) OVER (
            PARTITION BY experiment_id
            ORDER BY epoch
            ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS best_so_far,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY experiment_id ORDER BY epoch
        ) - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY experiment_id,
            CASE WHEN val_loss = MIN(val_loss) OVER (
                PARTITION BY experiment_id
                ORDER BY epoch
                ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
            ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
            ORDER BY epoch
        ) AS streak_no_improvement
    FROM training_epochs
)
SELECT
    e.experiment_name,
    ed.epoch,
    ed.val_loss,
    ed.streak_no_improvement,
    CASE
        WHEN ed.streak_no_improvement >= 5 THEN 'Would trigger early stop (patience=5)'
        ELSE 'Still learning'
    END AS early_stop_status
FROM epoch_data ed
JOIN experiments e ON ed.experiment_id = e.id
WHERE ed.streak_no_improvement >= 3
ORDER BY ed.experiment_id, ed.epoch;

-- ============================================================
-- QUERY 4: Hyperparameter impact analysis
-- ============================================================
WITH experiment_results AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (te.experiment_id)
        te.experiment_id,
        e.hyperparams->>'optimizer' AS optimizer,
        (e.hyperparams->>'learning_rate')::FLOAT AS lr,
        (e.hyperparams->>'batch_size')::INT AS batch_size,
        (e.hyperparams->>'dropout_rate')::FLOAT AS dropout,
        te.val_accuracy AS final_accuracy
    FROM training_epochs te
    JOIN experiments e ON te.experiment_id = e.id
    WHERE e.status = 'completed'
    ORDER BY te.experiment_id, te.epoch DESC
)
SELECT
    optimizer,
    ROUND(AVG(lr)::NUMERIC, 6) AS avg_lr,
    ROUND(AVG(batch_size)::NUMERIC, 0) AS avg_batch,
    ROUND(AVG(final_accuracy)::NUMERIC, 4) AS avg_accuracy,
    ROUND(STDDEV(final_accuracy)::NUMERIC, 4) AS accuracy_stddev,
    COUNT(*) AS num_experiments,
    ROUND(MAX(final_accuracy)::NUMERIC, 4) AS best_accuracy
FROM experiment_results
GROUP BY optimizer
ORDER BY avg_accuracy DESC;
Chapter Summary
Window functions perform calculations across related rows without collapsing them — unlike GROUP BY
ROW_NUMBER gives unique ranks, RANK skips after ties, DENSE_RANK does not skip
LAG and LEAD access values from previous and next rows — essential for trend analysis
The frame clause (ROWS BETWEEN ... AND ...) precisely controls which rows are included in a window
CTEs with WITH make complex queries readable by naming intermediate steps — they can be chained and reused within the same query
Recursive CTEs use UNION ALL to reference themselves — the anchor member starts the recursion, the recursive member extends it, always add a depth limit
CASE expressions add conditional logic anywhere in SQL — especially powerful inside aggregations to pivot data
String functions clean and normalize dirty data; date functions enable time series and cohort analysis
JSONB in PostgreSQL supports indexed, queryable semi-structured data storage
EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals what the database actually does — indexes eliminate sequential scans on large tables
Cheat Sheet

-- Window function syntax
fn() OVER (
    PARTITION BY col
    ORDER BY col
    ROWS BETWEEN X PRECEDING AND Y FOLLOWING
)

-- Ranking
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)  -- unique
RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)  -- skips after tie
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)  -- no skip
NTILE(4)     OVER (ORDER BY y)                  -- quartiles

-- Offset
LAG(col, 1, default)  OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)
LEAD(col, 1, default) OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y)

-- Aggregate as window
SUM(col)   OVER (PARTITION BY x ORDER BY y ROWS BETWEEN ...)
AVG(col)   OVER (...)
COUNT(*)   OVER (...)
MIN/MAX(col) OVER (...)

-- CTE
WITH name AS (SELECT ...)
SELECT * FROM name;

-- Multiple CTEs
WITH a AS (...), b AS (SELECT * FROM a WHERE ...)
SELECT * FROM b;

-- Recursive CTE
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT ... FROM t WHERE base_condition  -- anchor
    UNION ALL
    SELECT ... FROM t JOIN tree ON ...      -- recursive
    WHERE depth < 50                        -- safety limit
)
SELECT * FROM tree;

-- CASE
CASE WHEN cond THEN val ELSE other END
CASE col WHEN val1 THEN r1 WHEN val2 THEN r2 END

-- JSON (PostgreSQL)
col->>'key'         -- extract as text
col->'key'          -- extract as JSON
col ? 'key'         -- key exists
col @> '{"k":"v"}'  -- contains

-- Useful string functions
TRIM / LTRIM / RTRIM
UPPER / LOWER / INITCAP
LEFT(str, n) / RIGHT(str, n)
SUBSTRING(str FROM n FOR len)
REPLACE(str, from, to)
SPLIT_PART(str, delim, n)
LENGTH(str)
CONCAT(a, b, c)

-- Useful date functions
NOW() / CURRENT_DATE
DATE_TRUNC('month', col)
EXTRACT(YEAR FROM col)
col + INTERVAL '7 days'
AGE(date1, date2)
Revision Notes
Window function evaluates after WHERE/GROUP BY but before ORDER BY — cannot be filtered with WHERE, must wrap in CTE
PARTITION BY in window = the group; without it, the entire table is one window
ROW_NUMBER never ties; RANK skips; DENSE_RANK does not skip — know all three cold
LAG default value prevents NULLs on the first row — always provide one
CTE with WITH is evaluated once per reference in most databases (PostgreSQL materializes by default)
Recursive CTEs always need both an anchor member and a recursive member, always use UNION ALL not UNION
JSONB (binary JSON) is faster to query than JSON in PostgreSQL — always prefer JSONB
EXPLAIN ANALYZE = plan + actual times; EXPLAIN = plan only (no execution)
Avoid functions on indexed columns in WHERE — they prevent index use
NULLIF(denominator, 0) prevents division-by-zero errors — use it whenever dividing
