# transfer_learning_classifier.py
# End-to-end transfer learning pipeline with Grad-CAM interpretability check

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchvision import models, transforms
import numpy as np

IMAGENET_MEAN = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406]
IMAGENET_STD = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]

class TransferLearningClassifier:
    def __init__(self, num_classes, freeze_backbone=True, device="cpu"):
        self.device = device
        self.model = models.resnet18(weights=models.ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1)

        if freeze_backbone:
            for param in self.model.parameters():
                param.requires_grad = False

        self.model.fc = nn.Linear(self.model.fc.in_features, num_classes)
        self.model.to(device)

        trainable_params = [p for p in self.model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
        self.optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(trainable_params, lr=1e-3)
        self.criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

        # Grad-CAM setup on the last conv layer
        self.target_layer = self.model.layer4[-1].conv2
        self.gradients = None
        self.activations = None
        self.target_layer.register_forward_hook(self._save_activation)
        self.target_layer.register_full_backward_hook(self._save_gradient)

    def _save_activation(self, module, input, output):
        self.activations = output.detach()

    def _save_gradient(self, module, grad_input, grad_output):
        self.gradients = grad_output[0].detach()

    def train_step(self, images, labels):
        self.model.train()
        images, labels = images.to(self.device), labels.to(self.device)

        self.optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = self.model(images)
        loss = self.criterion(outputs, labels)
        loss.backward()
        self.optimizer.step()

        preds = outputs.argmax(dim=1)
        accuracy = (preds == labels).float().mean().item()
        return loss.item(), accuracy

    def evaluate(self, images, labels):
        self.model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            images, labels = images.to(self.device), labels.to(self.device)
            outputs = self.model(images)
            loss = self.criterion(outputs, labels)
            preds = outputs.argmax(dim=1)
            accuracy = (preds == labels).float().mean().item()
        return loss.item(), accuracy

    def explain_prediction(self, image_tensor):
        """Generate a Grad-CAM heatmap for a single image"""
        self.model.eval()
        image_tensor = image_tensor.unsqueeze(0).to(self.device).requires_grad_(True)

        output = self.model(image_tensor)
        predicted_class = output.argmax(dim=1).item()

        self.model.zero_grad()
        output[0, predicted_class].backward()

        weights = self.gradients.mean(dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True)
        cam = F.relu((weights * self.activations).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True))
        cam = cam.squeeze().cpu().numpy()
        cam = (cam - cam.min()) / (cam.max() - cam.min() + 1e-8)

        return cam, predicted_class


def generate_dummy_batch(batch_size=16, num_classes=5):
    """Simulate a labeled image batch for demonstration purposes"""
    images = torch.rand(batch_size, 3, 224, 224)
    labels = torch.randint(0, num_classes, (batch_size,))
    return images, labels


def main():
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    num_classes = 5

    print(f"Using device: {device}\n")
    classifier = TransferLearningClassifier(num_classes=num_classes,
                                             freeze_backbone=True, device=device)

    print("Training (feature extraction — frozen backbone)...\n")
    for epoch in range(5):
        train_images, train_labels = generate_dummy_batch(num_classes=num_classes)
        loss, acc = classifier.train_step(train_images, train_labels)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1} | Loss: {loss:.4f} | Accuracy: {acc:.2%}")

    print("\nEvaluating on a held-out simulated batch...")
    val_images, val_labels = generate_dummy_batch(num_classes=num_classes)
    val_loss, val_acc = classifier.evaluate(val_images, val_labels)
    print(f"Validation Loss: {val_loss:.4f} | Validation Accuracy: {val_acc:.2%}")

    print("\nGenerating Grad-CAM explanation for a single sample...")
    sample_image = val_images[0]
    heatmap, predicted_class = classifier.explain_prediction(sample_image)
    print(f"Predicted class: {predicted_class}")
    print(f"Grad-CAM heatmap shape: {heatmap.shape}")
    print(f"Heatmap value range: [{heatmap.min():.3f}, {heatmap.max():.3f}]")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Introduction

Object detection localizes objects with a rectangular bounding box — a coarse approximation of shape. Image segmentation goes a level deeper: it classifies every single pixel in an image, producing a precise, pixel-accurate map of where objects are and what they are.

This precision matters enormously in domains where a rough box isn't good enough — medical imaging (exact tumor boundary matters for treatment planning), autonomous driving (exact drivable road surface matters for safety), and satellite imagery (exact land parcel boundaries matter for analysis). This chapter covers the major segmentation paradigms and the architectures that made pixel-level prediction practical at scale.
Semantic Segmentation vs Instance Segmentation
The Three Segmentation Tasks

Original Image: A photo with 3 people and a dog

Semantic Segmentation:
  Every pixel labeled by CLASS only
  → all 3 people get the same "person" label (indistinguishable from each other)
  → dog pixels get "dog" label
  → background gets "background" label

Instance Segmentation:
  Every pixel labeled by CLASS + INDIVIDUAL INSTANCE
  → person 1, person 2, person 3 are separately identified
  → dog is its own instance

Panoptic Segmentation:
  Combines both: instance-level for "countable" objects (people, dog),
  semantic-level for "stuff" categories (sky, road, grass) that have no
  discrete instances
Why This Distinction Matters

Semantic segmentation is a per-pixel classification problem — conceptually similar to Chapter 61's classification, just applied densely across every pixel instead of the whole image. Instance segmentation is fundamentally harder: it must also solve the detection problem (find and separate individual object instances) before or during segmentation.
FCN and U-Net
Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN)

Before FCN (2015), CNN classifiers ended in fully-connected layers, which discard spatial structure — they can tell you what is in an image but not where. FCN's key insight: replace the fully-connected layers with convolutional layers throughout, preserving spatial information end-to-end, and add an upsampling path to bring the output back to the original image resolution.

Input Image (H x W x 3)
      │
Downsampling path (standard CNN — conv + pooling, reduces spatial size)
      │
Bottleneck: low-resolution, high-channel feature map
      │
Upsampling path (transposed convolutions — restores spatial size)
      │
Output: (H x W x num_classes) — per-pixel class scores

FCN's downsampling repeatedly shrinks the image (via pooling/strided convs) while increasing channel depth to capture semantic meaning, then upsamples back to full resolution using transposed convolutions (sometimes called "deconvolutions") to recover a dense, per-pixel prediction map.
The Problem FCN Left Unsolved: Detail Loss

Because downsampling aggressively compresses spatial detail into a small bottleneck, the naive upsampling path in plain FCN struggles to recover fine boundary details — segmentation edges tend to come out blurry or blocky, especially for small or thin objects.
U-Net: Skip Connections for Precise Localization

U-Net (originally designed for biomedical image segmentation, 2015) solves FCN's detail-loss problem with skip connections that directly copy feature maps from the downsampling path to the corresponding upsampling stage, at matching resolution.

Input Image
                     │
    ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
    │         ENCODER (Downsampling)   │
    │  Conv+Pool → Conv+Pool → Conv+Pool│
    └───────┬──────────┬──────────┬────┘
            │          │          │
        (skip)      (skip)     (skip)
            │          │          │
    ┌───────┴──────────┴──────────┴────┐
    │         DECODER (Upsampling)     │
    │  UpConv+Concat → UpConv+Concat   │
    └────────────────┬──────────────────┘
                     │
              Output Segmentation Map

This gives U-Net the classic symmetric "U" shape it's named after: the encoder captures what is in the image at increasingly abstract levels, while the skip-connected decoder recovers precisely where the boundaries are, by directly reusing high-resolution detail from the corresponding encoder stage rather than trying to reconstruct it purely from the compressed bottleneck.
U-Net in PyTorch

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class DoubleConv(nn.Module):
    """Two consecutive 3x3 convolutions — the basic U-Net building block"""
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.conv(x)


class UNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels=3, num_classes=1, features=[64, 128, 256, 512]):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder_blocks = nn.ModuleList()
        self.decoder_blocks = nn.ModuleList()
        self.upconvs = nn.ModuleList()
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)

        # Encoder (downsampling path)
        channels = in_channels
        for feature in features:
            self.encoder_blocks.append(DoubleConv(channels, feature))
            channels = feature

        # Bottleneck
        self.bottleneck = DoubleConv(features[-1], features[-1] * 2)

        # Decoder (upsampling path) — built in reverse
        for feature in reversed(features):
            self.upconvs.append(
                nn.ConvTranspose2d(feature * 2, feature, kernel_size=2, stride=2)
            )
            self.decoder_blocks.append(DoubleConv(feature * 2, feature))   # *2 due to skip concat

        # Final 1x1 conv maps to the desired number of output classes
        self.final_conv = nn.Conv2d(features[0], num_classes, kernel_size=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        skip_connections = []

        # Encoder pass — save output before each pooling step
        for block in self.encoder_blocks:
            x = block(x)
            skip_connections.append(x)
            x = self.pool(x)

        x = self.bottleneck(x)
        skip_connections = skip_connections[::-1]   # Reverse for easy indexing

        # Decoder pass — upsample, concat matching skip connection, then convolve
        for i in range(len(self.upconvs)):
            x = self.upconvs[i](x)
            skip = skip_connections[i]

            # Handle any size mismatch from rounding during pooling
            if x.shape != skip.shape:
                x = nn.functional.interpolate(x, size=skip.shape[2:])

            x = torch.cat([skip, x], dim=1)   # Skip connection: concatenate along channels
            x = self.decoder_blocks[i](x)

        return self.final_conv(x)


# Example usage
model = UNet(in_channels=3, num_classes=1)   # Binary segmentation (e.g., tumor vs background)
dummy_input = torch.rand(2, 3, 256, 256)
output = model(dummy_input)
print(output.shape)   # torch.Size([2, 1, 256, 256]) — per-pixel logit for the foreground class
U-Net Training Loop (Binary Segmentation)

import torch.nn.functional as F

model = UNet(in_channels=3, num_classes=1)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

def dice_loss(pred, target, smooth=1e-6):
    """
    Dice loss — commonly used alongside or instead of BCE for segmentation,
    especially with class imbalance (e.g., small tumor region vs large background)
    """
    pred = torch.sigmoid(pred)
    pred_flat = pred.view(-1)
    target_flat = target.view(-1)

    intersection = (pred_flat * target_flat).sum()
    dice = (2. * intersection + smooth) / (pred_flat.sum() + target_flat.sum() + smooth)
    return 1 - dice

def train_step(images, masks):
    """images: (batch, 3, H, W), masks: (batch, 1, H, W) with values 0 or 1"""
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    logits = model(images)

    bce = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, masks)
    dice = dice_loss(logits, masks)
    loss = bce + dice   # Combined loss is a common practical choice

    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()
Mask R-CNN
Extending Faster R-CNN for Instance Segmentation

Mask R-CNN (2017) adds a third branch to the Faster R-CNN architecture from Chapter 62: alongside the existing classification and bounding-box regression heads, it adds a small FCN-style mask prediction head that outputs a binary segmentation mask for each detected object.

Image → Backbone CNN → Feature Map
                            │
              Region Proposal Network (RPN)
                            │
                  RoIAlign (per proposed region)
                            │
        ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
        │                   │                   │
  Classification      Bounding Box         Mask Prediction
     Head               Regression Head    (small FCN, per class)

The classification and box heads work exactly as in Faster R-CNN. The new mask head predicts a small (e.g., 28×28) binary mask for each RoI, independently for each possible class, and only the mask corresponding to the predicted class is used at inference — this decouples what the object is (classification) from what shape it has (mask), which the authors found works better than trying to predict a multi-class mask directly.
RoIAlign: The Critical Fix Over RoI Pooling

The original Faster R-CNN's RoI Pooling used integer rounding when mapping proposed regions onto the feature map grid, introducing small misalignments between the proposed region and the extracted features. For bounding boxes this misalignment is usually tolerable, but for pixel-precise masks it causes visible, sometimes serious quality degradation.

RoIAlign fixes this by using bilinear interpolation instead of rounding, precisely aligning extracted features with the exact proposed region coordinates — this single change was a major contributor to Mask R-CNN's mask quality and is now a standard technique whenever pixel-level precision matters.

# Mask R-CNN is typically used via a pretrained implementation rather than
# built from scratch — torchvision provides a ready-to-use version

import torchvision
from torchvision.models.detection import maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2

model = maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2(weights="DEFAULT")
model.eval()

# Inference
images = [torch.rand(3, 480, 640)]   # List of tensors, one per image
predictions = model(images)

pred = predictions[0]
print(pred.keys())          # dict_keys(['boxes', 'labels', 'scores', 'masks'])

DeepLab
The Atrous (Dilated) Convolution Insight

Standard CNNs use pooling to enlarge the receptive field (how much of the input each neuron "sees"), but pooling also reduces spatial resolution — directly conflicting with segmentation's need for dense, full-resolution output. DeepLab's key innovation is atrous (dilated) convolution, which enlarges the receptive field without any pooling or resolution loss, by inserting gaps between kernel elements.

Standard 3x3 convolution kernel positions:  X X X
                                             X X X
                                             X X X

Dilated 3x3 convolution (dilation=2):       X . X . X
                                             . . . . .
                                             X . X . X
                                             . . . . .
                                             X . X . X

A dilation rate of r inserts r-1 zeros between adjacent kernel weights, expanding the effective receptive field to cover a much larger area using the same number of parameters and the same output resolution as a standard convolution.

import torch.nn as nn

# Standard convolution
standard_conv = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1, dilation=1)

# Dilated convolution — same kernel size, much larger receptive field
dilated_conv = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=2, dilation=2)
dilated_conv_large = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=4, dilation=4)
Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP)

DeepLab applies several parallel atrous convolutions with different dilation rates on the same feature map, then concatenates their outputs — this captures context at multiple scales simultaneously (small dilation for fine detail, large dilation for broader context), which is especially valuable since objects in real images appear at wildly varying sizes.

class ASPP(nn.Module):
    """Simplified Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling module"""
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.branch1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, 1)  # 1x1, no dilation
        self.branch2 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, 3, padding=6, dilation=6)
        self.branch3 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, 3, padding=12, dilation=12)
        self.branch4 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, 3, padding=18, dilation=18)
        self.project = nn.Conv2d(out_channels * 4, out_channels, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        b1 = self.branch1(x)
        b2 = self.branch2(x)
        b3 = self.branch3(x)
        b4 = self.branch4(x)
        combined = torch.cat([b1, b2, b3, b4], dim=1)
        return self.project(combined)
SAM (Segment Anything Model)
A New Paradigm: Promptable Segmentation

SAM (Meta AI, 2023) introduced a fundamentally different approach: instead of training a model for one fixed set of classes, SAM is trained to segment any object, given a "prompt" indicating what to segment — a point, a bounding box, or a rough mask.

Input: Image + Prompt (e.g., a single click point on an object)
Output: A precise segmentation mask for whatever object the point falls on
Why This Matters

SAM was trained on over a billion masks across 11 million images, giving it strong zero-shot generalization — it can segment objects and categories it never saw during training, without any fine-tuning. This makes it exceptionally useful for rapid dataset annotation (click once, get a precise mask instead of drawing one by hand) and for interactive segmentation tools.

SAM's Practical Role in a 2026 CV Workflow

SAM is rarely the final production model for a fixed-category task — it's far more commonly used as an annotation accelerator (dramatically speeding up dataset labeling for a task-specific model like U-Net or Mask R-CNN) or as an interactive tool in products where a user points at what they want segmented (photo editing, medical annotation tools).
Implementation and Applications
Choosing an Architecture for Your Task
Real-World Applications
Medical imaging — tumor/organ boundary delineation (U-Net's original domain), where pixel-precise boundaries directly affect treatment decisions.
Autonomous driving — drivable surface, lane markings, and pedestrian segmentation, often using panoptic segmentation for full scene understanding.
Satellite/aerial imagery — land use classification, building footprint extraction, agricultural monitoring (semantic segmentation over very large images).
Content-aware photo editing — background removal, object isolation ("magic eraser"-style tools), frequently powered by SAM or similar promptable models.
Manufacturing quality control — precise defect region segmentation on product images, where the extent of a defect matters, not just its presence.
Common Mistakes

Using standard cross-entropy loss alone on heavily imbalanced segmentation masks. When the foreground object occupies a small fraction of the image (e.g., a small tumor), cross-entropy alone can be dominated by the easy, abundant background pixels. Dice loss, or a combined BCE + Dice loss, is standard practice for this reason.

Ignoring skip connections in a custom encoder-decoder segmentation model. Without them, fine boundary detail is lost in the bottleneck, and models like plain FCN produce visibly blurry, blocky segmentation boundaries.

Confusing semantic and instance segmentation requirements. If the task requires counting or tracking individual objects, semantic segmentation alone is insufficient, since it merges all objects of the same class into one undifferentiated region — Mask R-CNN or a similar instance-aware model is required.

Expecting SAM to work well for highly specialized domains out of the box. SAM's zero-shot generalization is strong for natural-image-like objects, but it can underperform a task-specific fine-tuned model on very specialized domains (certain medical modalities, satellite imagery) where object boundaries differ significantly from its training distribution.

Evaluating segmentation quality with accuracy alone. Pixel accuracy can look deceptively high even for a poor model, simply because background pixels usually dominate the image. IoU (per-class and mean) and Dice coefficient are the standard, more informative segmentation metrics.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation?

Semantic segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel but does not distinguish between separate objects of the same class — all pixels belonging to "person," for example, get the same label regardless of how many people are present. Instance segmentation additionally separates individual object instances, so each person in the image is identified as a distinct entity with their own mask.
Why does U-Net use skip connections?

The encoder (downsampling) path compresses the image into an abstract, low-resolution bottleneck, losing fine spatial detail along the way. Skip connections copy feature maps from each encoder stage directly to the matching decoder stage, giving the decoder access to high-resolution detail it would otherwise have to reconstruct from scratch, resulting in much sharper, more precise segmentation boundaries.
What is SAM and how is it different from a typical segmentation model?

SAM (Segment Anything Model) is a promptable segmentation model — instead of being trained on a fixed set of classes, it takes a prompt (like a point or box) and segments whatever object is indicated, generalizing to object categories it never explicitly saw during training. Typical segmentation models like U-Net or Mask R-CNN are trained for a fixed, predefined set of classes.
Intermediate Level
Explain how Mask R-CNN extends Faster R-CNN to perform instance segmentation.

Mask R-CNN adds a third parallel head to Faster R-CNN's existing classification and bounding-box regression heads: a small FCN-style mask prediction head that outputs a binary mask for each region of interest, predicted independently per class. It also replaces RoI Pooling with RoIAlign, using bilinear interpolation instead of integer rounding to precisely align extracted features with the region's true coordinates — critical for producing pixel-accurate masks rather than just boxes.
What problem do atrous (dilated) convolutions solve in DeepLab, and how do they solve it?

Standard CNNs typically use pooling to expand the receptive field, but pooling reduces spatial resolution, which conflicts with segmentation's need for dense, full-resolution predictions. Atrous convolutions expand the receptive field by inserting gaps between kernel elements, without any pooling or loss of resolution, letting the network see a wider context at the same output resolution and parameter count as a standard convolution.
Why is Dice loss often preferred over plain cross-entropy for segmentation tasks with class imbalance?

Dice loss is directly based on the overlap between predicted and ground-truth regions (similar in spirit to IoU), which naturally focuses on getting the minority foreground region right, regardless of how small it is relative to the image. Cross-entropy treats every pixel independently and equally, so when background pixels vastly outnumber foreground pixels, the loss can be dominated by the easy background majority, causing the model to under-prioritize the harder, smaller foreground region.
Advanced Level
Why does RoIAlign produce meaningfully better masks than RoI Pooling, given that both are used for the same purpose?

RoI Pooling maps a proposed region onto the feature map grid using integer-based rounding at each step (both when dividing the region into bins and when pooling within each bin), introducing small but real spatial misalignments between the extracted features and the true region boundaries. For bounding box regression, these small misalignments are largely tolerable since box coordinates are inherently a coarse approximation. For pixel-level mask prediction, however, these same misalignments directly translate into misaligned mask boundaries, which is highly visible and damaging to mask quality — RoIAlign avoids this entirely by using bilinear interpolation to sample feature values at exact, non-rounded coordinates.
How would you decide between fine-tuning a U-Net from scratch versus using SAM-generated masks as training data for a specialized domain like satellite imagery?

If speed of initial annotation is the primary bottleneck and some domain gap with SAM's training distribution is tolerable, using SAM to rapidly generate initial masks (which can then be manually corrected rather than drawn from scratch) can save enormous annotation time before training a dedicated model. If SAM's zero-shot masks prove unreliable on the specific domain — which is common in specialized imagery quite different from natural photos — investing directly in manually annotated data and training a dedicated architecture like U-Net or DeepLab from the start may be more reliable, since SAM's masks might introduce systematic errors that get baked into any model trained purely on its output.
Explain why panoptic segmentation requires combining ideas from both semantic and instance segmentation rather than using either approach alone.

Real scenes contain two fundamentally different categories of content: "things" — countable, distinct objects like people or cars, which benefit from instance-level separation — and "stuff" — uncountable, amorphous regions like sky, road, or grass, which have no natural notion of a countable instance and are better handled with per-pixel class labels alone. Pure instance segmentation struggles to sensibly represent "stuff" categories (there's no natural way to count "instances" of sky), while pure semantic segmentation cannot distinguish between individual "thing" instances (multiple people become one undifferentiated blob). Panoptic segmentation architectures combine an instance segmentation branch for "things" with a semantic segmentation branch for "stuff," merging both into one consistent output.

# medical_segmentation.py
# U-Net-based binary segmentation pipeline for medical lesion/tumor detection
# Simulates a realistic training and evaluation workflow

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import numpy as np

class DoubleConv(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, 3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
            nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, 3, padding=1),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
            nn.ReLU(inplace=True),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.conv(x)


class UNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels=1, num_classes=1, features=[32, 64, 128, 256]):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder_blocks = nn.ModuleList()
        self.decoder_blocks = nn.ModuleList()
        self.upconvs = nn.ModuleList()
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2, 2)

        channels = in_channels
        for feature in features:
            self.encoder_blocks.append(DoubleConv(channels, feature))
            channels = feature

        self.bottleneck = DoubleConv(features[-1], features[-1] * 2)

        for feature in reversed(features):
            self.upconvs.append(nn.ConvTranspose2d(feature * 2, feature, 2, stride=2))
            self.decoder_blocks.append(DoubleConv(feature * 2, feature))

        self.final_conv = nn.Conv2d(features[0], num_classes, kernel_size=1)

    def forward(self, x):
        skips = []
        for block in self.encoder_blocks:
            x = block(x)
            skips.append(x)
            x = self.pool(x)

        x = self.bottleneck(x)
        skips = skips[::-1]

        for i in range(len(self.upconvs)):
            x = self.upconvs[i](x)
            skip = skips[i]
            if x.shape != skip.shape:
                x = F.interpolate(x, size=skip.shape[2:])
            x = torch.cat([skip, x], dim=1)
            x = self.decoder_blocks[i](x)

        return self.final_conv(x)


def dice_coefficient(pred, target, smooth=1e-6):
    """Evaluation metric — NOT used as the loss directly here (see combined loss below)"""
    pred = (torch.sigmoid(pred) > 0.5).float()
    intersection = (pred * target).sum()
    return (2. * intersection + smooth) / (pred.sum() + target.sum() + smooth)


def iou_score(pred, target, smooth=1e-6):
    pred = (torch.sigmoid(pred) > 0.5).float()
    intersection = (pred * target).sum()
    union = pred.sum() + target.sum() - intersection
    return (intersection + smooth) / (union + smooth)


def combined_loss(pred, target):
    bce = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(pred, target)
    pred_sig = torch.sigmoid(pred)
    intersection = (pred_sig * target).sum()
    dice_loss = 1 - (2. * intersection + 1e-6) / (pred_sig.sum() + target.sum() + 1e-6)
    return bce + dice_loss


def generate_synthetic_scan_batch(batch_size=8, img_size=128):
    """
    Simulates grayscale medical scans with a circular 'lesion' region.
    In practice this would be real MRI/CT slices with radiologist-annotated masks.
    """
    images = torch.randn(batch_size, 1, img_size, img_size) * 0.1 + 0.5
    masks = torch.zeros(batch_size, 1, img_size, img_size)

    for i in range(batch_size):
        cx, cy = np.random.randint(30, img_size - 30, size=2)
        radius = np.random.randint(8, 20)

        yy, xx = np.meshgrid(np.arange(img_size), np.arange(img_size), indexing="ij")
        lesion_mask = (xx - cx) ** 2 + (yy - cy) ** 2 <= radius ** 2

        images[i, 0][lesion_mask] += 0.3   # Lesion appears slightly brighter
        masks[i, 0] = torch.tensor(lesion_mask, dtype=torch.float32)

    return images, masks


def train_and_evaluate():
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    model = UNet(in_channels=1, num_classes=1, features=[16, 32, 64])
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

    print("Training U-Net on simulated lesion segmentation data...\n")

    for epoch in range(30):
        images, masks = generate_synthetic_scan_batch(batch_size=8, img_size=128)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        logits = model(images)
        loss = combined_loss(logits, masks)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        if (epoch + 1) % 5 == 0:
            with torch.no_grad():
                dice = dice_coefficient(logits, masks).item()
                iou = iou_score(logits, masks).item()
            print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:2d} | Loss: {loss.item():.4f} | "
                  f"Dice: {dice:.4f} | IoU: {iou:.4f}")

    # Final evaluation on a fresh synthetic test batch
    print("\nFinal evaluation on held-out simulated scans:")
    test_images, test_masks = generate_synthetic_scan_batch(batch_size=16, img_size=128)
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        test_logits = model(test_images)
        test_dice = dice_coefficient(test_logits, test_masks).item()
        test_iou = iou_score(test_logits, test_masks).item()

    print(f"Test Dice Coefficient: {test_dice:.4f}")
    print(f"Test IoU Score:        {test_iou:.4f}")

    if test_dice >= 0.85:
        print("\n✓ Strong segmentation performance — boundaries well captured")
    elif test_dice >= 0.60:
        print("\n⚠ Moderate performance — consider more training or data augmentation")
    else:
        print("\n✗ Weak performance — review architecture, loss function, or data quality")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    train_and_evaluate()

Box regression head  -> bounding box
Mask head (new)      -> per-class binary mask, uses RoIAlign

point prompt, box prompt, rough mask prompt -> precise output mask

Vision Transformer (ViT) Architecture
The Core Idea: Images as Sequences of Patches

CNNs process images using convolutions, which have a built-in inductive bias for locality — nearby pixels are assumed to be related. Vision Transformer (ViT), introduced in 2020, makes a bold claim: if you have enough data, you don't need that built-in bias at all — a standard Transformer encoder, with no convolutions, can learn visual patterns directly, provided images are reshaped into something a Transformer already knows how to process: a sequence of tokens.

Image (224x224x3)
      │
Split into fixed-size patches (e.g., 16x16)
      │
196 patches total (14x14 grid) — each treated as a "token"
      │
Flatten each patch + linear projection → patch embedding
      │
Add positional embeddings (same idea as Chapter 58)
      │
Prepend a learnable [CLS] token
      │
Feed the full sequence through a standard Transformer Encoder
      │
Use the [CLS] token's final representation for classification
Patch Embedding

An image of size 224×224×3, split into 16×16 patches, produces (224/16) × (224/16) = 14 × 14 = 196 patches. Each patch is flattened into a vector of length 16×16×3 = 768 and linearly projected into the model's embedding dimension — mathematically, this projection is equivalent to a single strided convolution.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class PatchEmbedding(nn.Module):
    """
    Splits an image into patches and linearly projects each into an embedding.
    Implemented efficiently as a single strided convolution.
    """
    def __init__(self, img_size=224, patch_size=16, in_channels=3, embed_dim=768):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_patches = (img_size // patch_size) ** 2

        # A conv with kernel_size == stride == patch_size splits the image into
        # non-overlapping patches and linearly projects each one in a single operation
        self.projection = nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels, embed_dim, kernel_size=patch_size, stride=patch_size
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (batch, channels, H, W)
        x = self.projection(x)              # (batch, embed_dim, H/patch, W/patch)
        x = x.flatten(2)                    # (batch, embed_dim, num_patches)
        x = x.transpose(1, 2)               # (batch, num_patches, embed_dim)
        return x


# Example
patch_embed = PatchEmbedding(img_size=224, patch_size=16, embed_dim=768)
dummy_image = torch.rand(2, 3, 224, 224)
patches = patch_embed(dummy_image)
print(patches.shape)   # torch.Size([2, 196, 768]) — 196 patch "tokens"
The [CLS] Token

Borrowed directly from BERT (Chapter 69), ViT prepends a learnable [CLS] token to the sequence of patch embeddings. This token has no fixed image content of its own — through self-attention, it aggregates information from all patches over the course of the encoder, and its final representation is used as the whole image's summary vector for classification.

class VisionTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, img_size=224, patch_size=16, in_channels=3,
                 embed_dim=768, num_heads=12, num_layers=12, num_classes=1000):
        super().__init__()
        self.patch_embed = PatchEmbedding(img_size, patch_size, in_channels, embed_dim)
        num_patches = self.patch_embed.num_patches

        self.cls_token = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, 1, embed_dim))
        self.pos_embedding = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, num_patches + 1, embed_dim))

        encoder_layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
            d_model=embed_dim, nhead=num_heads, dim_feedforward=embed_dim * 4,
            batch_first=True
        )
        self.encoder = nn.TransformerEncoder(encoder_layer, num_layers=num_layers)

        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)
        self.classifier = nn.Linear(embed_dim, num_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        batch_size = x.shape[0]
        x = self.patch_embed(x)                              # (batch, num_patches, embed_dim)

        cls_tokens = self.cls_token.expand(batch_size, -1, -1)
        x = torch.cat([cls_tokens, x], dim=1)                 # Prepend [CLS] token
        x = x + self.pos_embedding                            # Add positional embeddings

        x = self.encoder(x)                                   # Standard Transformer encoder
        x = self.norm(x)

        cls_output = x[:, 0]                                  # Take only the [CLS] token's output
        return self.classifier(cls_output)


# Example usage
vit = VisionTransformer(num_classes=10)
dummy_image = torch.rand(2, 3, 224, 224)
logits = vit(dummy_image)
print(logits.shape)   # torch.Size([2, 10])
Why ViT Needs Large-Scale Pretraining

CNNs' convolutional inductive bias (locality, translation invariance) acts as a built-in assumption that's usually correct for images, which helps CNNs learn effectively even from moderately sized datasets. ViT has no such built-in assumption — it must learn these patterns purely from data. As a result, ViT trained from scratch on small-to-medium datasets typically underperforms CNNs, but outperforms them when pretrained on very large datasets (hundreds of millions of images), since the Transformer's lack of built-in bias becomes an advantage once there's enough data to learn better, less-constrained patterns directly.
Using a Pretrained ViT

from torchvision import models

CLIP: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining
The Core Idea

CLIP (OpenAI, 2021) trains two separate encoders — an image encoder (typically a ViT or CNN) and a text encoder (a Transformer, like the ones in Chapter 69) — to project images and their matching text captions into the same shared embedding space, such that a matching image-text pair ends up close together, and non-matching pairs end up far apart.

"A photo of a golden retriever"  ──► Text Encoder ──► Text Embedding  ┐
                                                                        │  Compare via
        [Image of a dog]         ──► Image Encoder ──► Image Embedding ┘  cosine similarity
Contrastive Pretraining

CLIP is trained on hundreds of millions of (image, caption) pairs scraped from the internet — no manual class labels required. For a batch of N image-text pairs, CLIP computes the cosine similarity between every image embedding and every text embedding in the batch, producing an N × N similarity matrix.

The training objective pushes the diagonal entries (correct image-text matches) to be high, and all off-diagonal entries (incorrect pairings, sampled naturally just from being in the same batch) to be low — this is a form of contrastive learning, using the symmetric cross-entropy loss (InfoNCE) applied in both directions (image→text and text→image).

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def clip_contrastive_loss(image_embeddings, text_embeddings, temperature=0.07):
    """
    image_embeddings, text_embeddings: (batch_size, embed_dim), L2-normalized
    """
    # Cosine similarity matrix, scaled by a learned/fixed temperature
    logits = (image_embeddings @ text_embeddings.T) / temperature

    batch_size = image_embeddings.shape[0]
    labels = torch.arange(batch_size)   # Ground truth: image i matches text i (the diagonal)

    loss_image_to_text = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels)
    loss_text_to_image = F.cross_entropy(logits.T, labels)

    return (loss_image_to_text + loss_text_to_image) / 2


# Example usage
batch_size, embed_dim = 8, 512
image_emb = F.normalize(torch.rand(batch_size, embed_dim), dim=-1)
text_emb = F.normalize(torch.rand(batch_size, embed_dim), dim=-1)

loss = clip_contrastive_loss(image_emb, text_emb)
print(f"CLIP contrastive loss: {loss.item():.4f}")
Why This Training Approach Is Powerful

Because CLIP learns from naturally occurring image-caption pairs rather than a fixed, manually annotated set of classes, it develops a much richer, more flexible visual-semantic understanding — it isn't limited to recognizing a predefined list of 1,000 ImageNet categories, but can, in principle, understand any concept expressible in natural language that appeared meaningfully in its training data.
Zero-Shot Image Classification with CLIP

CLIP's most striking practical property: it can classify images into arbitrary, never-trained-on categories, simply by comparing the image embedding against text embeddings of candidate class descriptions.

# Using OpenAI's CLIP via the official library (pip install openai-clip or open_clip_torch)
import torch
import clip
from PIL import Image

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model, preprocess = clip.load("ViT-B/32", device=device)

image = preprocess(Image.open("photo.jpg")).unsqueeze(0).to(device)

# Arbitrary candidate labels — CLIP was never explicitly trained to distinguish these
candidate_labels = ["a photo of a cat", "a photo of a dog", "a photo of a bird", "a photo of a car"]
text_tokens = clip.tokenize(candidate_labels).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    image_features = model.encode_image(image)
    text_features = model.encode_text(text_tokens)

    image_features = F.normalize(image_features, dim=-1)
    text_features = F.normalize(text_features, dim=-1)

    similarity = (100.0 * image_features @ text_features.T).softmax(dim=-1)

for label, prob in zip(candidate_labels, similarity[0].tolist()):
    print(f"{label}: {prob:.2%}")
Notice there is no training step here at all — this is a genuinely zero-shot classification, working purely by comparing embeddings in the shared space CLIP learned during pretraining.
BLIP and Image Captioning
Extending Beyond Matching to Generation

CLIP is excellent at matching images to text but cannot generate new text — its text encoder only produces embeddings, not fluent captions. BLIP (Bootstrapping Language-Image Pretraining) extends the multimodal idea to generative tasks like image captioning and visual question answering, by combining an image encoder with a text decoder capable of generating fluent, free-form text conditioned on image features.

Image → Image Encoder → Image Features
                              │
                    Cross-Attention (image features as K, V)
                              │
Text Decoder (autoregressive, causal — same pattern as Chapter 58's decoder)
                              │
              Generated Caption: "a golden retriever running on a beach"

This cross-attention pattern — a text decoder attending to image features exactly the way the original Transformer's decoder attended to the encoder's output in Chapter 58 — is the standard architectural bridge used across essentially all modern vision-language generation models.

# Using a pretrained BLIP model via HuggingFace Transformers
from transformers import BlipProcessor, BlipForConditionalGeneration
from PIL import Image

processor = BlipProcessor.from_pretrained("Salesforce/blip-image-captioning-base")
model = BlipForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("Salesforce/blip-image-captioning-base")

image = Image.open("photo.jpg").convert("RGB")
inputs = processor(image, return_tensors="pt")

output_ids = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=30)
caption = processor.decode(output_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

print(f"Generated caption: {caption}")
BLIP vs CLIP — Complementary Roles
Multimodal AI Applications
Image Search and Retrieval

CLIP embeddings enable text-to-image search: embed a large image collection once (offline), then at query time, embed a natural-language search query and find images with the closest embeddings — no manual tagging required, and the query can be an arbitrary natural-language description.

def build_image_index(image_paths, model, preprocess, device):
    """Precompute and store embeddings for a collection of images (done once, offline)"""
    embeddings = []
    for path in image_paths:
        image = preprocess(Image.open(path)).unsqueeze(0).to(device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            emb = model.encode_image(image)
            emb = F.normalize(emb, dim=-1)
        embeddings.append(emb.cpu())
    return torch.cat(embeddings, dim=0)   # (num_images, embed_dim)


def text_to_image_search(query_text, image_embeddings, image_paths, model, device, top_k=5):
    """Find the top-k images best matching a natural-language query"""
    text_tokens = clip.tokenize([query_text]).to(device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        text_emb = model.encode_text(text_tokens)
        text_emb = F.normalize(text_emb, dim=-1).cpu()

    similarities = (image_embeddings @ text_emb.T).squeeze(1)
    top_indices = similarities.argsort(descending=True)[:top_k]

    return [(image_paths[i], similarities[i].item()) for i in top_indices]
Content Moderation

CLIP-style embeddings can flag images similar to known problematic content categories, described purely in natural language, without needing a dedicated classifier retrained for every new policy category — a significant practical advantage when moderation guidelines evolve frequently.
Multimodal LLMs

Modern multimodal LLMs (GPT-4V-style, Claude with vision, Gemini) build on the same core idea as CLIP/BLIP: a vision encoder produces image features, which are projected into the same space the language model's token embeddings live in, letting the language model attend to visual information using the exact same attention mechanism from Chapter 58, just with a mixed sequence of text and image tokens.
Implementation and Fine-Tuning
Fine-Tuning ViT for a Custom Classification Task

from torchvision import models, transforms
import torch.nn as nn

def build_finetuned_vit(num_classes, freeze_backbone=True):
    model = models.vit_b_16(weights=models.ViT_B_16_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1)

    if freeze_backbone:
        for param in model.parameters():
            param.requires_grad = False

    # Replace the classification head — same transfer learning pattern as Chapter 61
    model.heads.head = nn.Linear(model.hidden_dim, num_classes)
    return model


model = build_finetuned_vit(num_classes=5, freeze_backbone=True)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.heads.head.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# ViT-specific preprocessing (patch size expects a fixed input resolution)
vit_transform = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize(256),
    transforms.CenterCrop(224),
    transforms.ToTensor(),
    transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.5, 0.5, 0.5], std=[0.5, 0.5, 0.5]),
])
Fine-Tuning CLIP for Domain-Specific Retrieval

Full CLIP fine-tuning is uncommon at the fresher/intern level (it requires large batch sizes for effective contrastive learning), but a lighter, common practical approach is training a small linear or MLP "adapter" layer on top of frozen CLIP embeddings for a domain-specific task — cheaper, faster, and often sufficient.
Common Mistakes

Training ViT from scratch on a small dataset. Without CNN's built-in inductive bias, ViT typically underperforms a CNN when trained from scratch on limited data. Always start from a pretrained checkpoint unless you have access to a genuinely large dataset.

Forgetting to L2-normalize embeddings before computing CLIP similarity. CLIP's contrastive objective and cosine similarity calculations assume normalized embeddings — skipping normalization produces similarity scores that don't behave as expected and can silently degrade retrieval or classification quality.

Expecting CLIP to generate text. CLIP's text encoder only produces embeddings for matching/retrieval — it has no decoder and cannot generate novel captions. Use BLIP (or a similar encoder-decoder vision-language model) for generation tasks.

Using CLIP's zero-shot classification on categories that differ greatly from its training distribution. CLIP's zero-shot performance depends heavily on how well a concept was represented in its internet-scale pretraining data — highly specialized domains (rare medical conditions, proprietary product categories) often perform poorly without fine-tuning or a domain-specific adapter.

Assuming a bigger patch size in ViT is always better or worse. Smaller patches (e.g., 8×8) create more tokens and capture finer detail but increase compute quadratically (self-attention cost scales with sequence length, per Chapter 58); larger patches (e.g., 32×32) are cheaper but coarser. This is a genuine trade-off, not a free win in either direction.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
How does Vision Transformer convert an image into a format a Transformer can process?

ViT splits the image into fixed-size, non-overlapping patches (e.g., 16×16 pixels), flattens each patch, and linearly projects it into an embedding vector — treating each patch as a "token," analogous to a word token in NLP. Positional embeddings are added since attention itself has no sense of spatial order, and a learnable [CLS] token is prepended to aggregate information for classification.
What is CLIP and what makes its training approach different from a typical image classifier?

CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder jointly to place matching image-caption pairs close together in a shared embedding space, using contrastive learning on naturally occurring internet image-text pairs. Unlike a typical classifier trained on a fixed, manually labeled set of classes, CLIP requires no manual class labels and can generalize to arbitrary categories described in natural language.
What is zero-shot classification, and how does CLIP achieve it?

Zero-shot classification means classifying into categories the model was never explicitly trained to distinguish, with no additional training. CLIP achieves this by embedding candidate class descriptions as text (e.g., "a photo of a dog") and comparing them via cosine similarity to an image's embedding — the model picks whichever text description is closest in the shared embedding space.
Intermediate Level
Why does ViT typically underperform CNNs on small datasets but outperform them at large scale?

CNNs have a strong built-in inductive bias (locality and translation invariance via convolution) that helps them learn effectively even with limited data. ViT has little to no such built-in bias — it must learn these patterns purely from data through self-attention. This makes ViT less data-efficient on small datasets, but the lack of a restrictive built-in assumption becomes an advantage once pretrained on very large datasets, where ViT can learn more flexible, less-constrained patterns than a CNN's fixed inductive bias would allow.
Explain CLIP's contrastive loss and why it uses an N×N similarity matrix during training.

For a batch of N image-text pairs, CLIP computes a similarity score between every image embedding and every text embedding, producing an N×N matrix. The diagonal represents genuinely matching pairs and is pushed to be maximally similar, while all off-diagonal entries (naturally mismatched pairings that occur just from being in the same batch) are pushed to be dissimilar. This is computed and averaged in both directions — image-to-text and text-to-image — using cross-entropy loss with the diagonal as the correct label.
What is the architectural difference between CLIP and BLIP, and why does it matter for their respective capabilities?

CLIP uses two independent encoders (image and text) with no cross-attention between them, producing embeddings that can be compared via similarity — well-suited for matching and retrieval, but structurally incapable of generating text. BLIP adds a text decoder that cross-attends to image features (the same encoder-decoder cross-attention pattern from Chapter 58's Transformer), enabling it to generate novel, fluent text conditioned on an image — the architectural difference directly explains why BLIP can caption images and CLIP cannot.
Advanced Level
Why is the [CLS] token's final representation, rather than an average of all patch tokens, typically used for classification in ViT?

The [CLS] token has no fixed content of its own and is free to aggregate whatever information self-attention determines is most relevant across all patches over the course of the encoder — it isn't tied to representing any specific spatial region the way a patch token is. This mirrors BERT's use of [CLS] for sentence-level representations in NLP. In practice, averaging patch tokens (global average pooling) can also work reasonably well and is used in some ViT variants, but the [CLS] token approach was the original design and remains common, partly for consistency with the established Transformer pretraining paradigm from NLP.
How does the temperature parameter in CLIP's contrastive loss affect training, and what would happen with a poorly chosen value?

The temperature scales the similarity scores before the softmax in the contrastive loss — a lower temperature makes the softmax distribution sharper (more confident, more peaked around the highest-similarity pair), while a higher temperature makes it softer/flatter. Too low a temperature can make training unstable, with gradients dominated by a small number of very confident (or overconfident) pairs; too high a temperature can make the loss signal too weak to meaningfully separate matching from non-matching pairs, slowing or stalling learning. In practice, CLIP often learns the temperature as a trainable parameter rather than fixing it manually, letting the model find an appropriate scale during training.
Explain the trade-off in ViT's patch size choice, connecting it to the quadratic cost of self-attention discussed in Chapter 58.

Smaller patches produce a longer sequence of tokens (e.g., 8×8 patches on a 224×224 image yield 784 tokens, versus 196 for 16×16 patches), capturing finer visual detail but incurring self-attention's quadratic cost in sequence length — both compute and memory grow substantially. Larger patches reduce sequence length and computational cost but discard finer spatial detail, since each token now represents a coarser region of the image. This is the direct visual analog of the sequence-length scaling trade-off from Chapter 58, and is a genuine architectural decision made based on the target resolution, available compute budget, and how much fine-grained detail the task requires.

Mini Project: CLIP-Powered Visual Search Engine

# clip_visual_search.py
# A text-to-image search engine using CLIP embeddings
# No manual tagging required — natural language queries directly find matching images

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import clip
from PIL import Image
import os
import json

class VisualSearchEngine:
    def __init__(self, model_name="ViT-B/32", device=None):
        self.device = device or ("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
        self.model, self.preprocess = clip.load(model_name, device=self.device)
        self.image_paths = []
        self.image_embeddings = None

    def index_images(self, folder_path):
        """Precompute embeddings for every image in a folder — done once, offline"""
        supported_ext = (".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")
        paths = [os.path.join(folder_path, f) for f in os.listdir(folder_path)
                  if f.lower().endswith(supported_ext)]

        embeddings = []
        print(f"Indexing {len(paths)} images...")

        for path in paths:
            try:
                image = self.preprocess(Image.open(path).convert("RGB")).unsqueeze(0).to(self.device)
                with torch.no_grad():
                    emb = self.model.encode_image(image)
                    emb = F.normalize(emb, dim=-1)
                embeddings.append(emb.cpu())
                self.image_paths.append(path)
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Skipping {path}: {e}")

        self.image_embeddings = torch.cat(embeddings, dim=0)
        print(f"Indexed {len(self.image_paths)} images successfully.\n")

    def search(self, query_text, top_k=5):
        """Search the indexed images using a natural-language query"""
        if self.image_embeddings is None:
            raise RuntimeError("No images indexed yet — call index_images() first.")

        text_tokens = clip.tokenize([query_text]).to(self.device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            text_emb = self.model.encode_text(text_tokens)
            text_emb = F.normalize(text_emb, dim=-1).cpu()

        similarities = (self.image_embeddings @ text_emb.T).squeeze(1)
        top_indices = similarities.argsort(descending=True)[:top_k]

        results = [
            {"path": self.image_paths[i], "similarity": round(similarities[i].item(), 4)}
            for i in top_indices
        ]
        return results

    def classify_zero_shot(self, image_path, candidate_labels):
        """Zero-shot classify a single image against arbitrary candidate labels"""
        image = self.preprocess(Image.open(image_path).convert("RGB")).unsqueeze(0).to(self.device)
        text_tokens = clip.tokenize(candidate_labels).to(self.device)

        with torch.no_grad():
            image_emb = F.normalize(self.model.encode_image(image), dim=-1)
            text_emb = F.normalize(self.model.encode_text(text_tokens), dim=-1)
            probs = (100.0 * image_emb @ text_emb.T).softmax(dim=-1).squeeze(0)

        return sorted(zip(candidate_labels, probs.tolist()), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)


def main():
    engine = VisualSearchEngine(model_name="ViT-B/32")

    # In practice: point this at a real folder of images
    # engine.index_images("my_photo_collection/")

    # Simulated search demonstration (requires a real indexed folder to actually run)
    print("Example queries you could run once images are indexed:")
    example_queries = [
        "a dog playing in the park",
        "a sunset over the ocean",
        "people at a birthday party",
        "a red sports car"
    ]
    for query in example_queries:
        print(f'  search("{query}")')

    print("\nExample zero-shot classification usage:")
    print('  engine.classify_zero_shot("photo.jpg", ["a cat", "a dog", "a bird"])')


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Cheat Sheet

# ViT pipeline
image -> patches (fixed size) -> flatten + linear projection -> patch embeddings
patch embeddings + [CLS] token + positional embeddings -> Transformer Encoder
[CLS] token output -> classification head

# CLIP pipeline
image -> Image Encoder -> image embedding  ┐
text  -> Text Encoder  -> text embedding   ┘ -> cosine similarity (shared space)

# CLIP contrastive loss (per batch of N pairs)
logits = (image_emb @ text_emb.T) / temperature
loss = (CrossEntropy(logits, diag_labels) + CrossEntropy(logits.T, diag_labels)) / 2

# Zero-shot classification
similarity = image_embedding · text_embedding(candidate_label)  for each candidate
predicted_label = argmax(similarity)

# BLIP pipeline (generation)
image -> Image Encoder -> image features
image features (K, V) + Text Decoder (causal, cross-attends to image) -> generated caption

# CLIP vs BLIP
CLIP -> matching / retrieval / zero-shot classification (no generation)
BLIP -> generation (captioning, VQA) via cross-attention decoder
Revision Notes
ViT patch embedding = single strided convolution (kernel = stride = patch size), mathematically equivalent to flatten + linear projection
[CLS] token = learnable, content-free token that aggregates global information via attention — same idea as BERT
ViT needs large-scale pretraining because it lacks CNN's convolutional inductive bias
CLIP = dual encoder + contrastive loss; no cross-attention between image and text encoders
CLIP embeddings must be L2-normalized before computing cosine similarity
Zero-shot classification = compare image embedding to text embeddings of candidate labels, no training needed
BLIP = image encoder + cross-attending text decoder; can generate captions, CLIP cannot
Multimodal LLMs = vision encoder features projected into LLM's embedding space, processed via standard attention
Patch size trade-off: smaller = finer detail, more tokens, quadratically more compute; larger = cheaper, coarser

Project 4: Document Scanner with OpenCV
Overview

A classical computer vision application (no deep learning required) that takes a photo of a physical document and produces a clean, perspective-corrected, scanned-looking output — the same core technique behind mobile scanning apps.
Architecture

Input photo of a document (at an angle, with background)
      │
Preprocessing: grayscale, Gaussian blur
      │
Edge Detection (Canny)
      │
Contour Detection → find the largest 4-sided contour (the document's edges)
      │
Perspective Transform (warp the 4 detected corners to a flat rectangle)
      │
Post-processing: adaptive thresholding for a clean "scanned" black-and-white look
      │
Output: flattened, cleaned document image
Tech Stack
Implementation Sketch

import cv2
import numpy as np

def scan_document(image_path):
    image = cv2.imread(image_path)
    orig = image.copy()

    gray = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
    edged = cv2.Canny(blurred, 75, 200)

    contours, _ = cv2.findContours(edged.copy(), cv2.RETR_LIST, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
    contours = sorted(contours, key=cv2.contourArea, reverse=True)[:5]

    doc_contour = None
    for c in contours:
        peri = cv2.arcLength(c, True)
        approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(c, 0.02 * peri, True)
        if len(approx) == 4:               # Found a 4-cornered shape — likely the document
            doc_contour = approx
            break

    if doc_contour is None:
        raise ValueError("Could not detect a document boundary in the image.")

    # Perspective transform using the four detected corner points (implementation
    # detail: order corners, then cv2.getPerspectiveTransform + cv2.warpPerspective)
    warped = four_point_transform(orig, doc_contour.reshape(4, 2))

    # Final clean "scanned" look
    warped_gray = cv2.cvtColor(warped, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    scanned = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(
        warped_gray, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C, cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 11, 10
    )
    return scanned

Project 5: License Plate Recognition System
Overview

A two-stage pipeline: first detect the location of a license plate within an image of a vehicle, then read the alphanumeric text on the plate using OCR — a widely used pattern in parking systems, toll systems, and traffic enforcement.
Architecture

Input image (vehicle photo)
      │
Stage 1: License Plate Detection
   (YOLOv8 fine-tuned on plate-only class, OR classical contour-based
    approach using edge detection + aspect-ratio filtering)
      │
Crop detected plate region
      │
Stage 2: Preprocessing for OCR
   (grayscale, thresholding, noise removal, resizing)
      │
Stage 3: OCR (Tesseract or EasyOCR) extracts the plate text
      │
Output: bounding box + recognized plate string + confidence
Tech Stack
Dataset
Public datasets like "Car License Plate Detection" (Kaggle) provide annotated plate bounding boxes suitable for fine-tuning YOLOv8's detection stage.
Implementation Sketch

from ultralytics import YOLO
import easyocr
import cv2

plate_detector = YOLO("license_plate_yolov8.pt")   # Fine-tuned on plate-only class
ocr_reader = easyocr.Reader(["en"])

def recognize_plate(image_path):
    image = cv2.imread(image_path)
    results = plate_detector(image, conf=0.4)

    plates_found = []
    for result in results:
        for box in result.boxes:
            x1, y1, x2, y2 = map(int, box.xyxy[0].tolist())
            plate_crop = image[y1:y2, x1:x2]

            # Preprocess crop for cleaner OCR
            gray_crop = cv2.cvtColor(plate_crop, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
            _, thresh_crop = cv2.threshold(gray_crop, 0, 255,
                                            cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

            ocr_result = ocr_reader.readtext(thresh_crop)
            plate_text = " ".join([res[1] for res in ocr_result])
            confidence = float(box.conf[0])

            plates_found.append({
                "bounding_box": [x1, y1, x2, y2],
                "plate_text": plate_text,
                "detection_confidence": round(confidence, 3)
            })

    return plates_found

Common Mistakes Across All Five Projects

Skipping error analysis on real, messy test images. All five projects will look deceptively good on clean, curated test images. Always test with intentionally difficult inputs (blurry, angled, poorly lit, partially occluded) before claiming a project "works."

Weak README documentation. A project without a clear README — setup steps, sample input/output, architecture summary — is invisible to a recruiter skimming GitHub. Treat the README as part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.
Overstating model performance or domain readiness. Especially for the medical imaging project, be precise and honest about what a small personal-project dataset does and doesn't prove.

Not connecting the project to a deployment surface. A model sitting in a Jupyter notebook demonstrates far less than the same model wrapped in a FastAPI endpoint or Streamlit demo — the deployment step is a large part of what separates a "student project" from an "engineer's project" in a portfolio.

Ignoring licensing on pretrained models and datasets used. Some pretrained weights and datasets carry usage restrictions (research-only, non-commercial); note this clearly in your README, especially for anything involving face recognition or personal data.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
Why include a document scanner project that uses no deep learning at all in a CV portfolio?

It demonstrates strength in classical computer vision fundamentals — edge detection, contour analysis, geometric transformations — which remain relevant in many production pipelines (as a fast, deterministic pre-processing step before or instead of a deep model) and shows interviewers you understand OpenCV beyond just calling cv2.imread().
Why does the license plate recognition project use two separate models (detector + OCR) instead of one end-to-end model?

Detection (finding where the plate is) and text recognition (reading what the plate says) are different tasks requiring different architectures — a detector is optimized for localization, while OCR models are optimized for recognizing characters and sequences. Splitting them into a two-stage pipeline also makes each stage independently debuggable and replaceable, which is standard practice for this kind of task.
Intermediate Level
For the face recognition project, why compare face embeddings with cosine/Euclidean distance instead of training a classifier for each known person?

Embedding-based comparison allows adding a new known person by simply computing and storing one new embedding, with no retraining required. A classifier approach would require retraining (or at least significant modification) every time a new identity needs to be added, which doesn't scale well for a system where the set of known people changes over time.
Why does the medical X-ray project require more careful augmentation choices than a general-purpose image classifier?

Certain augmentations that are harmless for general object recognition can be clinically meaningless or misleading for medical images — for example, horizontal flipping could reverse anatomical laterality (left vs. right), and could teach the model spurious patterns that don't reflect real diagnostic reasoning. Augmentation choices should always be validated against the specific domain's semantics, not applied as generic defaults.
Advanced Level
How would you extend the real-time object detection project (Project 2) to handle sustained high-throughput video, and what bottlenecks would you anticipate?

Key considerations: batching frames where possible rather than processing one at a time, ensuring the model is loaded once and kept warm rather than reloaded per request, using a lighter YOLO variant (nano/small) if latency is critical, and considering asynchronous processing (a queue between frame capture and inference) to avoid blocking the video capture thread. The main anticipated bottlenecks are GPU throughput at high frame rates and I/O overhead from repeatedly encoding/decoding frames if streaming over a network — this connects directly to production model-serving concerns covered in Part 12.
What would you change about the license plate recognition pipeline if you needed it to work reliably across multiple countries with different plate formats?

You would likely need country/region-specific OCR post-processing (different plate formats have different character counts, layouts, and sometimes non-Latin scripts), potentially a plate-format classifier as an additional stage to route each detected plate to the appropriate OCR/validation logic, and a broader, more diverse training dataset for the detection stage to handle varying plate shapes, colors, and mounting positions across regions.

Introduction

Natural Language Processing begins with a hard truth: computers don't understand text. They understand numbers. Every technique in this Part — from a simple Naive Bayes classifier to a full LLM — depends on first converting raw, messy human language into a structured, numerical form a model can process.

This chapter covers that first, essential layer: text preprocessing. It's tempting to think of preprocessing as "boring plumbing" before the "real" modeling work — but poor preprocessing decisions silently degrade every downstream model, from classical bag-of-words methods to modern Transformers. Even LLM tokenization (Chapter 72) is a direct descendant of the fundamentals in this chapter.
Text Preprocessing Pipeline
The Standard Pipeline

Raw Text
    │
Lowercasing (optional, task-dependent)
    │
Tokenization (split into words/sentences/subwords)
    │
Removing punctuation / special characters (optional, task-dependent)
    │
Stop word removal (optional, task-dependent)
    │
Stemming or Lemmatization (optional, task-dependent)
    │
Clean, structured tokens → ready for vectorization (Chapter 67)

The word "optional" appears repeatedly here for a reason: unlike a fixed formula, preprocessing is a series of task-dependent decisions. A sentiment analysis pipeline might lowercase everything; a Named Entity Recognition pipeline must preserve capitalization, since "Apple" (company) vs "apple" (fruit) is exactly the kind of distinction capitalization helps resolve.
A Full Pipeline Example

import re
import nltk
from nltk.corpus import stopwords
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer, WordNetLemmatizer
from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize

# One-time downloads (run once in your environment)
# nltk.download('punkt')
# nltk.download('stopwords')
# nltk.download('wordnet')

def preprocess_text(text, lowercase=True, remove_punct=True,
                     remove_stopwords=True, lemmatize=True):
    """
    A configurable text preprocessing pipeline.
    Each step is toggleable because the 'right' preprocessing depends on the task.
    """
    if lowercase:
        text = text.lower()

    if remove_punct:
        text = re.sub(r'[^\w\s]', '', text)

    tokens = word_tokenize(text)

    if remove_stopwords:
        stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))
        tokens = [t for t in tokens if t not in stop_words]

    if lemmatize:
        lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
        tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(t) for t in tokens]

    return tokens


sample_text = "The quick brown foxes were jumping over the lazy dogs!"
processed = preprocess_text(sample_text)
print(processed)
# ['quick', 'brown', 'fox', 'jumping', 'lazy', 'dog']
Tokenization (Word, Sentence, Subword)
Why Tokenization Comes First

Tokenization splits raw text into discrete units — tokens — that become the basic building blocks for everything downstream. Every other preprocessing step, and every vectorization technique in Chapter 67, operates on tokens, not raw character strings.
Word Tokenization

from nltk.tokenize import word_tokenize

text = "Don't stop believin' — it's only $9.99!"
tokens = word_tokenize(text)
print(tokens)
# ['Do', "n't", 'stop', 'believin', "'", '—', 'it', "'s", 'only', '$', '9.99', '!']
Notice how word_tokenize handles contractions ("Don't" → "Do" + "n't") and separates punctuation and currency symbols as their own tokens — naive text.split() would not handle any of this correctly.

# Naive splitting — fails on punctuation, contractions, and edge cases
naive_tokens = text.split()
print(naive_tokens)
# ["Don't", 'stop', "believin'", '—', "it's", 'only', '$9.99!']
# Notice: punctuation stuck to words, contractions not split
Sentence Tokenization

from nltk.tokenize import sent_tokenize

paragraph = "Dr. Smith works at A.I. Corp. He arrived at 9 a.m. Everyone was excited."
sentences = sent_tokenize(paragraph)
print(sentences)
# ['Dr. Smith works at A.I. Corp.', 'He arrived at 9 a.m.', 'Everyone was excited.']

Sentence tokenization is genuinely difficult because periods serve multiple purposes — ending a sentence, marking an abbreviation ("Dr."), or being part of an acronym ("A.I."). Robust sentence tokenizers use statistical models trained to distinguish these cases, not simple regex splitting on periods.
Subword Tokenization

Modern LLMs and Transformers (Chapter 72) don't use word-level tokenization at all — they use subword tokenization, which splits rare or unknown words into smaller, meaningful pieces. This solves the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem: a word-level vocabulary can never cover every possible word (especially rare words, typos, or new terms), but a subword vocabulary can represent virtually any word by combining smaller known pieces.

# Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) concept — the algorithm behind GPT's tokenizer
# (Full implementation and detail covered in Chapter 72)

# Word-level tokenization struggles with unseen/rare words:
word_level = ["unbelievably"]   # Either in vocabulary or not — no middle ground

# Subword tokenization breaks it into known, reusable pieces:
subword_level = ["un", "believ", "ably"]   # Each piece likely appears in many other words

# This is conceptually how a Hugging Face tokenizer works in practice:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("unbelievably")
print(tokens)
# ['unbelievable', '##ly']  — BERT's WordPiece splits into a known root + suffix
Normalization (Lowercasing, Stemming, Lemmatization)
Lowercasing

text = "The Transformer Architecture Changed NLP Forever"
print(text.lower())
# "the transformer architecture changed nlp forever"

Lowercasing reduces vocabulary size by treating "The" and "the" as the same token, which helps classical models generalize with less data. However, it destroys information: "US" (the country) and "us" (the pronoun) become indistinguishable. Modern subword tokenizers and case-sensitive models (like cased BERT variants) often skip this step deliberately, particularly for tasks like Named Entity Recognition where case carries meaning.
Stemming
Stemming crudely chops word endings using rule-based heuristics, without necessarily producing a real word.

from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer

stemmer = PorterStemmer()
words = ["running", "runs", "ran", "easily", "fairly", "studies", "studying"]

for word in words:
    print(f"{word} -> {stemmer.stem(word)}")

# running -> run
# runs -> run
# ran -> ran        <- Stemming CANNOT handle irregular forms
# easily -> easili  <- Not even a real word!
# fairly -> fairli  <- Not even a real word!
# studies -> studi
# studying -> studi
Stemming is fast (simple rule-based suffix stripping) but crude — it can produce non-words ("easili") and fails on irregular forms ("ran" is not reduced to "run").
Lemmatization
Lemmatization uses actual vocabulary and morphological analysis (often via part-of-speech context) to reduce a word to its true dictionary root form (the lemma).

from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer

lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
words = ["running", "runs", "ran", "studies", "studying", "better"]

for word in words:
    print(f"{word} -> {lemmatizer.lemmatize(word, pos='v')}")   # pos='v' = treat as verb

# running -> run
# runs -> run
# ran -> run          <- Correctly handles irregular forms!
# studies -> study
# studying -> study
# better -> better    <- Needs pos='a' (adjective) to correctly map to 'good'
print(lemmatizer.lemmatize("better", pos="a"))
# better -> good
Stemming vs Lemmatization — When to Use Each
Stop Words and Punctuation
What Are Stop Words?

Stop words are extremely common words ("the," "is," "at," "which," "on") that typically carry little distinguishing meaning for many NLP tasks, since they appear in nearly every document regardless of topic.

from nltk.corpus import stopwords

stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))
print(len(stop_words))    # 179 (NLTK's default English stop word list)
print(list(stop_words)[:10])

text = "the movie was not very good and I would not recommend it"
tokens = text.split()
filtered = [t for t in tokens if t not in stop_words]
print(filtered)
# ['movie', 'good', 'recommend']
The Critical Danger: Stop Word Removal Can Destroy Meaning

Notice in the example above: "not" was removed as a stop word, completely flipping the sentence's sentiment from negative to what now reads as a positive fragment ("movie good recommend"). For sentiment analysis, negation words are often among the most important tokens in the entire sentence — removing them as generic stop words is a classic, damaging mistake.

# A safer approach for sentiment-sensitive tasks: exclude negations from the stop word list
negation_words = {"not", "no", "never", "n't", "cannot", "none"}
safe_stop_words = stop_words - negation_words

filtered_safe = [t for t in tokens if t not in safe_stop_words]
print(filtered_safe)
# ['not', 'movie', 'good', 'not', 'recommend']  — negation preserved

Whether to remove punctuation is also task-dependent:

text = "Wow!!! This is amazing... right?"

# Aggressive punctuation removal — loses emotional/emphasis signal
