Chapter Summary
Classical NLP converts variable-length text into fixed-length numerical vectors through a pipeline of preprocessing, tokenization, and feature extraction
Bag-of-Words loses word order entirely but provides a simple effective baseline; TF-IDF improves it by downweighting common uninformative words using IDF scores
N-grams capture local word order — critical for negation ("not good"), named entities ("New York"), and domain phrases
Naive Bayes is the fastest text classifier — trains in milliseconds, scales to millions of documents, and remains competitive on small datasets where deep learning overfits
Logistic Regression with TF-IDF is the go-to baseline for text classification — interpretable coefficients, good calibration, strong performance with L1/L2 regularization
Linear SVM historically achieves state-of-the-art performance on text classification — the maximum margin principle is well-suited to high-dimensional sparse feature spaces
CRF models the joint probability over label sequences — capturing transitions between consecutive labels — making it far superior to independent token classifiers for NER and POS tagging
The BIO tagging scheme represents multi-word entities as sequences of Begin-Inside-Outside tags — span-level F1 is the correct evaluation metric for NER, not token-level accuracy
Classical NLP wins in production when labeled data is scarce, inference latency is critical, interpretability is required, or resources are constrained

All modern NLP representations — attention weights, contextual embeddings, positional encodings — can be understood as learned generalizations of the manual features classical NLP required engineers to design

Introduction

Every chapter before this one built toward a single destination: the Transformer. You have already seen the self-attention mechanism and the encoder-decoder architecture in Part 8. This chapter takes that architecture and shows how it was specialized into two major families that reshaped NLP — and eventually all of AI.

BERT proved that a transformer encoder, pre-trained on massive unlabeled text, could be fine-tuned for almost any language understanding task with only a small labeled dataset. GPT proved that a transformer decoder, trained simply to predict the next word, could generate coherent text and eventually reason, converse, and follow instructions.

Understanding both families deeply is non-negotiable for any AI/ML engineer in 2026. RAG systems, chatbots, search engines, content moderation, and every LLM API you will ever call trace their architecture directly back to the ideas in this chapter.
BERT Architecture Deep Dive

BERT stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, introduced by Google in 2018. Its core insight was that most NLP tasks benefit from understanding a word using context from both directions — the words before it and the words after it — rather than only reading left to right.
Why Bidirectionality Matters
Consider the sentence: "The bank raised interest rates after the river bank flooded."

To understand the first "bank," a purely left-to-right model only has "The" as context. A bidirectional model sees the entire sentence, including "interest rates" appearing after it and "river... flooded" appearing later, allowing it to correctly disambiguate the two different meanings of "bank."
Architecture Overview

BERT uses only the encoder half of the original Transformer architecture (from Part 8, Chapter 58). It stacks multiple encoder layers, each containing multi-head self-attention followed by a feedforward network, with residual connections and layer normalization throughout.

Input: [CLS] The bank raised rates [SEP]
         │
         ▼
   Token Embeddings + Segment Embeddings + Position Embeddings
         │
         ▼
   Transformer Encoder Layer 1  (Self-Attention + FFN)
         │
   Transformer Encoder Layer 2
         │
        ...
         │
   Transformer Encoder Layer 12  (BERT-base)
         │
         ▼
   Contextual Embeddings for every token
BERT-base: 12 encoder layers, 12 attention heads, 768 hidden dimensions, ~110 million parameters. BERT-large: 24 encoder layers, 16 attention heads, 1024 hidden dimensions, ~340 million parameters.
Input Representation
BERT combines three embeddings for every input token:
Token embeddings — the meaning of the subword token itself (using WordPiece tokenization)
Segment embeddings — which sentence the token belongs to (Sentence A or Sentence B), used for tasks involving sentence pairs
Position embeddings — where the token sits in the sequence, since self-attention has no inherent sense of order

from transformers import BertTokenizer

tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")

text = "The bank raised interest rates."
encoded = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

print(encoded["input_ids"])
print(tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(encoded["input_ids"][0]))
# ['[CLS]', 'the', 'bank', 'raised', 'interest', 'rates', '.', '[SEP]']
The special tokens matter:
[CLS] — placed at the start of every input; its final hidden state is used as an aggregate sequence representation for classification tasks
[SEP] — separates sentences (used in sentence-pair tasks like question answering) and marks the end of input
Pre-training and Fine-tuning
This two-stage paradigm is the single most important idea in modern NLP, and it is worth understanding deeply because it applies equally to LLMs in Part 11.
Pre-training
BERT is pre-trained on massive unlabeled text corpora (English Wikipedia + BooksCorpus, roughly 3.3 billion words) using two self-supervised objectives:
Masked Language Modeling (MLM). Randomly mask 15% of input tokens and train the model to predict the original token using bidirectional context.

Input:  The [MASK] raised interest rates after the meeting.
Target: The bank raised interest rates after the meeting.

Of the masked 15%: 80% are replaced with [MASK], 10% are replaced with a random token, and 10% are left unchanged. This mixture prevents the model from simply learning to recognize the [MASK] token and ignoring everything else, and forces it to build a genuine contextual representation of every token.

Next Sentence Prediction (NSP). Given two sentences A and B, predict whether B actually follows A in the original text, or is a random sentence. This was intended to help the model understand relationships between sentences (useful for tasks like question answering), though later research (RoBERTa) showed this objective contributes less than originally believed.
Fine-tuning

After pre-training, BERT already "understands" language broadly. Fine-tuning adapts this general understanding to a specific downstream task using a much smaller labeled dataset — often just thousands of examples instead of billions of words.

Pre-trained BERT (general language understanding)
         │
         ▼
  Add a small task-specific head (1-2 layers)
         │
         ▼
  Fine-tune ALL parameters on labeled task data
         │
         ▼
  Task-specific BERT (e.g., sentiment classifier)

This is dramatically more efficient than training a model from scratch for every task — the expensive part (learning language itself) happens once, and adapting it to a new task takes hours instead of weeks.
Why This Paradigm Changed NLP

Before BERT, most NLP systems required task-specific architectures and large labeled datasets built from scratch. BERT showed that a single pre-trained model could achieve state-of-the-art results across eleven different NLP benchmarks with only minor architectural changes and modest fine-tuning data. This established "pre-train then fine-tune" as the default strategy — the same strategy that underlies GPT, T5, and every modern LLM.
Sentence-BERT

Raw BERT is poor at producing sentence-level embeddings for similarity comparison. Averaging BERT's token embeddings, or using the [CLS] token directly, produces embeddings that perform worse than simple word-embedding-based approaches (like averaging GloVe vectors) on semantic similarity tasks.
The Problem Sentence-BERT Solves

To find the most similar pair among 10,000 sentences using raw BERT, you would need to feed every possible pair through the full BERT model — roughly 50 million inference passes, taking hours or days. This is impractical for real-world search, clustering, or RAG retrieval systems.
The Sentence-BERT Solution

Sentence-BERT (SBERT) fine-tunes BERT using a siamese network structure: two identical BERT encoders (sharing weights) process two sentences independently, producing two fixed-size embeddings. A pooling layer (typically mean pooling over token embeddings) converts BERT's variable-length output into a single fixed-size vector.

Sentence A ──► BERT ──► Mean Pooling ──► Embedding A ──┐
                                                          ├──► Cosine Similarity
Sentence B ──► BERT ──► Mean Pooling ──► Embedding B ──┘

Once trained, computing sentence embeddings requires only one forward pass per sentence. Comparing 10,000 sentences drops from ~50 million BERT inference passes to just 10,000, with similarity computed via simple cosine similarity between pre-computed vectors.

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
from sentence_transformers.util import cos_sim

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

sentences = [
    "The stock market rallied after the earnings report.",
    "Shares surged following strong quarterly results.",
    "The chef prepared a delicious pasta dish."
]

embeddings = model.encode(sentences)

similarity_01 = cos_sim(embeddings[0], embeddings[1])
similarity_02 = cos_sim(embeddings[0], embeddings[2])

print(f"Similarity (finance vs finance): {similarity_01.item():.4f}")
print(f"Similarity (finance vs cooking): {similarity_02.item():.4f}")

This is the exact mechanism behind embedding models used in every RAG pipeline you will build in Part 11 — Sentence-BERT and its successors (BGE, E5, text-embedding-3) all use this siamese fine-tuning approach.
RoBERTa, DistilBERT, and ALBERT
BERT sparked a wave of follow-up models, each addressing a different limitation.
RoBERTa (Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach)
Facebook AI showed that BERT was significantly undertrained. RoBERTa uses the identical architecture but changes the training recipe:
Removes the Next Sentence Prediction objective entirely (found to add little value)
Trains on 10x more data (160GB vs 16GB) for far longer
Uses dynamic masking (different tokens masked each epoch, rather than fixed masks applied once during preprocessing)
Uses much larger batch sizes
Result: RoBERTa consistently outperforms BERT on downstream benchmarks with the same architecture, purely from better training.
DistilBERT (Distilled BERT)

DistilBERT uses knowledge distillation to compress BERT into a smaller, faster model. A smaller "student" model is trained to mimic the output probability distributions of the full "teacher" BERT model, not just the hard labels.
40% fewer parameters than BERT-base (66M vs 110M)
60% faster inference
Retains ~97% of BERT's language understanding performance on benchmark tasks
This is the model of choice when latency or deployment cost matters more than squeezing out the last percentage point of accuracy — a common tradeoff in production systems.
ALBERT (A Lite BERT)
ALBERT reduces BERT's parameter count through two architectural changes rather than distillation:
Factorized embedding parameterization — decouples the size of the vocabulary embedding from the size of the hidden layers, using a smaller embedding dimension projected up to the hidden dimension
Cross-layer parameter sharing — all encoder layers share the same weights, dramatically reducing total parameters

ALBERT achieves comparable or better accuracy than BERT with far fewer parameters, though inference speed is not necessarily faster (the same computation still happens per layer, just with shared weights).

GPT Architecture Deep Dive
While BERT uses the transformer encoder, GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) uses the transformer decoder — and this single architectural choice leads to fundamentally different capabilities.
Decoder-Only Architecture

Input:  "The bank raised"
          │
          ▼
   Token + Position Embeddings
          │
          ▼
   Masked Self-Attention Layer 1   (can only see PAST tokens)
          │
   Masked Self-Attention Layer 2
          │
         ...
          │
   Masked Self-Attention Layer N
          │
          ▼
   Predict next token: "interest"
Causal (Masked) Self-Attention

GPT uses causal masking in its self-attention: each token can only attend to itself and tokens before it, never tokens after it. This is enforced by masking out (setting to negative infinity before softmax) all attention scores pointing to future positions.

import torch

def causal_mask(seq_len):
    """
    Creates a mask that prevents a position from attending to future positions.
    Upper triangular positions are masked with -inf before softmax.
    """
    mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(seq_len, seq_len), diagonal=1)
    mask = mask.masked_fill(mask == 1, float('-inf'))
    return mask

seq_len = 5
mask = causal_mask(seq_len)
print(mask)
# Row i can only attend to columns 0...i (no future positions)

This causal structure is exactly why GPT is naturally suited to generation: at inference time, the model predicts one token at a time, appends it to the sequence, and repeats — each new prediction only ever depends on what has already been generated, never on future tokens it hasn't produced yet.
BERT vs GPT: The Fundamental Difference
Why GPT Scaled So Well

GPT's training objective — simply predict the next token — requires no labeled data of any kind. Any text on the internet becomes training data automatically. This made it trivial to scale training data far beyond what BERT-style objectives typically used, and this scalability, combined with the decoder architecture's natural fit for generation, is what led directly to GPT-2, GPT-3, GPT-4, and the modern LLM landscape covered in Part 11.
T5 and Seq2Seq Models

T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) takes a different unifying approach: instead of choosing encoder-only or decoder-only, it uses the full encoder-decoder architecture from the original Transformer paper, and reframes every NLP task as converting input text to output text.
The Text-to-Text Framework

Translation:      Input: "translate English to German: The house is big"
                  Output: "Das Haus ist groß"

Classification:   Input: "sentiment: This movie was fantastic!"
                  Output: "positive"

Summarization:    Input: "summarize: <long article text>"
                  Output: "<short summary>"

Question Answer:  Input: "question: What is the capital of France? context: ..."
                  Output: "Paris"

Every task — classification, translation, summarization, question answering — is expressed as plain text in, plain text out. This unification means a single model architecture, a single training procedure, and a single loss function (cross-entropy over generated tokens) can be applied to virtually any NLP task, simply by changing the text prefix and target format.
Architecture

T5 uses a standard encoder-decoder transformer: the encoder processes the input text bidirectionally (like BERT), and the decoder generates the output text autoregressively (like GPT), with cross-attention connecting the two.

from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5ForConditionalGeneration

tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained("t5-small")
model = T5ForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("t5-small")

input_text = "summarize: The quarterly earnings report showed a 15% increase in revenue, driven primarily by strong performance in the cloud computing division, while the hardware segment saw a modest decline due to supply chain constraints."

input_ids = tokenizer(input_text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
output_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=30)

summary = tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)
print(summary)
When to Choose Each Architecture Family
HuggingFace Transformers Library
HuggingFace's transformers library is the industry-standard interface for working with every model family in this chapter. It provides a consistent API across thousands of pre-trained models.
The Pipeline API (Fastest Path to Results)

from transformers import pipeline

# Sentiment analysis — model, tokenizer, and pre/post-processing all handled automatically
classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
result = classifier("The new product launch exceeded all our expectations!")
print(result)
# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9998}]

# Named Entity Recognition
ner = pipeline("ner", grouped_entities=True)
entities = ner("Sundar Pichai is the CEO of Google, based in Mountain View.")
for entity in entities:
    print(f"{entity['word']}: {entity['entity_group']} ({entity['score']:.2f})")

# Text generation
generator = pipeline("text-generation", model="gpt2")
output = generator("The future of artificial intelligence is", max_length=30, num_return_sequences=1)
print(output[0]["generated_text"])

# Zero-shot classification — classify into arbitrary labels without fine-tuning
zero_shot = pipeline("zero-shot-classification")
result = zero_shot(
    "This new smartphone has an incredible camera and battery life.",
    candidate_labels=["technology", "sports", "politics", "cooking"]
)
print(result["labels"][0], result["scores"][0])
Working with Models and Tokenizers Directly
The pipeline API is convenient but hides details. Production code typically works with the underlying model and tokenizer directly for full control.

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
import torch

model_name = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name)

text = "I was disappointed with the customer service experience."

inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)

probabilities = torch.softmax(outputs.logits, dim=-1)
predicted_class = torch.argmax(probabilities, dim=-1).item()

labels = model.config.id2label
print(f"Prediction: {labels[predicted_class]}")
print(f"Confidence: {probabilities[0][predicted_class]:.4f}")

The Auto* classes (AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, etc.) automatically detect the correct architecture from the model name or checkpoint, making code portable across different model families without changing a line beyond the model name string.
Fine-tuning BERT for Classification
This is the canonical fine-tuning workflow every AI/ML engineer should be able to write from memory.

from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification,
    TrainingArguments, Trainer
)
from datasets import load_dataset
import numpy as np
import evaluate

# --- Load Data ---
dataset = load_dataset("imdb")   # Binary sentiment classification dataset

# --- Load Tokenizer and Model ---
model_name = "bert-base-uncased"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_name, num_labels=2)

# --- Tokenize the Dataset ---
def tokenize_function(examples):
    return tokenizer(examples["text"], truncation=True, padding="max_length", max_length=256)

tokenized_datasets = dataset.map(tokenize_function, batched=True)

train_dataset = tokenized_datasets["train"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(2000))
eval_dataset = tokenized_datasets["test"].shuffle(seed=42).select(range(500))

# --- Define Evaluation Metric ---
accuracy_metric = evaluate.load("accuracy")

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return accuracy_metric.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)

# --- Training Configuration ---
training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./bert-sentiment-results",
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=16,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="accuracy",
    logging_steps=50,
)

# --- Train ---
trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=eval_dataset,
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
)

trainer.train()

# --- Evaluate ---
results = trainer.evaluate()
print(f"Final accuracy: {results['eval_accuracy']:.4f}")

# --- Save the fine-tuned model ---
trainer.save_model("./bert-sentiment-finetuned")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("./bert-sentiment-finetuned")

# --- Inference with the fine-tuned model ---
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline("sentiment-analysis", model="./bert-sentiment-finetuned")
print(classifier("This movie completely blew me away, incredible acting."))
Key Fine-tuning Hyperparameters to Understand
Common Mistakes

Using a learning rate meant for training from scratch. Fine-tuning pre-trained transformers requires learning rates 10-100x smaller (2e-5 vs 2e-3) than training from random initialization. Using a large learning rate destroys the pre-trained representations within the first few steps ("catastrophic forgetting").

Forgetting to freeze or handle the classification head correctly. When loading a pre-trained model for a new number of classes, the final classification layer is randomly initialized and must be trained; this is handled automatically by AutoModelForSequenceClassification, but engineers sometimes mistakenly load architectures that do not match their task.

Averaging BERT's raw token embeddings for sentence similarity. This produces poor results (sometimes worse than simple word averaging) because BERT was never trained with a sentence-level similarity objective. Always use Sentence-BERT or another embedding model explicitly trained for this purpose.

Ignoring the causal masking difference when adapting techniques between BERT and GPT. Padding strategies, attention masks, and generation logic differ meaningfully between encoder-only and decoder-only models; code copied from a BERT tutorial often needs real adaptation for GPT-style models.

Truncating inputs without considering task-appropriate strategy. For long documents, always truncating from the end can remove the most important content (e.g., a conclusion). Consider sliding-window approaches or extractive pre-filtering when documents exceed the model's max sequence length.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the key architectural difference between BERT and GPT?

BERT uses only the transformer encoder and processes text bidirectionally, seeing the entire input at once — this makes it well suited to understanding tasks like classification and question answering. GPT uses only the transformer decoder with causal (masked) self-attention, so each token can only attend to previous tokens — this makes it naturally suited to text generation, since it predicts one token at a time based only on what came before.
What is masked language modeling and why is it used to pre-train BERT?

Masked language modeling randomly hides 15% of input tokens and trains the model to predict the original token using the surrounding bidirectional context. It is used because it forces the model to build a genuine contextual understanding of language from unlabeled text at massive scale, without requiring any human-labeled data, producing general-purpose representations that transfer well to downstream tasks.
What does the [CLS] token represent in BERT?

[CLS] is a special token prepended to every input sequence. After passing through all encoder layers, its final hidden state is used as an aggregate representation of the entire sequence, commonly fed into a classification head for tasks like sentiment analysis or natural language inference.
Intermediate Level
Why does RoBERTa outperform BERT despite using the identical architecture?

RoBERTa demonstrated that BERT was significantly undertrained. By removing the Next Sentence Prediction objective, training on ten times more data, using dynamic masking instead of static masking applied once during preprocessing, and training with much larger batch sizes for longer, RoBERTa extracts substantially more performance from the same architecture purely through a better training recipe.
Why can't you directly average BERT's token embeddings to get a good sentence embedding, and how does Sentence-BERT solve this?

BERT was pre-trained with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction, neither of which directly optimizes for producing sentence embeddings where semantic similarity corresponds to embedding distance. Sentence-BERT fine-tunes BERT using a siamese network structure on sentence-pair similarity data (such as natural language inference datasets), explicitly training the pooled output so that cosine similarity between embeddings reflects semantic similarity, and making large-scale similarity search computationally feasible.
Explain how T5 unifies different NLP tasks into a single framework.

T5 converts every NLP task into a text-to-text format by prepending a task-specific prefix to the input (e.g., "translate English to German:", "summarize:", "sentiment:") and training the encoder-decoder model to generate the appropriate text output. This means a single model architecture, training procedure, and loss function can handle classification, translation, summarization, and question answering simultaneously, simplifying both training infrastructure and multi-task learning.
Advanced Level
Why is causal masking implemented as additive negative infinity before the softmax, rather than simply zeroing out attention weights after softmax?

If invalid positions were zeroed out after the softmax, the remaining valid attention weights would not sum to 1, breaking the probabilistic interpretation of attention as a weighted average. By adding negative infinity to the raw attention scores before the softmax, those positions become exactly zero after the softmax is applied (since e^-∞ = 0), while the remaining valid positions are automatically renormalized to sum to 1, preserving a mathematically correct probability distribution over only the permitted (past) positions.
Compare the parameter efficiency strategies of DistilBERT and ALBERT, and explain why they lead to different inference speed characteristics despite both reducing parameter count.

DistilBERT reduces parameters by removing layers entirely (6 layers instead of 12) via knowledge distillation, so at inference time there is genuinely less computation to perform — this directly reduces both parameter count and latency. ALBERT reduces parameters through cross-layer weight sharing and factorized embeddings, but the same number of layers of computation still occur at inference time — the model is smaller to store and can be more efficient to train, but does not proportionally speed up inference the way removing layers does, since inference speed depends on computation performed, not parameters stored.

Mini Project: Multi-Label Support Ticket Classifier

# support_ticket_classifier.py
# Fine-tunes DistilBERT for multi-label classification of customer support tickets
# Demonstrates a realistic production fine-tuning scenario

from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification,
    TrainingArguments, Trainer
)
import torch
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, accuracy_score

LABELS = ["billing", "technical", "account", "feature_request", "urgent"]

# Simulated labeled dataset — in production this would be loaded from a database
raw_data = [
    {"text": "I was charged twice for my subscription this month", "labels": [1, 0, 0, 0, 1]},
    {"text": "The app crashes every time I try to upload a file", "labels": [0, 1, 0, 0, 1]},
    {"text": "I can't log into my account after resetting my password", "labels": [0, 0, 1, 0, 1]},
    {"text": "It would be great if you added dark mode to the app", "labels": [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]},
    {"text": "My invoice shows an incorrect amount, please review", "labels": [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]},
    {"text": "Can you add support for exporting data to CSV?", "labels": [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]},
]

model_name = "distilbert-base-uncased"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    model_name,
    num_labels=len(LABELS),
    problem_type="multi_label_classification"
)

class TicketDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, data, tokenizer, max_length=128):
        self.data = data
        self.tokenizer = tokenizer
        self.max_length = max_length

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.data)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        item = self.data[idx]
        encoding = self.tokenizer(
            item["text"], truncation=True, padding="max_length",
            max_length=self.max_length, return_tensors="pt"
        )
        return {
            "input_ids": encoding["input_ids"].squeeze(),
            "attention_mask": encoding["attention_mask"].squeeze(),
            "labels": torch.tensor(item["labels"], dtype=torch.float)
        }

dataset = TicketDataset(raw_data, tokenizer)

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    predictions = (torch.sigmoid(torch.tensor(logits)) > 0.5).int().numpy()
    return {
        "f1_micro": f1_score(labels, predictions, average="micro", zero_division=0),
        "exact_match": accuracy_score(labels, predictions)
    }

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./ticket-classifier",
    num_train_epochs=5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,
    learning_rate=3e-5,
    logging_steps=1,
    eval_strategy="no",
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=dataset,
)

trainer.train()

def classify_ticket(text, threshold=0.5):
    """Classify a new support ticket into one or more categories"""
    inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, padding=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**inputs)

    probabilities = torch.sigmoid(outputs.logits)[0]
    predicted_labels = [
        LABELS[i] for i, prob in enumerate(probabilities) if prob > threshold
    ]

    print(f"\nTicket: {text}")
    print(f"Predicted categories: {predicted_labels}")
    for label, prob in zip(LABELS, probabilities):
        print(f"  {label}: {prob:.3f}")

    return predicted_labels

# Test on new tickets
classify_ticket("The website keeps timing out and I need this fixed urgently")
classify_ticket("I'd love to see a mobile app version of this product")
What this project teaches:

Multi-label classification (a ticket can belong to multiple categories simultaneously) using problem_type="multi_label_classification", which applies a sigmoid instead of softmax over the output logits
Building a custom PyTorch Dataset class for HuggingFace's Trainer
Realistic production use case: automatic routing and prioritization of support tickets
Chapter Summary
BERT uses a bidirectional transformer encoder, pre-trained with Masked Language Modeling and Next Sentence Prediction, making it ideal for language understanding tasks
The pre-train then fine-tune paradigm allows a single model to be adapted to many downstream tasks with small labeled datasets, and underlies all modern NLP and LLM development
Sentence-BERT uses a siamese network structure to produce sentence embeddings where cosine similarity reflects semantic similarity, making large-scale semantic search computationally feasible
RoBERTa improves BERT through better training alone; DistilBERT compresses BERT through knowledge distillation for speed; ALBERT reduces parameters through weight sharing and factorized embeddings
GPT uses a decoder-only architecture with causal self-attention, naturally suited to autoregressive text generation
T5 unifies all NLP tasks into a text-to-text framework using a full encoder-decoder architecture
HuggingFace Transformers provides a consistent, production-ready API (pipeline, AutoTokenizer, AutoModel*) across all these architectures
Fine-tuning requires small learning rates (2e-5 to 5e-5), few epochs, and careful handling of the randomly-initialized task-specific head

Revision Notes
BERT = bidirectional encoder, MLM + NSP pre-training, [CLS] token for classification
Fine-tuning learning rates must be small (2e-5 to 5e-5) — large LR causes catastrophic forgetting
Sentence-BERT = siamese BERT fine-tuned for embedding similarity; never average raw BERT token embeddings for similarity tasks
RoBERTa = BERT + better training recipe (more data, no NSP, dynamic masking)
DistilBERT = knowledge distillation, fewer layers, genuinely faster inference
ALBERT = parameter sharing + factorized embeddings, smaller storage but not necessarily faster inference
GPT = decoder-only, causal masking, next-token prediction, naturally suited to generation
T5 = encoder-decoder, every task reframed as text-to-text with task prefixes
HuggingFace pipeline() for quick results; AutoTokenizer/AutoModel* for production control

Introduction

The previous chapters built the theoretical and architectural foundation of NLP — tokenization, embeddings, and transformers. This chapter is where that foundation becomes products. Every application in this chapter appears constantly in real AI/ML engineering roles: a fintech company needs sentiment analysis on customer reviews, a legal tech startup needs NER to extract entities from contracts, a healthcare company needs summarization of clinical notes, and a global e-commerce platform needs machine translation.

A recurring theme in this chapter is choice: for every task, you now have three tiers of solution available — a classical statistical approach, a fine-tuned transformer, and a prompted LLM (covered in depth in Part 11). Knowing when each tier is the right engineering decision is what separates a senior engineer from someone who only knows how to call an API.
Text Classification
Text classification assigns predefined categories to text — the most common and most economically valuable NLP task in industry.
The Three-Tier Decision Framework
Tier 1: Classical Baseline

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

texts = [
    "This product exceeded my expectations, highly recommend!",
    "Terrible quality, broke after one day of use.",
    "Average product, does what it says, nothing special.",
    "Absolutely love it, best purchase this year!",
    "Waste of money, would not buy again.",
]
labels = ["positive", "negative", "neutral", "positive", "negative"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    texts, labels, test_size=0.2, random_state=42
)

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), max_features=5000)),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])

pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = pipeline.predict(X_test)
print(classification_report(y_test, predictions, zero_division=0))

Why this still matters: a logistic regression baseline trains in seconds, runs inference in microseconds, and is fully interpretable (you can inspect exactly which words drive each prediction). Always build this baseline first — it tells you whether the problem needs a transformer at all, and gives you a number to beat.
Tier 2: Fine-tuned Transformer (Recap Reference)

The complete fine-tuning workflow for text classification was covered in Chapter 69. The same Trainer-based pipeline applies directly to any classification application in this chapter — sentiment, topic categorization, intent classification, and more.
Tier 3: LLM Zero-Shot Classification

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

def classify_with_llm(text, categories):
    prompt = f"""Classify the following text into exactly one of these categories: {', '.join(categories)}.
Respond with only the category name, nothing else.

Text: "{text}"
Category:"""

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content.strip()

categories = ["billing", "technical", "account", "feature_request"]
result = classify_with_llm("My card was charged twice for the same order", categories)
print(result)
Sentiment Analysis
Sentiment analysis is a specialization of text classification, but deserves its own treatment because of nuances that trip up production systems.
Beyond Positive/Negative
Real production sentiment systems typically need more granularity than a binary label:

from transformers import pipeline

# Fine-grained sentiment (1-5 stars) rather than binary positive/negative
sentiment_analyzer = pipeline(
    "sentiment-analysis",
    model="nlptown/bert-base-multilingual-uncased-sentiment"
)

reviews = [
    "It's okay, does the job but nothing impressive.",
    "Absolutely phenomenal, changed how I work every day.",
    "Broke within a week, very disappointed.",
]

for review in reviews:
    result = sentiment_analyzer(review)[0]
    print(f"{review}\n  → {result['label']} (confidence: {result['score']:.3f})\n")
Handling Negation and Sarcasm
Two well-known failure modes in sentiment analysis:

# Negation flips sentiment but shares almost all the same words
examples = [
    "This is a great product",              # positive
    "This is not a great product",           # negative — negation flips it
    "I wouldn't say this is a bad product",  # positive — double negation
]

# Sarcasm often uses positive words to express negative sentiment
sarcastic_examples = [
    "Oh great, my flight got cancelled again. Just wonderful.",   # negative, despite "great"/"wonderful"
]

# Classical bag-of-words models struggle badly with both patterns.
# Transformer models handle negation reasonably well (due to attention over full context)
# but sarcasm remains a genuinely hard, mostly unsolved problem requiring
# world knowledge and tone understanding — even large LLMs are not perfectly reliable here.
Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA)

Real reviews often express different sentiment toward different aspects of a product in the same sentence: "The camera is amazing but the battery life is terrible." Standard sentiment analysis would average these into a confusing neutral score. ABSA extracts sentiment per aspect.

def simple_aspect_sentiment(text, aspects, sentiment_pipeline):
    """
    A lightweight ABSA approach: for each aspect, extract the sentence
    fragment mentioning it and classify that fragment independently.
    """
    import re
    results = {}
    sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text)

    for aspect in aspects:
        relevant = [s for s in sentences if aspect.lower() in s.lower()]
        if relevant:
            combined = " ".join(relevant)
            sentiment = sentiment_pipeline(combined)[0]
            results[aspect] = sentiment
        else:
            results[aspect] = None

    return results

sentiment_analyzer = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
text = "The camera is absolutely amazing and takes stunning photos. However, the battery life is terrible and dies within a few hours."
aspects = ["camera", "battery"]

results = simple_aspect_sentiment(text, aspects, sentiment_analyzer)
for aspect, sentiment in results.items():
    print(f"{aspect}: {sentiment}")

Production ABSA systems typically use models fine-tuned specifically for joint aspect-extraction-and-sentiment (a sequence labeling task), rather than this simplified sentence-splitting heuristic — but the heuristic is a reasonable and fast starting point.
Named Entity Recognition

NER identifies and classifies named entities in text — people, organizations, locations, dates, monetary values — and is foundational for information extraction, search, and knowledge graph construction.
Using a Pre-trained NER Pipeline

from transformers import pipeline

ner = pipeline("ner", grouped_entities=True)

text = """Tim Cook, CEO of Apple, announced during a press conference in Cupertino 
that the company would invest $10 billion in AI infrastructure by 2027, 
partnering with Microsoft and OpenAI on the initiative."""

entities = ner(text)

for entity in entities:
    print(f"{entity['word']:20s} → {entity['entity_group']:6s} (confidence: {entity['score']:.3f})")
Typical output categories:
Custom NER for Domain-Specific Entities

Generic NER models recognize generic categories. Real applications often need domain-specific entities — a legal document processor needs to extract "CONTRACT_PARTY" and "EFFECTIVE_DATE"; a medical system needs "DRUG_NAME" and "DOSAGE". This requires fine-tuning a token classification model on labeled domain data.

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForTokenClassification
import torch

# Conceptual structure of a fine-tuned domain NER model
# (fine-tuning process follows the same Trainer pattern as Chapter 69,
#  but with per-token labels instead of per-sequence labels)

model_name = "path/to/fine-tuned-legal-ner-model"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(model_name)

text = "This Agreement is effective as of January 1, 2026, between Acme Corp and Beta Industries."

tokens = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**tokens)

predictions = torch.argmax(outputs.logits, dim=-1)
predicted_labels = [model.config.id2label[p.item()] for p in predictions[0]]

word_tokens = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(tokens["input_ids"][0])
for token, label in zip(word_tokens, predicted_labels):
    if label != "O":   # "O" means "Outside" any entity
        print(f"{token}: {label}")

BIO Tagging Scheme: Token classification models use the BIO scheme to mark entity boundaries: B-eginning of an entity, I-nside an entity (continuation), O-utside any entity. For example, "New York City" would be tagged B-LOC I-LOC I-LOC, allowing the model to distinguish adjacent entities of the same type.
Question Answering
Extractive Question Answering
Extractive QA finds the answer as a literal span of text within a given context passage — the model does not generate new words, it points to where the answer already exists.

from transformers import pipeline

qa_pipeline = pipeline("question-answering", model="deepset/roberta-base-squad2")

context = """
The Transformer architecture was introduced in the paper "Attention Is All You Need" 
in 2017 by researchers at Google. It relies entirely on attention mechanisms, 
eliminating the need for recurrence and convolutions. This architecture became 
the foundation for models like BERT, GPT, and T5.
"""

questions = [
    "When was the Transformer architecture introduced?",
    "What mechanism does the Transformer rely on?",
    "Who introduced the Transformer architecture?"
]

for question in questions:
    result = qa_pipeline(question=question, context=context)
    print(f"Q: {question}")
    print(f"A: {result['answer']} (confidence: {result['score']:.3f})\n")

Extractive QA models (typically fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa variants on datasets like SQuAD) output a start position and end position within the context, and the answer is simply the substring between them. This means extractive QA can never produce an answer that isn't literally present in the source text — a useful safety property for grounding, but a limitation when the answer requires synthesis across multiple parts of the context.
Abstractive Question Answering

Abstractive QA generates a natural language answer, potentially synthesizing information rather than only extracting a span. This is what modern LLM-based question answering (and RAG systems in Part 11) typically do.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

def abstractive_qa(question, context):
    prompt = f"""Answer the question based only on the context provided. 
If the answer is not in the context, say "I cannot find this information in the provided context."

Context: {context}

Question: {question}
Answer:"""

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        temperature=0
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

context = "The Transformer architecture, introduced in 2017, eliminated recurrence entirely in favor of attention mechanisms, enabling far greater parallelization during training compared to RNNs and LSTMs."

answer = abstractive_qa("Why was the Transformer faster to train than RNNs?", context)
print(answer)
Extractive vs Abstractive comparison:
Text Summarization
Extractive Summarization
Extractive summarization selects and stitches together the most important existing sentences from the source text, rather than generating new ones.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
import re

def extractive_summarize(text, num_sentences=3):
    """
    Simple extractive summarization using TF-IDF sentence scoring.
    Ranks sentences by their similarity to the overall document.
    """
    sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text.strip())

    if len(sentences) <= num_sentences:
        return text

    vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
    sentence_vectors = vectorizer.fit_transform(sentences)

    # Score each sentence by average similarity to all other sentences
    similarity_matrix = cosine_similarity(sentence_vectors)
    scores = similarity_matrix.sum(axis=1)

    ranked_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:num_sentences]
    ranked_indices = sorted(ranked_indices)   # preserve original order

    summary = " ".join([sentences[i] for i in ranked_indices])
    return summary

document = """
Artificial intelligence has transformed numerous industries in recent years. 
Healthcare providers now use AI for diagnostic imaging and drug discovery. 
Financial institutions leverage machine learning for fraud detection and algorithmic trading. 
The retail sector uses recommendation systems to personalize shopping experiences. 
However, these advances also raise concerns about job displacement and algorithmic bias. 
Researchers continue to work on making AI systems more transparent and fair. 
Governments worldwide are developing regulatory frameworks to govern AI deployment. 
The pace of AI innovation shows no signs of slowing down.
"""

summary = extractive_summarize(document, num_sentences=3)
print(summary)
Abstractive Summarization
Abstractive summarization generates new sentences that capture the meaning of the source, often more concise and readable than extractive summaries, at the cost of higher hallucination risk.

Summarization Evaluation: ROUGE

from rouge_score import rouge_scorer

reference_summary = "AI has transformed healthcare, finance, and retail, though it raises concerns about jobs and bias."
generated_summary = "AI has changed many industries including healthcare and finance, but raises job and fairness concerns."

scorer = rouge_scorer.RougeScorer(["rouge1", "rouge2", "rougeL"], use_stemmer=True)
scores = scorer.score(reference_summary, generated_summary)

for metric, score in scores.items():
    print(f"{metric}: Precision={score.precision:.3f}, Recall={score.recall:.3f}, F1={score.fmeasure:.3f}")

ROUGE-1 measures unigram (single word) overlap, ROUGE-2 measures bigram overlap, and ROUGE-L measures the longest common subsequence — capturing sentence-level structure similarity. Higher scores indicate closer overlap with a human-written reference summary, though ROUGE has well-known limitations: it rewards word overlap even when a paraphrased summary captures the meaning perfectly with completely different words.

from sacrebleu import corpus_bleu

BLEU measures n-gram precision between machine translation output and one or more human reference translations. Like ROUGE, it penalizes valid paraphrases that use different but equally correct wording, which is why human evaluation remains important for production translation quality assessment.
Information Extraction
Information extraction pulls structured data (relationships, facts, key-value pairs) out of unstructured text — the technique behind resume parsers, invoice processors, and contract analyzers.

import re
from transformers import pipeline

def extract_invoice_fields(text):
    """
    Combines regex (for highly structured patterns) with NER
    (for named entities) — a common real-world information extraction pattern.
    """
    patterns = {
        "invoice_number": r"Invoice\s*#?:?\s*(\w+-?\d+)",
        "amount": r"\$\s?([\d,]+\.\d{2})",
        "date": r"(\d{1,2}[/-]\d{1,2}[/-]\d{2,4})",
        "email": r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+"
    }

    extracted = {}
    for field, pattern in patterns.items():
        match = re.search(pattern, text)
        extracted[field] = match.group(1) if match else None

    ner = pipeline("ner", grouped_entities=True)
    entities = ner(text)
    extracted["organizations"] = [e["word"] for e in entities if e["entity_group"] == "ORG"]

    return extracted

invoice_text = """
Invoice #: INV-20264521
Date: 03/15/2026
Bill To: Acme Corporation
Amount Due: $4,250.00
Contact: billing@acmecorp.com
"""

result = extract_invoice_fields(invoice_text)
for field, value in result.items():
    print(f"{field}: {value}")

The professional pattern: regex handles highly structured, predictable formats (invoice numbers, dates, emails, currency amounts) reliably and with zero training cost. NER handles free-text entity extraction where format is not fixed. Modern systems increasingly use LLMs with structured output (function calling, covered in Part 11) for the hardest extraction cases where regex and NER both fall short — for example, extracting nested contractual obligations from legal prose.
Common Mistakes
Applying binary sentiment analysis where aspect-based analysis is needed. Averaging conflicting sentiments in one sentence produces a misleadingly neutral score that hides genuinely useful signal.

Using extractive summarization when synthesis is required, or abstractive summarization when hallucination is unacceptable. Choosing the wrong summarization tier for the risk profile of the application (e.g., using abstractive summarization for legal or medical documents) can introduce fabricated information into critical output.

Evaluating translation or summarization quality using only automated metrics. BLEU and ROUGE correlate imperfectly with human judgment, especially for creative paraphrasing; production systems should include periodic human evaluation, not rely on automated scores alone.

Ignoring domain shift in NER. A generic NER model trained on news text will perform poorly on legal, medical, or technical domain text where entity types and writing style differ substantially — domain-specific fine-tuning is often necessary.

Not handling the "no answer" case in extractive QA. Real-world questions are frequently not answerable from the given context; production systems must handle low-confidence scores explicitly rather than always returning the highest-scoring (but potentially wrong) span.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
What is the difference between extractive and abstractive summarization?

Extractive summarization selects and combines existing sentences directly from the source text without altering their wording. Abstractive summarization generates new sentences that capture the meaning of the source, potentially using entirely different words and synthesizing information across sentences, at higher risk of introducing inaccuracies.
What does the BIO tagging scheme represent in Named Entity Recognition?

BIO stands for Beginning, Inside, and Outside. Each token in a sequence is labeled B- at the start of an entity, I- for tokens continuing that same entity, and O for tokens outside any entity. This scheme allows models to correctly distinguish adjacent, separate entities of the same type.
Why is BLEU score not a perfect measure of translation quality?

BLEU measures n-gram overlap between a machine translation and reference translations. A translation can be entirely correct and fluent while using different word choices or sentence structure than the reference, resulting in a low BLEU score despite being a high-quality translation. This is why BLEU should be supplemented with human evaluation.
Intermediate Level
Explain the tradeoffs between the three-tier approach (classical, fine-tuned transformer, LLM prompting) for text classification.

Classical approaches (TF-IDF + logistic regression) train and run near-instantly, are fully interpretable, and need minimal labeled data, but their accuracy ceiling is lower and they struggle with nuanced language. Fine-tuned transformers achieve higher accuracy and handle context and nuance well but require hundreds to thousands of labeled examples and a training/deployment pipeline. LLM prompting requires no training data at all and adapts instantly to new categories, but has higher per-request latency and cost, and can be less consistent without careful prompt engineering. The right choice depends on data availability, latency/cost constraints, and how often categories change.
Why is extractive question answering generally preferred over abstractive question answering in compliance-sensitive applications?

Extractive QA outputs a literal span of text copied directly from the provided context, meaning the answer is guaranteed to exist verbatim in the source document — there is no mechanism by which the model can fabricate information. Abstractive QA generates new text and can synthesize or subtly alter facts, introducing hallucination risk. In domains like legal, medical, or financial compliance, where an incorrect fabricated answer carries real consequences, the traceability and grounding of extractive QA is often required even at the cost of reduced flexibility.
How would you build an aspect-based sentiment analysis system for a product with multiple distinct features being discussed in reviews?

A lightweight approach splits reviews into sentences or clauses, identifies which sentences mention which product aspects (using keyword matching or a fine-tuned aspect-extraction model), and runs sentiment classification independently on each aspect-relevant fragment. A more robust production approach fine-tunes a joint sequence-labeling model that simultaneously identifies aspect terms and their associated sentiment polarity in a single pass, trained on aspect-annotated review data (such as the SemEval ABSA datasets).
Advanced Level
Discuss the failure modes of ROUGE and BLEU as automated evaluation metrics, and describe an alternative evaluation approach that addresses these limitations.

ROUGE and BLEU are both based on surface-level n-gram overlap between generated text and reference text, meaning they penalize valid paraphrases and synonyms even when meaning is preserved, and can reward outputs that share words with the reference while missing its actual meaning. They also do not directly measure factual correctness, fluency, or hallucination. Alternative approaches include embedding-based metrics like BERTScore, which compares semantic similarity of contextual embeddings rather than exact word overlap; LLM-as-judge evaluation, where a strong model is prompted to score outputs against criteria like faithfulness and relevance (covered in depth in Part 11's Chapter 83); and human evaluation panels, which remain the gold standard despite being slower and more expensive to run at scale.

# feedback_analysis_pipeline.py
# End-to-end NLP application combining sentiment analysis, NER, 
# and information extraction on customer feedback data

from transformers import pipeline
import re
from collections import Counter

class FeedbackAnalyzer:
    def __init__(self):
        print("Loading models...")
        self.sentiment_pipeline = pipeline(
            "sentiment-analysis",
            model="nlptown/bert-base-multilingual-uncased-sentiment"
        )
        self.ner_pipeline = pipeline("ner", grouped_entities=True)
        print("Models loaded.\n")

    def analyze_sentiment(self, text):
        result = self.sentiment_pipeline(text[:512])[0]   # truncate to model limit
        star_rating = int(result["label"][0])
        return {
            "star_rating": star_rating,
            "sentiment": "positive" if star_rating >= 4 else "negative" if star_rating <= 2 else "neutral",
            "confidence": result["score"]
        }

    def extract_entities(self, text):
        entities = self.ner_pipeline(text)
        return {
            "organizations": [e["word"] for e in entities if e["entity_group"] == "ORG"],
            "people": [e["word"] for e in entities if e["entity_group"] == "PER"],
            "locations": [e["word"] for e in entities if e["entity_group"] == "LOC"]
        }

    def extract_mentioned_issues(self, text, issue_keywords):
        """Simple keyword-based issue detection — a lightweight information extraction step"""
        text_lower = text.lower()
        return [issue for issue in issue_keywords if issue in text_lower]

    def analyze_feedback_batch(self, feedback_list, issue_keywords):
        results = []
        for feedback in feedback_list:
            sentiment = self.analyze_sentiment(feedback)
            entities = self.extract_entities(feedback)
            issues = self.extract_mentioned_issues(feedback, issue_keywords)

            results.append({
                "text": feedback,
                "sentiment": sentiment,
                "entities": entities,
                "issues": issues
            })
        return results

    def generate_report(self, results):
        print("=" * 70)
        print("  CUSTOMER FEEDBACK ANALYSIS REPORT")
        print("=" * 70)

        total = len(results)
        sentiment_counts = Counter(r["sentiment"]["sentiment"] for r in results)
        all_issues = [issue for r in results for issue in r["issues"]]
        issue_counts = Counter(all_issues)

        print(f"\nTotal feedback analyzed: {total}")
        print(f"\nSentiment Breakdown:")
        for sentiment, count in sentiment_counts.items():
            pct = (count / total) * 100
            print(f"  {sentiment:10s}: {count:3d} ({pct:.1f}%)")

        if issue_counts:
            print(f"\nTop Reported Issues:")
            for issue, count in issue_counts.most_common(5):
                print(f"  {issue:20s}: {count} mentions")

        negative_feedback = [r for r in results if r["sentiment"]["sentiment"] == "negative"]
        if negative_feedback:
            print(f"\nSample Negative Feedback Requiring Attention:")
            for r in negative_feedback[:3]:
                print(f"  - \"{r['text'][:80]}...\"")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    analyzer = FeedbackAnalyzer()

    feedback_samples = [
        "The delivery from FastShip was late and the packaging from Acme Corp was damaged.",
        "Absolutely love this product, works perfectly every time!",
        "Customer service was unhelpful and the app keeps crashing on my phone.",
        "Decent product but the price is a bit high compared to competitors.",
        "The battery life is terrible and it stopped charging after two weeks.",
        "Fast shipping and great quality, will buy again from this store.",
    ]

    issue_keywords = ["delivery", "packaging", "battery", "crashing", "price", "customer service"]

    results = analyzer.analyze_feedback_batch(feedback_samples, issue_keywords)
    analyzer.generate_report(results)

# summarization_api.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
from transformers import pipeline
import re

app = FastAPI(title="Document Summarization API")
summarizer = pipeline("summarization", model="facebook/bart-large-cnn")

class SummarizeRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str
    max_length: int = 130
    min_length: int = 30

def chunk_text(text: str, max_words: int = 800) -> list[str]:
    """Splits long text into chunks at sentence boundaries, respecting model context limits"""
    sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text)
    chunks, current_chunk, word_count = [], [], 0

    for sentence in sentences:
        words_in_sentence = len(sentence.split())
        if word_count + words_in_sentence > max_words and current_chunk:
            chunks.append(" ".join(current_chunk))
            current_chunk, word_count = [], 0
        current_chunk.append(sentence)
        word_count += words_in_sentence

    if current_chunk:
        chunks.append(" ".join(current_chunk))

    return chunks

@app.post("/summarize")
async def summarize_document(request: SummarizeRequest):
    chunks = chunk_text(request.text)

    chunk_summaries = []
    for chunk in chunks:
        result = summarizer(chunk, max_length=request.max_length,
                            min_length=request.min_length, do_sample=False)
        chunk_summaries.append(result[0]["summary_text"])

    combined_summary = " ".join(chunk_summaries)

    # If multiple chunks were summarized, run a second pass to condense further
    if len(chunk_summaries) > 1:
        final_result = summarizer(combined_summary, max_length=request.max_length,
                                  min_length=request.min_length, do_sample=False)
        final_summary = final_result[0]["summary_text"]
    else:
        final_summary = combined_summary

    return {
        "original_word_count": len(request.text.split()),
        "summary_word_count": len(final_summary.split()),
        "compression_ratio": round(len(final_summary.split()) / len(request.text.split()), 3),
        "summary": final_summary
    }

# resume_parser.py
import re
import spacy
from rapidfuzz import fuzz

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")

SKILLS_TAXONOMY = [
    "Python", "Java", "JavaScript", "SQL", "React", "PyTorch", "TensorFlow",
    "Machine Learning", "Deep Learning", "AWS", "Docker", "Kubernetes",
    "Git", "FastAPI", "Django", "NLP", "Computer Vision", "LangChain"
]

def extract_contact_info(text: str) -> dict:
    email_match = re.search(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+", text)
    phone_match = re.search(r"(\+?\d{1,3}[-.\s]?)?\(?\d{3}\)?[-.\s]?\d{3}[-.\s]?\d{4}", text)
    linkedin_match = re.search(r"linkedin\.com/in/[\w-]+", text)

    return {
        "email": email_match.group(0) if email_match else None,
        "phone": phone_match.group(0) if phone_match else None,
        "linkedin": linkedin_match.group(0) if linkedin_match else None
    }

def extract_name(text: str) -> str:
    """Assumes the candidate's name appears in the first few lines as a PERSON entity"""
    first_section = "\n".join(text.strip().split("\n")[:5])
    doc = nlp(first_section)
    for ent in doc.ents:
        if ent.label_ == "PERSON":
            return ent.text
    return None

def extract_skills(text: str, threshold: int = 85) -> list[str]:
    """Fuzzy matches resume text against a known skills taxonomy"""
    text_lower = text.lower()
    found_skills = []

    for skill in SKILLS_TAXONOMY:
        if skill.lower() in text_lower:
            found_skills.append(skill)
        else:
            # Fuzzy match catches variations like "Pytorch" vs "PyTorch"
            words = text.split()
            for word in words:
                if fuzz.ratio(word.lower(), skill.lower()) > threshold:
                    found_skills.append(skill)
                    break

    return sorted(set(found_skills))

def extract_experience_years(text: str) -> int:
    """Extracts stated years of experience if explicitly mentioned"""
    match = re.search(r"(\d+)\+?\s*years?\s*(of)?\s*experience", text, re.IGNORECASE)
    return int(match.group(1)) if match else None

def parse_resume(text: str) -> dict:
    return {
        "name": extract_name(text),
        "contact": extract_contact_info(text),
        "skills": extract_skills(text),
        "years_experience": extract_experience_years(text)
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample_resume = """
    Priya Sharma
    priya.sharma@email.com | +1-555-234-5678 | linkedin.com/in/priyasharma

    SUMMARY
    Machine Learning Engineer with 4 years of experience building production ML systems.

    SKILLS
    Python, PyTorch, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, AWS, Docker, FastAPI, SQL

    EXPERIENCE
    ML Engineer, TechCorp (2022-Present)
    """

    result = parse_resume(sample_resume)
    print(result)

Common Mistakes Across NLP Projects
Skipping input validation on uploaded documents. Production NLP services must gracefully handle empty files, corrupted PDFs, non-English text, or malformed input rather than crashing.

Loading models on every request instead of caching them. Model loading is expensive; always cache loaded models (@st.cache_resource in Streamlit, module-level globals in FastAPI, or a proper model server) so they load once per process, not once per request.
Hardcoding similarity thresholds without validation. The FAQ chatbot's SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD should be tuned against real user queries and a labeled "should escalate" dataset, not chosen arbitrarily.

Ignoring multi-page or multi-column PDF extraction issues. Real-world resumes and reports often have complex layouts that naive PDF text extraction garbles — always spot-check extracted text against the source document.

Building projects with no README or setup instructions. A project a recruiter cannot run in under 5 minutes effectively does not exist as a portfolio piece — always include clear installation and usage instructions.
Interview Questions
Beginner Level
Why is caching model loading important in a production NLP API?

Loading a transformer model involves reading potentially hundreds of megabytes to gigabytes of weights from disk and initializing them into memory, which can take several seconds. If this happens on every incoming request, latency becomes unacceptable and server resources are wasted. Caching ensures the model loads once when the service starts and is reused across all subsequent requests.
In the FAQ chatbot project, why use Sentence-BERT embeddings instead of simple keyword matching?

Keyword matching fails when users phrase questions differently than the FAQ text (for example, "I forgot my password" vs. "How do I reset my password?") despite having the same intent. Sentence-BERT embeddings capture semantic meaning, so questions with similar meaning but different wording still produce similar embeddings and match correctly via cosine similarity.
Intermediate Level
How would you handle a resume parser encountering resumes in languages other than English?

The parser would need language detection (using a library like langdetect or fasttext) as a first step, then route non-English resumes to language-appropriate NER models (spaCy provides multilingual models) or a multilingual transformer, since an English-only NER model will perform poorly or fail to recognize entities in other languages. Skills matching would also need a multilingual or translated taxonomy.
In the summarization API, why is recursive summarization (summary-of-summaries) necessary, and what are its risks?

Transformer models have a maximum context window, so very long documents must be split into chunks that fit within this limit, each chunk summarized independently, and then those chunk summaries combined and summarized again to produce a single coherent final summary. The risk is information loss and compounding inaccuracy: each summarization pass can drop details or subtly distort meaning, and running this recursively across multiple passes can accumulate these errors, potentially losing important information that appeared in only one chunk.
Advanced Level
How would you scale the FAQ chatbot's retrieval system from 5 FAQs to 50,000 FAQs, and what would change architecturally?

At small scale, computing cosine similarity against all FAQ embeddings in memory (as done in this project) is fast enough. At 50,000+ FAQs, this brute-force approach becomes a bottleneck, so the architecture would shift to an approximate nearest neighbor index (FAISS, or a managed vector database like Pinecone or Qdrant, covered in Part 11 Chapter 75) using algorithms like HNSW to achieve sub-linear search time. Additionally, at this scale you would likely introduce a reranking stage, where the top-k candidates from fast vector search are re-scored with a more expensive but more accurate cross-encoder model before returning the final answer, and periodically re-embed the FAQ base if the underlying embedding model is updated.
